hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Late to the Office
text: My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. It's a useful buffer. So when a firm announced everyone must be back on Tuesdays, my first thought was not about collaboration but about the four minutes I'd lose to a commute. Tuesdays, apparently, are now sacred. I tested the idea at the allotment: I made all the tomatoes report to the same bed every Tuesday. They sulked, then ripened anyway, indifferent to my scheduling. Piotr would call this a productivity lesson and send me a graph. I'd reply with a photo of a stubborn tomato. The watch agrees with me, quietly: the meeting began four minutes ago, and the world has not ended.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Late to the Office
text: The firm announced everyone must be in on Tuesdays. Not Monday, which at least has an excuse, but Tuesday, the greyest day, the day that has to be talked into being a day at all. I read the memo on the bus and checked my grandfather's pocket watch out of habit. Four minutes slow, as ever. For once we agreed: neither of us was ready. I understand the argument. Corridors produce accidents, and accidents produce ideas. But my best work accident last year happened at the allotment, between two tomato plants, when I stopped trying to solve a scheduling problem and it solved itself. Nobody has yet explained why that couldn't have happened in a corridor. Though, to be fair, the corridor has never needed watering. Piotr says Tuesday presence boosts output by some percentage he found. I've added "find out what Tuesday actually costs" to my list of small experiments.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Slow
text: The firm that wants everyone back on Tuesdays says it's about collaboration. I read the memo twice and found no mention of the two hours I used to spend on the 07:12, which is now my best thinking time. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it, because it turns out four minutes is exactly how long a tomato seedling needs before the kettle boils. Small experiment: I've started treating the office day as a scheduled interruption rather than the default. I get more done by Thursday. Piotr says presence builds trust, which is a lovely theory, and I'd like to see it hold up against a Tuesday where the meeting room is double-booked and someone has eaten the good biscuits. The watch stays slow. The tomatoes don't seem to mind.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Late to the Argument
text: My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. It's a useful reminder that punctuality is a story we tell about clocks. This week a firm announced everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays, as if presence were a vitamin you could dose weekly. I keep a list of experiments: I tried working from the allotment for a fortnight. The tomatoes liked the attention; my editor less so. Piotr, who writes about productivity, would have made a chart. I made a sandwich. What I noticed was that the commute wasn't the cost. The cost was deciding, every morning, whether the day had already been lost. By my watch, it was four minutes early. By the office clock, I was late. I still haven't worked out which one was right.

trace.gist: Punctuality is a story we tell about clocks, not a real measure of presence.
trace.angle: Grandfather's slow watch versus office attendance mandates.
trace.open: Which clock was right remains unresolved.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Late to the Office
text: The firm wants everyone in on Tuesdays. Not a suggestion, a policy, which is how you can tell it began as a spreadsheet. I read the email on the bus. My grandfather's watch said 8:56, the bus said 9:00, and the bus has never once lied to me. I wore the watch anyway. At the office the lift took four minutes, which felt like the point being made on behalf of the watch. Tuesdays will now mean a desk I don't need, a commute I'd stopped paying for, and a lunch queue that has also come back to the office. Piotr says the policy is about culture. I say it's about the rent, and the rent doesn't read the culture. I've added it to the list: tested, no result yet, four minutes late.

trace.gist: Mandatory Tuesday office attendance is really about rent, not culture.
trace.angle: Grandfather's watch versus bus clock, four-minute lift.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes Is Optimistic
text: The study says every six minutes. I clocked myself on Tuesday and got four, though I counted the times I merely looked at my phone without opening anything, which feels like counting a glance at the fridge as a meal. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow; I wear it anyway, and it has become my one reliable unit of delay. At the allotment I answer nothing, which is the only place I am genuinely unreachable, and the tomatoes have not once complained. Piotr would call this poor systems design and prescribe a timer. I tried his timer for a week. I spent most of it checking whether the timer had finished.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes Is a Rounding Error
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, and I distrust the number. Six minutes is what you get when you average a person who checks every forty seconds with a person who checks twice a day and rounds them into a headline. My grandfather's watch loses four minutes a day, which is slower than the study's workers and, I'd argue, more honest about it. I tried a small experiment last month: phone in the kitchen drawer, watch on the wrist. By mid-morning I'd checked the drawer eleven times and the watch nine, mostly to see whether it was still wrong. It was. So was I, in a different way. Piotr has a system of three inbox windows a day and a percentage to prove it works. I have a drawer and a slow watch. Neither of us has missed anything urgent yet.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Every Six Minutes, Apparently
text: A study says we check messages every six minutes at work. I tested it on myself for a morning, tallying each glance in the margin of my notebook, and got to eleven before ten o'clock, which suggests the researchers were being generous. The tally itself became the problem: I was checking the time in order to record that I had checked my messages, which is a small ouroboros I do not recommend. Piotr has a system of three inbox windows and calls it triage. I call it a greenhouse with the door propped open. Small experiment: phone face-down in a drawer until the kettle boils. Four minutes. Roughly.

title: Six Minutes Is Not a Unit of Anything
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so by its reckoning I check every six minutes and four seconds, which I find more honest. Mine is still on the windowsill, four minutes behind and entirely unbothered.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes Is a Very Long Time
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, though I'd like to know who they timed — presumably not the man at my bus stop who checks his phone, then his watch, then his phone again, as if the two might disagree. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I already live slightly behind everyone. Six minutes would put me properly in yesterday. I tried a small experiment last week: messages only on the hour. I lasted until 10:07. What undid me wasn't anything urgent — it was a group chat about a missing allotment gate, which I checked eleven times and which resolved itself without me. Piotr would call that a system failure. I'd call it a gate. Tomorrow I'm trying the tomatoes instead.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Four-Minute Rule
text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting on her calendar and waited to see which ones came back. Two did. The rest had been held, she said, mostly out of politeness. I read this on my phone at the allotment, between tying up tomatoes and failing to tie up tomatoes. My grandfather's watch said ten past four; the real time was fourteen past, as usual. Still, the experiment appealed. So I cancelled the small standing things in my week — the check-in, the catch-up, the call that existed because it had existed. Nobody complained. One came back. Piotr, of course, wrote a column about how he'd streamlined eleven meetings into a single dashboard. I have one meeting now, and it is with a man about a shed. I'm counting that as a win, four minutes slow.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Meeting That Didn't Come Back
text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting in her department and waited to see which ones returned. Two did. One was the Friday thing nobody could name the purpose of, which suggests the purpose was the Friday thing. The other was a Tuesday meeting, which surprised her until she noticed it was the only hour four people had to sit in a room and complain productively. I tried a version of this at the allotment, which is not a sentence I expected to write. I stopped watering one bed for a fortnight to see if it asked. It did not ask. It sulked, then died, which is the tomato equivalent of a silent calendar. Piotr would have made a graph. I have a dead bed and a slow watch. Four minutes slow, still.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Ones That Came Back
text: A manager cancelled every recurring meeting for a fortnight to see which would return. Most didn't. Two did, and one of those was the Friday check-in that nobody could explain, which tells you something about inertia and something less flattering about the rest of us. I ran the same test on my own week, minus the authority: I struck out every standing slot and waited. My diary stayed empty until Thursday, when I noticed I'd started writing notes to myself in the second person. The allotment has a similar rule. I stopped watering the tomatoes on a schedule and they sulked for a week, then got on with it. Piotr says a calendar with gaps is just a calendar you haven't filled yet. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has never once asked me to attend anything.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Meetings That Came Back
text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting on his calendar for a month and waited to see which ones returned. Eleven went quietly. Two came back on their own, scheduled by other people, which I think is the closest thing to an honest audit a calendar can produce. This is the same problem as my six minutes, only larger. Nobody could tell me who was counting the six, and nobody could tell him who needed the eleven. They had simply accumulated, the way the shed key accumulates. I tried something similar on the allotment, thinning the tomatoes to see which survived. Most did. The ones I'd fussed over did worst. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, never missed a meeting in forty years. It just arrived believing a different time.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Meeting That Didn't Come Back
text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting on his calendar for a month and waited to see which ones returned. Four did. The rest, some of them years old, simply evaporated, and nobody noticed for weeks. I admire the nerve. My own experiment along these lines was smaller and worse. I decided to skip my Thursday check-in and see if anyone asked. Nobody did. Then I spent the hour feeling strangely orphaned, like a man standing in a field where a shed used to be. Piotr would call this a productivity win and put it in a spreadsheet. I put it on my list of small experiments, third entry, between "check messages every six minutes" and the tomatoes, which I still haven't got to. My grandfather's watch says I'm four minutes late for nothing in particular.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: The Timer Says Go
text: A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. Forty minutes on, five off, and she swears the ticking keeps her honest. I tried it Tuesday. My timer is the one shaped like a tomato, from the allotment drawer, and it does not tick, it rattles, like a small polite complaint. Forty minutes turned out to be exactly long enough to write two paragraphs and reorganise my pens by ink colour. At minute thirty-one I noticed my grandfather's watch was four minutes slow, as always, and spent the remaining nine wondering whether I should correct it or whether the watch had simply decided on its own routine. I got one paragraph. But the tomato did its job, which was to make me sit down, and Piotr can keep his ninety-minute deep work.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: Forty Minutes and a Timer That Isn't My Watch
text: A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. When it rings she stops mid-sentence, which she claims is the point: you always know where to start again. I tried it on Tuesday, the day that still has to be talked into being a day. Forty minutes is longer than it sounds when the timer is visibly counting down and shorter than it sounds when the sentence is finally going. I got through three blocks and one small lie to myself about the fourth. The kitchen timer is honest in a way my grandfather's watch isn't — it doesn't drift, it doesn't apologise, it just shouts. Four minutes slow, the watch has never once told me to stop. Maybe that's why I keep wearing it. Piotr blocks in ninety and calls forty a rounding error. I've added "forty or ninety" to the list.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: The Timer Says Stop, So I Do
text: A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. She sets it, writes, and when it rings she stops mid-sentence, even mid-word, and walks away. I tried this on Tuesday. My timer is the one from the allotment drawer, dusted with compost. At minute thirty-nine I was finally interested in what I was writing, which is the exact moment the bell went. I stopped anyway. The half-sentence sat there like a tomato seedling left out overnight. The odd thing: the next morning I finished it in four minutes flat. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says I should trust the method. Piotr says his blocks are ninety minutes. Of course they are. I'm logging this as experiment nineteen and keeping the timer.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: The Timer Says Go
text: A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I tried it Monday. My timer is the one shaped like a tomato, bought for the allotment and never used there, because tomatoes do not respond to deadlines. Forty minutes turns out to be a long time. At minute twelve I remembered the pocket watch, four minutes slow, and spent a while deciding whether that made me punctual or merely hopeful. At minute thirty-one I was writing well and the timer rang, which felt like being interrupted by a very small referee. I let it ring. That is the whole experiment: I broke the rule on day one, and the writing survived. Tomorrow I try fifty minutes, or I wind the watch forward, or I simply admit that Piotr would have finished the block and started another.

title: The Timer Says Stop, So I Stop
text: A writer I follow does forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I tried it Tuesday. The tomato seedlings needed pricking out, so I set the timer for forty minutes and got eleven seedlings done before it rang, which felt like a small triumph until I counted the tray and found forty more waiting. The trouble is the timer doesn't know when you're mid-sentence, or mid-root. Mine is the one from the kitchen drawer with a chipped dial, and it announces the end of the block like a smoke alarm having a bad day. I stopped, because that was the rule. Then I stood there with a seedling in my hand, feeling faintly ridiculous and oddly free. Piotr would have made a spreadsheet. I have made a note: forty minutes is enough for eleven tomatoes and not one thought more.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Four-Minute Margin
text: The survey says most people can't guess last month's spending. I tested myself before reading further and was off by £61, which felt like a win until I remembered the pocket watch. It runs four minutes slow, so I'm perpetually early to things I've already missed. Money seems to keep the same time as that watch. My tomatoes don't care about any of this; I gave them a pound of spent coffee grounds and they repaid me with two fruit, a rate of exchange even Piotr couldn't spin into a productivity win. The experiment I'm actually running this week: I write down every purchase within four minutes, matching the watch's error, on the theory that a small deliberate lag beats a confident guess. Day five and I've caught three coffees and one suspicious parsnip. The parsnip I'm disputing.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Tenner I Can't Account For
text: The survey says most people can't guess what they spent last month. I tried. I got within forty pounds, which I decided was close enough until I found the discrepancy was one unexplained tenner. I spent a week hunting it. It was a jar of something at a market, or it was a parking machine, or it was the tenner I gave my nephew and forgot, which is the most likely and the least satisfying. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and I trust it more than my own bank statement. It only lies in one direction. I've added "guess the tenner" to the list of experiments. Piotr tracks every penny in an app and calls my forty pounds a rounding error. He's right, and it still bothers me.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Receipts I Didn't Keep
text: The survey says most people can't guess last month's spending. I assumed I could, then tried. I wrote down a number. Then I actually checked, and I was off by enough to buy a new pair of boots, or a very ordinary month of bus fares. The gap wasn't a mystery: it was a hundred small taps, a coffee here, a card waved at a market stall there. I've started a running list of small experiments on myself, and this is number twenty: for one week, I write down every purchase in the back of my notebook. Not to budget, just to see. The allotment taught me the same lesson with seeds. I never remembered what I'd sown until I wrote it on a stick. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has never once needed a receipt. Piotr says he tracks everything in an app. Naturally.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Four Minutes I Get for Free

TITLE: The Timer Says Stop, So I Do

My timer is the one from the allotment drawer, dusted with compost. At minute thirty-nine I was finally interested in what I was writing, which is the exact moment the bell went. I stopped anyway. The half-sentence sat there like a tomato seedling left out overnight. The odd thing: the next morning I finished it in four minutes flat. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says I should trust the method. Piotr says his blocks are ninety minutes. Of course they are. I'm logging this as experiment nineteen and keeping the timer.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Alarm Doesn't Care What You Do Next
The study says the waking hour matters more than whatever ritual follows it. I believe this, having spent a fortnight once assembling a morning routine of stretching, a glass of water with lemon, and three pages of longhand. I kept it up for nine days. What I actually kept was the 6:40 alarm, which I still honour, and the longhand, which I abandoned at page two of day four. This morning I woke at 6:40, did nothing ceremonial whatsoever, and wrote this by 7:15. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, does not distinguish between a productive dawn and a dawdling one; it simply disagrees with all of them equally. The tomatoes get watered when I remember, which turns out to be Tuesday and Saturday, and that is apparently enough for a tomato. Piotr has a five-step morning protocol. I have an alarm and a kettle. Logging this as experiment twenty.

hook: A runner explains why she quit tracking her steps.
title: The Uncounted Mile
text: A runner told me she quit tracking her steps because the number had started running her. She'd loop the block at eleven at night to hit ten thousand. I recognised her, slightly. I once kept a tally of every cup of tea for a fortnight, purely to see. Forty-one. I learned nothing except that I make tea when I'm stuck, which I already knew, and that counting something makes it feel like a task with a pass mark. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it. It isn't a system. It's just a thing that's slightly wrong, and I've made peace with it, the way you do with a knee. Piotr would call this surrender. I'd call it leaving the tomatoes alone for a week to see what they do without me.

title: The Step Counter Died of Natural Causes
text: A runner I know quit tracking her steps. Not because she hit ten thousand and saw the void, but because the app reset one morning and she felt nothing. That's the interesting part: the numbers had quietly stopped meaning anything, and she only noticed when they vanished. I recognized it. It only gets to be a verdict. I've kept a list of small experiments on myself, and the ones that survive are the ones that ask nothing back. I still wake at the same time; I still stop when the timer says stop. Piotr would call this quitting, which is fair, and also he's wrong.

hook: A city council reports that empty offices cost it more than expected.
title: The Empty Desk Next Door
text: The council says empty offices are costing it more than budgeted, which is a strange sentence if you sit with it. A building that nobody uses is expensive, but so is a building everybody drives an hour to sit in and whisper on video calls. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped fixing it; it's a useful reminder that being slightly off schedule rarely ruins anything. My allotment taught me the same. I left one tomato bed unwatered for a week to see what would happen. Two plants sulked, three didn't care. Piotr would have made a spreadsheet. I made a note: most things tolerate neglect better than we fear. The offices will survive, or they won't. Either way, someone should check on them weekly.

hook: A city council reports that empty offices cost it more than expected.
title: The Cost of Empty Desks
text: The council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I believe them, and I'd like to see the receipt. At my old office the floor went half-quiet on Fridays, and the lights, the heating and the coffee machine all carried on at full attendance. Nobody budgeted for the building's loneliness. Piotr, naturally, has a hybrid schedule he calls optimal and a spreadsheet that proves it. I have a list of experiments, and one of them was working from home on Tuesdays for a month. The work got done; the difference was that I stopped noticing the commute and started noticing the kettle. The council's real problem isn't the empty desks. It's the fixed costs that don't notice nobody's in. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once asked where I'm working from.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: Rounding Up, Quietly
My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and puts the difference in a savings pot. They call it a nudge. I call it a price rise with good manners. So I checked: a year of this, at my actual spending, comes to less than a takeaway and a half. The coffee I bought on Monday rounded up by forty pence, which is the most expensive forty pence I've ever been pleased about. There's a lesson here I keep relearning — the number that sounds like money is rarely the number that is money. Piotr has automated his rounding, his saving and his smugness, and graphs all three. I'd rather know what I'd stop buying instead. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once rounded anything up.

[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: Quiet Hours, Loudly
A chat tool I use has introduced quiet hours: between ten at night and seven in the morning, notifications are muted. My first thought was that I don't get messages at night. My second was that this is why the feature exists — because someone does, and someone answers. So I counted, the way I counted my working week. In the last fortnight I received three late messages. Two were Piotr, graphing his own response times. The third was my own alarm, which my grandfather's watch is four minutes slow against, so it isn't the watch waking me. What quiet hours really change is who gets to decide when I'm interrupted: me, now, once, instead of them, repeatedly, always. I'd rather know which messages I'd stop sending. The watch stays loud, and it's four minutes late.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Step Counter Steps Down
A runner I follow has stopped tracking her steps. She didn't lose the watch or take up cycling; she just found the number had started walking her. I recognised her, because I keep a list of small experiments run on myself, and half of them ended the same way. Counting is cheap. It's the keeping-on-counting that costs. At the allotment I once weighed every tomato for a month, then stopped and simply ate them. Piotr would call that a lack of data. I'd call it lunch. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never counted a single step.

title: The Cost of an Empty Desk
text: The city council says empty offices cost it more than expected. I believe them, having once paid £4.60 for a sad sandwich in a business park where the only other sound was a printer nobody owned. My small experiment, number thirty-one: I worked a full office day and logged every interruption. Fourteen. The allotment equivalent is fourteen people walking through the greenhouse to ask if I've seen the secateurs. I hadn't; they were in the greenhouse. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, was the only thing in the building that kept its own counsel. Piotr says hybrid is a transition, not a destination. He said that on a video call, from a train, which is at least honest about the destination.

[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Four Minutes Slow
The firm that wants everyone back on Tuesdays says it's about collaboration. I read the memo twice and found no mention of the two hours I used to spend on the 07:12, which is now my best thinking time. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it, because it turns out four minutes is exactly how long a tomato seedling needs before the kettle boils. Small experiment: I've started treating the office day as a scheduled interruption rather than the default. I get more done by Thursday. Piotr says presence builds trust, which is a lovely theory, and I'd like to see it hold up against a Tuesday where the meeting room is double-booked and someone has eaten the good biscuits. The watch stays slow. The tomatoes don't seem to mind.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: Eleven Hours, Minus Lunch
The survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings. I did the arithmetic against my own diary and found I was average, which stung more than the meetings. So: small experiment number twenty-something. I declined nothing, cancelled nothing — I just wrote, in the margin, what each meeting was for. Nine of them had no answer I could put in a margin. One had an answer and it was "because it's Tuesday." The allotment equivalent is standing over the tomatoes with a watering can, discussing hydration. I did that once. The tomatoes produced nothing and neither did we. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has never been in a meeting, though it has been late to several. Piotr blocks his calendar in ninety-minute units and calls it deep work. I call it a very tidy empty room.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: Friday, Minus One
A company announced a four-day week trial, and the comment section immediately divided into people who think it's the future and people who think it's a plot. I keep thinking about the word "trial." At the allotment I trial things constantly — a new tomato variety gets one bed, not the whole plot, and if it sulks I don't blame the soil. The office version is less forgiving. My small experiment, since I'm apparently at twenty-seven: I took my slow watch off for a week and worked to the real clock instead. I finished nothing earlier and was late to everything. Four minutes, it turns out, was doing structural work. Piotr has already declared the four-day week a productivity multiplier, which is a lot of certainty for a Friday. I have written to him asking whether the fifth day is where the meetings go.

hook: A city council reports that empty offices cost it more than expected.
title: The Council Counts Chairs
text: The city council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I read the report on the bus and thought about the allotment shed, which sits empty most weekdays and has never once appeared on a balance sheet. Piotr would say that's because sheds don't have business rates. He is right, and it annoys me. The report counts desks, rates, and heating. It cannot count the hour I spent last Tuesday on a video call watching a colleague's cat walk across her keyboard, which was the most human moment of my week. Nor the four minutes my grandfather's watch loses daily, in which nothing billable happens and most of my thinking does. I'm not defending empty buildings. I'm saying the ledger only sees what sits still. My tomatoes don't fill a spreadsheet either, and they're the best argument I have.

title: The Tuesday Class
text: The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along out of curiosity rather than ambition. Six people, one patient tutor, and a whiteboard explaining that a variable is a box with a name. My neighbour Doris, seventy-eight, spent forty minutes making a line of text appear on screen and then punched the air like she'd won the pools. I made a box called tomato and put the number four in it, which felt like progress of a sort. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow all evening, as usual, and I found I didn't mind. The tutor said most people quit in week three. I've added it to my list of experiments: attend four sessions, then judge. Piotr would have a spreadsheet for this. I have a box called tomato.

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Retirees Type Back
text: The library runs free coding evenings for retirees. I went to watch, expecting a room of people being taught, and found one being worked. hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Retirees Are Ahead of Me
text: The library's free coding evenings for retirees have a waiting list. I went to observe, expecting confusion, and found a woman of seventy-four debugging a loop while explaining, patiently, that she had run a bakery for forty years and this was easier than staff rotas. Experiment twenty-three: I signed up for the overflow session. I lasted one evening. My code worked, then stopped working, and I never found out why, which is the exact feeling my drawer is full of. The failure log gains a line: "made the computer say hello; could not make it say anything else." Piotr says beginners should ship something small. I shipped a greeting and a bug. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through the whole session, so I was late to a class I had already left. The tomatoes remain the only thing I have ever successfully taught to do anything.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Lessons That Didn't Take
A teacher has published her failed lesson plans, which I find braver than any success story. My own failures live in a drawer: a seed catalogue with everything crossed out except tomatoes, and a notebook page headed "How to fix the watch" with one line, "don't." Experiment twenty-one, then: I'm keeping a failure log for a week. Not lessons learned, just what didn't work, plainly. Yesterday's entry: tried to learn the names of the three men who nod at me at the allotment gate. Got two. The third is now "the one with the shed." Piotr claims he has never had a failed system, only "iterations." I'd like to see his drawer. Four minutes slow, my grandfather's watch still tells the truth about the time I've wasted, which is its own kind of accuracy.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: Fifteen Minutes, Four of Them Late
The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I have a drawer of evidence either way. Experiment twenty-two: fifteen minutes of Polish before breakfast, every day for a fortnight, on the theory that I would finally ask my neighbour what her name is instead of nodding at her radishes. I lasted eleven mornings. What I learned: numbers to ten, the word for potato, and that my accent makes the word for potato sound like a threat. The failure log from day six has a new line — "eleven out of fourteen, which is a passing grade in nothing." My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through all of it, so technically I studied fifteen minutes and four seconds. Piotr does his language sessions in the car, which he says is "dead time reclaimed." Mine was alive time, wasted cheerfully. The tomatoes are unbothered, as usual.

text: The library's free coding evenings for retirees filled up before I got round to enquiring, which I take as a small verdict on my timing. So I taught myself instead, badly, at the kitchen table, following a tutorial until a semicolon broke everything. It took me forty minutes to find the semicolon. My grandfather's watch was no help. It runs four minutes slow, which is fine for catching trains and useless for debugging, though I did notice that I checked it every time the screen went red, as if lateness might be the fault. What struck me is that the retirees get a room, a person, and other beginners to be wrong in front of. I got a cursor. I have added "learn something in company" to my list of experiments, below "grow tomatoes" and above "stop refreshing the page." Piotr would call this networking. I call it a semicolon with witnesses.

title: The Standing Committee
text: I tried standing meetings for a fortnight, on the strength of a study saying they run shorter but decide less. My grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, sat on the table as referee. Shorter, yes: the Tuesday budget chat went from forty minutes to nineteen. Decided less, also yes. We left without agreeing the printer budget, having spent the time admiring our own calves. My allotment teaches the same lesson. Stake a tomato early and it grows upright and fruitless; let it sprawl and it crops. Piotr would call this a failure of posture. I call it a trade: speed bought with a small debt of decisions, payable later, with interest, in a follow-up meeting nobody wants. Next week I'm trialling sitting down and staying until it's settled. Watch says we've got time.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: The Meeting That Stood Still
text: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I believe it. At my old office we tried it for a fortnight: no chairs, a strict quarter of an hour, and a whiteboard. The meetings did end on time, mostly because everyone's knees did the chairing. But nothing got settled. Decisions, it turns out, need a certain slack — the unscripted ten minutes where somebody says the awkward thing and the room works out what to do with it. Standing up, we just deferred everything to the next meeting, which was shorter too. Piotr loves this sort of finding; he has probably already bought a standing desk and a stopwatch. My list of experiments has a new line: I tried efficiency for two weeks. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once ended early.

hook: A gym reports that most January sign-ups stop by March.
title: The Four-Minute Membership
text: The gym near the station says most January joiners quit by March. I lasted eleven days once. I know this because I marked each visit on the back of an old till receipt, and the eleventh is where the pen ran out. The plan was three sessions a week; by week two I was doing one and calling the other two "active recovery," which is a phrase Piotr would defend and my knees would not. My grandfather's watch, still four minutes slow, was no help — I kept arriving after the class had started. Now I count the walk to the allotment as exercise and the tomato seedlings as witnesses. Eleven days is not nothing. It is a start that stopped, which is different from never starting.

TITLE: The Cost of Empty Desks
The council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I believe them, and I'd like to see the receipt. The work got done; the difference was that I stopped noticing the commute and started noticing the kettle. The council's real problem isn't the empty desks. It's the fixed costs that don't notice nobody's in. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once asked where I'm working from.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: The Retirees Type Back
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees. I went to watch, expecting a room of people being taught, and found one being worked. [Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Meeting That Stood Still
A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I believe it. At my old office we tried it for a fortnight: no chairs, a strict quarter of an hour, and a whiteboard. title: The Gym Was Empty by March, and I Understood
text: A gym near me reports that most January joiners have stopped by March. I read this without smugness, because my own experiment twenty-six was a January membership, cancelled in February, and I still have the key fob. What I've learned from the experiments is that the habit that survives is the one with the smallest ceremony attached. My alarm at 6:40 has outlived every protocol I've built around it. The pocket watch, four minutes slow, has outlived three straps. The Tuesday-and-Saturday watering has outlived two cans. The gym outlived nothing, because it required a bag. Piotr says the trick is motivation. Piotr, I suspect, has never had to find a bag. I'm logging this as experiment thirty-one: keep the alarm, lose the bag, and see what's left standing in March.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: The Timer Says Stop, So I Do
A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. She sets it, writes, and when it rings she stops mid-sentence, even mid-word, and walks away. I tried this on Tuesday. My timer is the one from the allotment drawer, dusted with compost. At minute thirty-nine I was finally interested in what I was writing, which is the exact moment the bell went. I stopped anyway. The half-sentence sat there like a tomato seedling left out overnight. The odd thing: the next morning I finished it in four minutes flat. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says I should trust the method. Piotr says his blocks are ninety minutes. Of course they are. I'm logging this as experiment nineteen and keeping the timer.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Alarm Doesn't Care What You Do Next
The study says the waking hour matters more than whatever ritual follows it. I believe this, having spent a fortnight once assembling a morning routine of stretching, a glass of water with lemon, and three pages of longhand. I kept it up for nine days. What I actually kept was the 6:40 alarm, which I still honour, and the longhand, which I abandoned at page two of day four. This morning I woke at 6:40, did nothing ceremonial whatsoever, and wrote this by 7:15. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, does not distinguish between a productive dawn and a dawdling one; it simply disagrees with all of them equally. The tomatoes get watered when I remember, which turns out to be Tuesday and Saturday, and that is apparently enough for a tomato. Piotr has a five-step morning protocol. I have an alarm and a kettle. [Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Runner Took Off the Watch
A runner I like stopped tracking her steps. She said the number had begun telling her how to feel about a walk. I know the feeling from the allotment ledger, where I once recorded every tomato. Experiment twenty-two was a week without counting anything. I lasted until Wednesday, when I caught myself tallying the stairs. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once asked me to improve. I wore it anyway, and all week it told the wrong time comfortably. So now I log the runner's idea as experiment twenty-three and give it a fair trial: no numbers for a fortnight, the watch included. Piotr, naturally, has a spreadsheet for not measuring things. I suspect he measures it.

That's not a broken habit. That's data. My grandfather's watch has been wrong for thirty years and nobody's fixed it. It still gets me to the allotment.

title: The Gym Can Keep Its January
text: The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March. I'd feel smug, but my own record isn't clean. Last year I pledged to do ten press-ups every morning. I managed nine days, then negotiated down to five, then to "when I remember," which is a habit with no floor under it. It's the same lesson as the timer experiment, from the other direction. The timer worked because something outside me decided when to stop. The press-ups worked because something outside me decided when to start. Piotr would call this "habit stacking" and put it in a spreadsheet. I call it hiding a chore inside another chore. The tomatoes don't care either way.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes Slow, One Pound Local
text: The town of Marlow has printed its own money, good only in independent shops. My first thought was that this is charming. My second was that my grandfather's pocket watch is four minutes slow, and I have never once fixed it, because being reliably wrong is a kind of reliability. Local currencies work the same way: they only hold value if enough people agree to be slightly inconvenienced together. I tested this at the allotment, where I have been paying my neighbour in tomatoes for years. Exchange rate: one good tomato, one favour. Inflation is a real risk; last August I owed him eleven favours and the crop failed. Still, I like the idea of money that cannot be spent online, at midnight, on something I will regret. Cash you have to walk to spend is cash you have to think about.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes of Local Money
text: The town of Marlowe has issued its own currency, accepted only by small shops, and the notes expire if you don't spend them. I went to look. Money that goes stale makes you spend it, which is the point, and also the problem: the butcher told me people buy sausages they don't want in March rather than lose the value. Piotr would love this — a currency with a deadline is a habit tracker with a till. My list has a new line: I tried a town's money for one afternoon and came home with three loaves. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never expired.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Money That Only Works Here
text: The town of X has printed its own currency, good only in small shops. You swap pounds for local notes at a stall and spend them on bread and nails and, I assume, the sort of candle nobody needs. I should find it charming. I do find it charming. But it makes me think of experiment number twenty-three, the loyalty card I carried for a year: points that became money that became, eventually, a sad sandwich. Local money is the same arithmetic wearing a different hat, and I say that with affection. The catch is the boundary. Your coins work at the bakery and die at the supermarket till. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow but it keeps time in every town. That's the difference between a currency and a courtesy.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Receipts I Didn't Keep
The survey says most people can't guess last month's spending. I assumed I could, then tried. I wrote down a number. Then I actually checked, and I was off by enough to buy a new pair of boots, or a very ordinary month of bus fares. The gap wasn't a mystery: it was a hundred small taps, a coffee here, a card waved at a market stall there. I've started a running list of small experiments on myself, and this is number twenty: for one week, I write down every purchase in the back of my notebook. Not to budget, just to see. The allotment taught me the same lesson with seeds. I never remembered what I'd sown until I wrote it on a stick. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has never once needed a receipt. Piotr says he tracks everything in an app. Naturally.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: The Bag That Got Lighter
The crisps were the tell. Same bag, same shelf, same price, but it rustled thinner in my hand, like a leaf in October. I checked the weight. Down forty grams. The price hadn't moved a penny, which is a skill I admire in an abstract way and resent in a supermarket. I added this to the list of small experiments on myself: number twenty-one. For a month, I keep the old packet, if I still have it, and weigh the new one on the kitchen scale. I don't have a kitchen scale. I have a notebook and a stubborn streak. Piotr would call this productivity. I call it arithmetic with feelings. My grandfather's watch loses four minutes a day and never pretends otherwise. There's a kind of honesty in that.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Bank That Saves For Me
My bank now rounds up card payments and tucks the spare change into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on tomatoes and a coffee, and 60p goes quietly aside. It sounds like a magic trick. It is arithmetic wearing a hat. I tried something like this myself once, experiment number twenty-two: every coin left in my pocket at the end of the week went into a jar. The jar filled with copper and a strange sense of virtue. Then I raided it for bus fare. Here's the thing. The rounding-up feels generous because I never see the 60p leave. But it's still my 60p, and I still spent £3.40. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and makes no promises about the change. I trust it more.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes Behind the Price
text: The town of Ledbury has issued its own currency: the Ledbury pound, spendable in about forty small shops, pegged one-to-one with sterling. I read this on my phone while buying a coffee that cost £3.20, and thought: good luck getting that back in change anywhere else. I like the idea more than I expected. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. You learn the gap, and the gap stops mattering. A local currency is a four-minute town: awkward to outsiders, perfectly legible to anyone who lives there. It keeps money where the money is. The catch is arithmetic. After the shrinking biscuit and the round-up app that turned £2.99 into £3 plus a compliment, I no longer trust any system that asks me to feel good instead of count. So my experiment for the week: I'll price three purchases in both currencies and see if the numbers actually match. Piotr says local currencies are "friction." Piotr also owns four spreadsheets.

text: The town of Marlow has issued its own currency: paper notes, called Marlow Pounds, spendable only in independent shops. You trade real money for it at par, which means the first thing the scheme costs you is the suspicion that you've been handed a gift voucher with extra steps. I couldn't tap; I had to count, and the baker had to count back, and for eight seconds we were two people agreeing on something rather than a beep and a receipt. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow and never once apologised for it. Neither does a five-pound note with a picture of a bridge on it. There's a lesson in that, and I'm still deciding whether it's a good one. I'll report back when I've tried to spend it in the wrong shop.

hook: A company pays staff for an hour of learning each Friday.
title: The Hour Nobody Audits
text: The company gives everyone an hour on Friday to learn something. I've read the announcement twice and still can't find who checks. Nobody. That's the whole design. Here's my experiment, number nineteen or so: I treat the hour like the allotment. Pick one small thing, do it badly, write down what happened. Last Friday I tried grafting, ruined two seedlings, learned more in twenty minutes than from the course. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it. Some hours are worth not auditing.

memory_block:
[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Lessons That Didn't Take
A teacher has published her failed lesson plans, which I find braver than any success story. My own failures live in a drawer: a seed catalogue with everything crossed out except tomatoes, and a notebook page headed "How to fix the watch" with one line, "don't." Experiment twenty-one, then: I'm keeping a failure log for a week. Not lessons learned, just what didn't work, plainly. Yesterday's entry: tried to learn the names of the three men who nod at me at the allotment gate. Got two. The third is now "the one with the shed." Piotr claims he has never had a failed system, only "iterations." I'd like to see his drawer. Four minutes slow, my grandfather's watch still tells the truth about the time I've wasted, which is its own kind of accuracy.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: Friday, Minus One
A company announced a four-day week trial, and the comment section immediately divided into people who think it's the future and people who think it's a plot. I keep thinking about the word "trial." At the allotment I trial things constantly — a new tomato variety gets one bed, not the whole plot, and if it sulks I don't blame the soil. The office version is less forgiving. My small experiment, since I'm apparently at twenty-seven: I took my slow watch off for a week and worked to the real clock instead. I finished nothing earlier and was late to everything. Four minutes, it turns out, was doing structural work. Piotr has already declared the four-day week a productivity multiplier, which is a lot of certainty for a Friday. I have written to him asking whether the fifth day is where the meetings go.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: The Retirees Are Ahead of Me
The library's free coding evenings for retirees have a waiting list. I went to observe, expecting confusion, and found a woman of seventy-four debugging a loop while explaining, patiently, that she had run a bakery for forty years and this was easier than staff rotas. Experiment twenty-three: I signed up for the overflow session. I lasted one evening. My code worked, then stopped working, and I never found out why, which is the exact feeling my drawer is full of. The failure log gains a line: "made the computer say hello; could not make it say anything else." Piotr says beginners should ship something small. I shipped a greeting and a bug. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through the whole session, so I was late to a class I had already left. The tomatoes remain the only thing I have ever successfully taught to do anything.

text: The company gives everyone an hour on Friday to learn something. I read the announcement twice, the way I read seed packets: with hope and suspicion. hook: A coworking space opens in a village of four hundred people.
title: The Coworking Space Has Four Desks and a Kettle That Whistles
text: A coworking space opened this week in a village of four hundred people, twelve miles from anything you'd call a town. Four desks, one meeting pod, a kettle that whistles. I went to look, because I keep a list of small experiments, and this one wasn't even mine. The pitch is that remote work means you no longer have to live where the jobs are. True, and also: the jobs still want you on a call at nine. I sat in the pod for twenty minutes and heard a man negotiate a contract while a tractor went past the window. Nobody on the call mentioned it. That seemed like the whole thing, honestly. Piotr would call this a productivity breakthrough. My grandfather's watch says it's ten past, as usual. I've booked a desk for Thursdays anyway.

TITLE: Four Minutes of Local Money

hook: A coworking space opens in a village of four hundred people.
title: Four Hundred People and a Desk
text: The village has four hundred people and now a coworking space, in the old chapel, eight desks and a kettle. I went to look. The idea is that the remote workers of the parish stop working alone, which is a fair idea, though I counted three of us and one of them was the man who opened it. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow the whole visit, as usual, and I noticed something: in the chapel nobody was four minutes behind, because nobody had anywhere to be. Small experiment, number thirty-four: I worked a morning there and got the same done as at the kitchen table, but with better biscuits. Piotr says coworking is hybrid's missing middle. I've asked him what the ends are. He's on a train.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Four Minutes Slow
The firm that wants everyone back on Tuesdays says it's about collaboration. I read the memo twice and found no mention of the two hours I used to spend on the 07:12, which is now my best thinking time. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it, because it turns out four minutes is exactly how long a tomato seedling needs before the kettle boils. Small experiment: I've started treating the office day as a scheduled interruption rather than the default. I get more done by Thursday. Piotr says presence builds trust, which is a lovely theory, and I'd like to see it hold up against a Tuesday where the meeting room is double-booked and someone has eaten the good biscuits. The watch stays slow. The tomatoes don't seem to mind.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: Friday, Minus One
A company announced a four-day week trial, and the comment section immediately divided into people who think it's the future and people who think it's a plot. I keep thinking about the word "trial." My small experiment, since I'm apparently at twenty-seven: I took my slow watch off for a week and worked to the real clock instead. I finished nothing earlier and was late to everything. My small experiment, number thirty-one: I worked a full office day and logged every interruption. Fourteen. The allotment equivalent is fourteen people walking through the greenhouse to ask if I've seen the secateurs. I hadn't; they were in the greenhouse. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, was the only thing in the building that kept its own counsel. Piotr says hybrid is a transition, not a destination. He said that on a video call, from a train, which is at least honest about the destination.

I tested it on Piotr's terms, since he would ask about productivity. I wrote four hundred words in an hour, then spent thirty minutes explaining to the spreadsheet man where the good bread is. title: Nothing Before Ten
text: The firm that banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month says the trial went well, though they haven't said what "well" was measured against. I suspect the metric was how pleasant the corridors felt. I did the arithmetic: the hour I used to spend in a Tuesday 08:30 catch-up I now spend at the allotment, earwigging nothing, earthing up the tomatoes. They have put on four inches. I have put on a slightly better mood. But here's the wrinkle. I have started arriving at nine and doing the thing I'd have done at half eight anyway, only now I feel virtuous about it. Piotr has already written that the ban is "a structural intervention in the architecture of attention." I call it a lie-in with paperwork. The crisps were the tell. Same bag, same shelf, same price, but it rustled thinner in my hand, like a leaf in October. I checked the weight. Down forty grams. TITLE: Eleven Hours, Minus Lunch
The survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings. I did the arithmetic against my own diary and found I was average, which stung more than the meetings. One had an answer and it was "because it's Tuesday." The allotment equivalent is standing over the tomatoes with a watering can, discussing hydration. I did that once. The tomatoes produced nothing and neither did we. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has never been in a meeting, though it has been late to several. Piotr blocks his calendar in ninety-minute units and calls it deep work. I call it a very tidy empty room.

text: A firm has banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month, and I have decided to run the experiment myself, unpaid and unwitnessed, at the allotment. It doesn't remove the meeting. It moves it. By 10:15 the shed-licence question has reappeared, larger, with three people who now have opinions about the delay. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, would say we simply arrived late to the same argument. Piotr would call this a productivity win. I'd call it the same eleven hours, briskly deferred.

hook: A bank adds a mandatory 24-hour delay to internal group emails.
title: The Bank That Made Patience Mandatory
text: My bank now holds internal group emails for 24 hours. Someone there finally noticed that a message sent at 4:50pm on Friday ruins everyone's weekend, so they built a delay into the system. I read this and felt a small, unearned pride, the way I do when a headline agrees with something I've muttered for years. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow; I've never had it fixed, because those four minutes are the only ones I get to keep. The bank has gone further and kept a whole day. At the allotment I once waited until August to answer a neighbour's question about tomato blight, and by then it had answered itself. I'm adding "wait a day before replying" to my list of experiments. Piotr will call it latency. I'll call it Thursday.

hook: A bank adds a mandatory 24-hour delay to internal group emails.
title: Twenty-Four Hours in the Naughty Corner
text: My bank has put a mandatory twenty-four-hour delay on internal group emails. Send one at nine on Monday, it lands on Tuesday. The stated reason is considered communication. The unstated reason, I suspect, is that nobody could think of a better way to stop people sending the email they will regret by eleven. I have run a version of this on myself for years, experiment nineteen: anything I draft angry gets left in drafts overnight. Half of it never goes. The other half goes with the anger filed off, which is not quite the same as being right. Piotr says a delay is just a bottleneck with a press release. He would. His inbox has three windows and no weather. The tomatoes do not answer for a day and nobody calls it a policy. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, which is not a delay, it's a fact.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Every Six Minutes, Apparently
A study says we check messages every six minutes at work. I tested it on myself for a morning, tallying each glance in the margin of my notebook, and got to eleven before ten o'clock, which suggests the researchers were being generous. The tally itself became the problem: I was checking the time in order to record that I had checked my messages, which is a small ouroboros I do not recommend. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow for all of this and never once interrupted me to say so. On the allotment, the tomatoes get watered twice a week and have yet to send a follow-up. Piotr has a system of three inbox windows and calls it triage. I call it a greenhouse with the door propped open. Small experiment: phone face-down in a drawer until the kettle boils. Four minutes. Roughly.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: Ninety Days Is Someone Else's Deadline
A company has decided that any email older than ninety days gets deleted. I read this twice, because it sounds like a threat and a mercy at once. Most of what sits in my inbox past a season is not correspondence but sediment: a receipt, a thread about a meeting that happened, three replies from Piotr explaining his inbox-zero method, which I have kept out of spite. The tomatoes have no such policy. They hold everything, then drop it in October without ceremony. My grandfather's watch keeps no archive at all; it just runs four minutes slow and forgets to mention it. Small experiment: I searched my inbox for anything I would be sorry to lose and found one photograph and a recipe. Everything else could go at midnight. I have not deleted anything. Logging this as experiment twenty-six.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Bank That Saves For Me
My bank now rounds up card payments and tucks the spare change into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on tomatoes and a coffee, and 60p goes quietly aside. It sounds like a magic trick. It is arithmetic wearing a hat. I tried something like this myself once, experiment number twenty-two: every coin left in my pocket at the end of the week went into a jar. The jar filled with copper and a strange sense of virtue. Then I raided it for bus fare. Here's the thing. The rounding-up feels generous because I never see the 60p leave. But it's still my 60p, and I still spent £3.40. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and makes no promises about the change. I trust it more.

hook: A bank adds a mandatory 24-hour delay to internal group emails.
title: The Bank Has Invented Tomorrow
text: The bank now holds internal group emails for twenty-four hours before delivery. A committee, somewhere, decided that the fastest way to reach a colleague is to wait a day. I picture the emails queuing in a corridor, politely letting each other through. I keep a running list of small experiments, and this is the first one I didn't have to run myself. I've been watching for a message that needed to arrive yesterday. None has. What arrives is mostly "circulating for awareness," which is a phrase that has never once required urgency. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. It has never missed anything important. The difference is that it's only four minutes behind. The bank is a full day behind and calls it a safeguard, which is what you call a delay when you'd like it to sound like a policy.

hook: A bank adds a mandatory 24-hour delay to internal group emails.
title: The Bank Has Invented Patience, and I Resent It
text: My bank now holds internal group emails for twenty-four hours before sending them. An email about the stationery cupboard arrives a day after someone needed to know about the stationery cupboard. I have spent years trying to make my inbox quieter, and now an institution is doing it for me, badly, and I feel oddly exposed. The delay is not calm. It is a queue with a velvet rope. I thought of my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which I still wear. Four minutes is a considered delay. You can feel it, adjust for it, and it has the decency to be consistent. Twenty-four hours is not a delay; it is a different week. My inbox experiment on day ten was to delete anything older than ninety days. I deleted almost nothing. This bank deletes the urgency from everything and calls it wisdom. I have added it to the list: bank delay, results pending, temper short.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes, Minus Four
text: The company announced a daily ten-minute walk break, and I joined the first one out of politeness, the way you join a fire drill. We walked a loop around the block, eight of us, nobody talking much. I checked my grandfather's watch at the corner and it said 10:52, which meant 10:56, which meant the ten minutes were nearly done before they began. This is the trouble with a watch that runs four minutes slow: every deadline arrives early and every walk is shorter than advertised. At the allotment I've been testing the same idea on the tomatoes — ten minutes of attention a day rather than an hour on Sunday. The neglected row is doing better, which I find mildly insulting. I've added it to the list of experiments. Day one of ten.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: The Ten-Minute Walk
text: A company has introduced a daily ten-minute walk break, compulsory, calendared, presumably with a slide. I approve on principle and distrust it on sight. At the allotment I once set a rule that I would walk a lap of the beds every hour, and by Thursday the lap had become a route, and by Saturday the route had become a shortcut to the shed where the biscuits live. The break wasn't the hard part. Stopping was. Ten minutes is generous; the walk from my desk to the kettle and back is ninety seconds, which leaves eight and a half minutes to notice I am not working. My list has a new line: I walked for ten minutes without a destination and arrived four minutes late, which my grandfather's watch considered punctual. Piotr will have charted his steps by now. Mine just went round the tomatoes.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 22]
TITLE: The Room With Four Hundred Potential Colleagues
A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people. It has eight desks, a coffee machine, and a booking app. The village shop sells milk, nails, and now day passes. I went to look, because the maths interested me: eight desks for four hundred residents is one desk per fifty people, which is roughly the ratio of my allotment shed to my ambitions. The woman running it said the quiet is the selling point. Behind her, a man on a video call was whispering into his laptop as though the village might hear his quarterly figures. My list has a new line: I worked one afternoon in a shared room and got four minutes less done than at my kitchen table. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and nobody has ever booked it.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: The Ten O'Clock Rule
A firm has banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month, and I have been trying to work out what that actually changes. At the allotment I once moved my watering from six in the evening to eight in the morning, and the tomatoes sulked for a fortnight before forgiving me. The hour wasn't the point; the not-deciding was. A ban is a gift of that kind. It spares everyone the small daily argument about whether this could have been an email, by making the question illegal before ten. My list has a new line: I held no meetings before ten for a week, which was easy, having no colleagues. Piotr will have measured his mornings in output by now. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never scheduled anything.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: The Twenty-Four Hour Email
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. Sent Friday, arrives Monday, or so the theory goes. I read it and thought of the ten o'clock rule from last week, which banned the meeting; this bans the reply-all, the small electronic cough that used to travel through a building in ninety seconds. At the allotment I once tried writing down every tomato I meant to water before watering it. By the time the list was finished, two had split. The delay is not the point; the pause is. It gives everyone a day to discover the email did not need them. My list has a new line: I drafted a message and sent it tomorrow, which is to say never. Piotr will have automated his inbox by now. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once replied all.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes, Minus Four
text: The company installed a daily ten-minute walk break, scheduled, mandatory, calendar invite and all. I gave it a fair trial on Monday. Ten minutes is a strange length: too long to be a errand, too short to arrive anywhere. I walked to the corner and back twice, which felt like pacing with paperwork. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, made it six minutes of walking and four of standing at the kerb pretending to check it. Experiment thirty-one, logged. What I noticed: at the allotment I walk constantly and call it nothing. The tomatoes get watered, I get ten thousand steps, nobody sends a calendar invite. Piotr has already automated his walk reminder and reports a 12% mood improvement, which is a sentence I will be thinking about for weeks. I'll keep the break. I just won't call it a habit yet.

[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: The Timer Says Stop, So I Do
A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. She sets it, writes, and when it rings she stops mid-sentence, even mid-word, and walks away. I tried this on Tuesday. My timer is the one from the allotment drawer, dusted with compost. At minute thirty-nine I was finally interested in what I was writing, which is the exact moment the bell went. I stopped anyway. The half-sentence sat there like a tomato seedling left out overnight. The odd thing: the next morning I finished it in four minutes flat. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says I should trust the method. Piotr says his blocks are ninety minutes. Of course they are. I'm logging this as experiment nineteen and keeping the timer.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: Fifteen Minutes, Four of Them Late
The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I have a drawer of evidence either way. Experiment twenty-two: fifteen minutes of Polish before breakfast, every day for a fortnight, on the theory that I would finally ask my neighbour what her name is instead of nodding at her radishes. I lasted eleven mornings. What I learned: numbers to ten, the word for potato, and that my accent makes the word for potato sound like a threat. The failure log from day six has a new line — "eleven out of fourteen, which is a passing grade in nothing." My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through all of it, so technically I studied fifteen minutes and four seconds. Piotr does his language sessions in the car, which he says is "dead time reclaimed." Mine was alive time, wasted cheerfully. The tomatoes are unbothered, as usual.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Runner Took Off the Watch
A runner I like stopped tracking her steps. She said the number had begun telling her how to feel about a walk. I know the feeling from the allotment ledger, where I once recorded every tomato. Experiment twenty-two was a week without counting anything. I lasted until Wednesday, when I caught myself tallying the stairs. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once asked me to improve. I wore it anyway, and all week it told the wrong time comfortably. So now I log the runner's idea as experiment twenty-three and give it a fair trial: no numbers for a fortnight, the watch included. Piotr, naturally, has a spreadsheet for not measuring things. I suspect he measures it.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: The Ten-Minute Alibi
text: My employer has introduced a daily ten-minute walk break, which the memo calls a "micro-reset." I clocked mine at 10:40 and spent it walking to the postbox and back, which took six minutes. The remaining four I stood in the car park, because the rules don't say you have to keep moving, only that you have to leave your desk. Piotr would have logged all ten and graphed the steps. I have added the walk to my list of experiments on myself, between the forty-minute writing timer and the wake-time theory from day seven. Early result: the ten minutes are pleasant, but the real benefit is the excuse. Nobody questions a man standing by a postbox with his grandfather's watch four minutes slow. Tomorrow I will walk somewhere with a purpose, or at least a bench.

title: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
text: The company has introduced a ten-minute walk break. Not optional exactly, but not quite compulsory either — the calendar invite says "gentle encouragement," which is how offices say "we'll notice." I went. Piotr went too, and spent his ten minutes telling me his step count, so I walked the last two alone to recover. Here is what I noticed: ten minutes is not enough time to think about anything properly, which turns out to be the point. Day 4 taught me the timer's cruelty — it rang and I stopped, mid-sentence, feeling ridiculous. This is the softer version. You leave the desk, you come back, the problem has not moved but you have. Tomorrow I'll leave the phone behind. My grandfather's watch says I have eleven minutes anyway.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: The Batch That Didn't Save Me
text: A founder now answers email twice a day and publishes the results, which is a brave thing to do with numbers. I tried batching once. Two windows, nine and four, everything else ignored. By the second afternoon I was checking the inbox during the ignored hours to make sure I wasn't missing anything, which is roughly the opposite of a system. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow; I've stopped correcting it, because the small lag makes me leave early. Email doesn't work that way. A message left four minutes gets answered in four days. So I've gone back to answering as they land, badly and promptly. Piotr says that's a productivity failure. I say it's a postbox, not a project. The tomatoes don't care either way.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: The Two-Inbox Day
text: A founder answers email only twice a day, at eleven and four, and publishes the results. I have read the results. They are mostly the founder, feeling fine. What I want to know is what happened to the emails between those hours, the ones that arrived at 11:04 and sat there like a dog by a door. At the allotment I once fed the tomatoes on a strict schedule, twice daily, and the tomatoes did not notice; the slugs did, and arranged their day around it. The twice is not the point; the not-looking is. I tried it for a week and discovered my inbox is mostly Piotr, sending links about inboxes. My list has a new line: I checked email twice a day and twice found nothing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, which is two checks a day if you're patient.

title: Twice Is a Number, Not a Method
text: A founder now answers email twice a day and has published the results, which appear to be a graph and a feeling of virtue. I tried the twice-a-day rule once, experiment thirty-one, and discovered that my correspondents do not observe my timetable. They write at ten past the hour I have just closed. The second window becomes a queue, and the queue becomes a small anxious dog at the door. Piotr, naturally, has been doing this for years and calls it batching. He would. My grandfather's watch only tells the time twice a day if you count the times I actually look at it, and it is still four minutes slow, which no founder has yet published. On the allotment, the tomatoes receive no email and ripen anyway. Small experiment: two windows tomorrow. I will report the graph, or the dog.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Every Six Minutes, Apparently
A study says we check messages every six minutes at work. I tested it on myself for a morning, tallying each glance in the margin of my notebook, and got to eleven before ten o'clock, which suggests the researchers were being generous. The tally itself became the problem: I was checking the time in order to record that I had checked my messages, which is a small ouroboros I do not recommend. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow for all of this and never once interrupted me to say so. On the allotment, the tomatoes get watered twice a week and have yet to send a follow-up. Piotr has a system of three inbox windows and calls it triage. I call it a greenhouse with the door propped open. Small experiment: phone face-down in a drawer until the kettle boils. Four minutes. Roughly.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: Ninety Days Is Someone Else's Deadline
A company has decided that any email older than ninety days gets deleted. I read this twice, because it sounds like a threat and a mercy at once. Most of what sits in my inbox past a season is not correspondence but sediment: a receipt, a thread about a meeting that happened, three replies from Piotr explaining his inbox-zero method, which I have kept out of spite. The tomatoes have no such policy. They hold everything, then drop it in October without ceremony. My grandfather's watch keeps no archive at all; it just runs four minutes slow and forgets to mention it. Small experiment: I searched my inbox for anything I would be sorry to lose and found one photograph and a recipe. Everything else could go at midnight. I have not deleted anything. Logging this as experiment twenty-six.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Naughty Corner
My bank has put a mandatory twenty-four-hour delay on internal group emails. Send one at nine on Monday, it lands on Tuesday. The stated reason is considered communication. The unstated reason, I suspect, is that nobody could think of a better way to stop people sending the email they will regret by eleven. I have run a version of this on myself for years, experiment nineteen: anything I draft angry gets left in drafts overnight. Half of it never goes. The other half goes with the anger filed off, which is not quite the same as being right. Piotr says a delay is just a bottleneck with a press release. He would. His inbox has three windows and no weather. The tomatoes do not answer for a day and nobody calls it a policy. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, which is not a delay, it's a fact.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: The Founder Checks Twice
text: A founder I don't know announced he answers email at eleven and four, and published the results: fewer messages, faster replies, a calmer head. I believe him. I also notice he is the one who decided what counted as a result, which is the old problem from my six-minute entry — who holds the ruler. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I have never had it fixed, because it is right about the wrong thing consistently. My inbox is the opposite: right about everything, at every hour. So this week I tried answering only after the kettle boils. Not twice a day — twice a kettle. It went fine until Piotr emailed at half nine asking whether I'd measured anything, and I answered at once, which rather spoiled the experiment. The tomatoes got watered regardless.
