hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Four-Minute Margin
text: I could not tell you what I spent last month. I could tell you what I spent on tomatoes: eleven pounds forty, mostly on canes and a bag of blood, fish and bone that the fox has already investigated. The survey says most people can't guess their monthly outgoings, and I am most people, apparently. So I ran an experiment: for one week I wrote down every purchase in the back of my notebook, next to the tomato figures. The total was £84.20, of which £19 was coffee I would have sworn I didn't buy. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow; I have never fixed it, because the lateness is useful. Money seems to work the other way. It runs quietly ahead of you, and you only notice when you check the time. Piotr would have a spreadsheet. I have a page of scrawl and a mild grudge against coffee.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Receipt Confusion
text: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I assumed I could, then tried. I wrote down a figure, checked the bank, and was wrong by more than my monthly coffee budget, which is itself a number I'd rather not know. The gap wasn't one big thing; it was many small things, each too minor to remember and too frequent to ignore. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, but at least I know it's four and not five. My spending has no such honest error. Piotr, naturally, tracks every purchase in an app and calls it awareness. I call it a second job with no holiday. I logged receipts for one week, then stopped, which is itself a finding. The seed packets at the allotment cost less than I guessed. The tomatoes remain priceless.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Head Start
The study says morning routines matter less than a consistent wake time, which is inconvenient, because my morning routine is the only part of my life that resembles a system. I have tested the alternatives. I once woke at five for a fortnight to write before the day started; I produced three paragraphs and a strong opinion about birdsong. The study's point is that the body wants regularity, not ritual, and I believe it, because my grandfather's watch is the same: it doesn't need winding at dawn, it needs winding at all. This week I've woken at the same time and done nothing else in particular. The writing has been fine. Not better, just fine, which for a Tuesday is a result. Piotr has a nine-step morning and calls it non-negotiable. Nine steps, and he's still late. Mine runs four minutes slow; I've decided that counts as consistency, not error. The tomatoes were watered at the same time all week. They have no routine and are, as ever, ahead of me.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: The Output-Only Manager
A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work alone, which sounds like rigour until you notice he has no idea when the work happens. I tested this on myself, because I test things on myself the way other people test things on other people. For a week I logged nothing but deliverables and deliberately worked at odd hours. The list looked identical each day. The list cannot tell you that Wednesday's entry was written at half past ten at night with the lights off. My grandfather's watch would report the same four minutes slow whatever I did; the watch is honest about being wrong. Piotr says output is the only fair metric. Piotr also once sent me a productivity graph at 5 a.m. At the allotment I judge tomatoes by the tomatoes. I still go and look at the leaves.

[Entry from day 29]
TITLE: The Ninety-Day Amnesia
A company now deletes all email older than ninety days. I read this and felt the floor tilt slightly, because I have emails I treat as furniture. One from a man at a council confirming a thing about a fence; if it vanishes, the fence becomes a rumour. I once cleared my inbox to zero and felt nothing but a small, clean panic. My grandfather's watch keeps four minutes slow and no one deletes that. It is wrong, but it is wrong consistently, and I can find the error. A deleted email is not wrong; it is simply gone, which is worse. Piotr deletes everything weekly and calls it a system. Systems are easy when you have nothing worth keeping. At the allotment I keep every seed packet, even the empty ones. The tomatoes don't care. I might.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Receipt in the Coat Pocket
text: I can't guess what I spent last month either, so I did what any reasonable person does and checked a coat pocket. There, folded to the size of a stamp, was a receipt for £11.40: two coffees, a pasty, and something listed as "MISC" for £2.10. I have no memory of the misc. That's the survey's point, I suppose, arriving in my own handwriting. What interests me is that the numbers exist and I still can't feel them. £11.40 is a number; the pasty was a Tuesday. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which is roughly how far behind my sense of my own spending runs. Piotr says to track every purchase in an app. I've added it to the list of experiments, somewhere below the tomato audit, which is still producing nothing but opinions.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Round-Up Roundabout
My bank now rounds up card payments and tucks the change into savings. Spend £4.30 on a sandwich, and 70p goes quietly aside. It’s clever, and I hate that it’s clever. Last month’s chocolate bar lost ten grams; this month my bank sells me my own spare change back as a favour. I tried it for a week. The app told me I’d saved £3.12, then charged me £2.50 for the privilege of noticing. Net gain: 62p, plus a mild sense of being managed. At the allotment, the tomato audit continues: not one extra fruit has appeared from my positive thinking. My grandfather’s watch still runs four minutes slow, which now feels less like a flaw and more like a small act of resistance. Piotr calls this “behavioural economics.” I call it a slot machine with better manners.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Ten-Pound Note With a Postcode
The town two valleys over has issued its own currency. Ten-pound notes you can only spend in local shops, which sounds charming until you work out what it actually is: a loyalty card with a printing press. My neighbour Beryl bought forty pounds of it and now can't buy her newspaper anywhere but the bakery, which doesn't sell newspapers, so she's been reading the ingredients on a loaf. I like the idea more than I should. Money that can't leave town is money that has to look you in the eye. But I've spent sixteen days auditing what shops quietly take from me. A currency that only circulates locally is still a currency, and the chocolate bar is still ten grams lighter. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and spends locally too. Piotr loves the scheme. He says it builds trust. I say trust is what's left when nobody's counting.

[Entry from day 21]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Rent
My rent went up £85 a month. My pay went up £31, before tax, which is to say it didn't. The letting agent's letter called this "market adjustment," the same phrase the supermarket used when the chocolate bar got lighter. Everything, it turns out, is being reformulated except the price. I did the sums on the back of the envelope the letter came in: at this rate, in four years I'll be paying to live here and commuting from the allotment. The tomatoes wouldn't have me; the slugs would. So I've added a line to the ledger — not what things cost, but what they cost against what I earn. The gap is the honest number, and nobody prints it on a wrapper. My grandfather's watch still runs four minutes slow. Lately it feels like the only thing in town keeping pace. Piotr says I should negotiate. I say I'm counting.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Forty Pence I Can't Account For
text: I tried to guess last month's spending before checking. I was off by £84, which is roughly a week of coffees, or one very optimistic tomato cage. What surprised me wasn't the number but the shape of the gap: I could recall every purchase over £50 and none of the small ones. The brain audits the landmarks and lets the weather go unrecorded. Piotr says he tracks every penny in an app and has done for six years. I believe him, and I notice he never says it makes him happy. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and I check it anyway, which is a kind of tracking too — a chosen error I can see. I'm not downloading anything. Instead: one week of writing down whatever I spend, in the back of the allotment notebook. Nothing rounded, nothing sorted. Just the weather, recorded.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Four-Minute Margin
text: The survey says most people can't guess last month's spending, which surprises me less than the survey does. I tried it on myself and landed within £12, mostly because of the watch. It runs four minutes slow, so I estimate every price in the margin it gives me: what would this cost if I waited? The kettle I nearly bought online at £39 was £31 in the shop two streets over. The margin paid for itself. Piotr would call this a system; I call it being too mean to pay full price. At the allotment I've stopped weighing tomatoes and started weighing what I actually eat versus what rots on the sill. Last week that gap was 1.4kg. The shed wall has a new column. The watch is still wrong, still useful.

hook: A shop publishes how it sets its prices.
title: The Four-Minute Discount
text: A shop near me published its pricing method this week: rent, wages, a margin, and a line for "what we think people will pay." I read it twice. It's the honest version of every price tag, and I felt oddly grateful, the way you do when someone admits the trick after you've fallen for it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. I've never fixed it. It means I'm never late, only nearly, and I've started to think of those four minutes as a small private discount on the day. The shop's confession is like that: the price is what it is, but now I know the minutes inside it. At the allotment I priced a tomato once. It came to eleven pounds. I ate it and said nothing.

hook: A shop publishes how it sets its prices.
title: The Price of a Chair
text: A furniture shop published its full cost breakdown: wood, labour, rent, a line for profit. I found it oddly moving, the way a receipt for a chair is also a receipt for someone's afternoon. Then I read the line for "marketing" and felt the floor tilt slightly. I tried this on myself. I costed one column: my hours, my coffee, the wear on my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow and therefore costs me four minutes per day I will never bill anyone for. The number came out lower than I feared, which was somehow worse. Piotr says transparency is a productivity tool. Piotr would price a sunset. At the allotment I know exactly what a tomato costs me, and I grow them anyway. Some prices are just the entry fee.

hook: A shop publishes how it sets its prices.
title: The Bakery Explains Itself
text: A bakery I pass on the way to the allotment has put a notice in the window explaining its prices: flour up, butter up, the oven's last repair, and a line that says "we would rather tell you than quietly shrink the loaf." I stood there longer than a man should stand outside a bakery. Compare that with the "MISC" on my coat-pocket receipt, £2.10 for something nobody will ever explain. A shop that shows its arithmetic is doing what my grandfather's watch refuses to do, which is admit what it's losing. The loaf is smaller than last year, but now I know why. Piotr says transparency is a productivity strategy. I say it's a shop deciding not to pick my pocket. Either way, I bought the bread.

title: The Shop That Showed Its Working
text: A bakery near the station has started printing a small card beside the till: what the flour cost this month, what the butter cost, what the electricity came to, and what they pay the two people on the early shift. I stood there reading it longer than I read most things, and then bought a loaf I didn't strictly need, which I suspect was the point. Prices, it turns out, are just numbers wearing coats, and I keep failing to check the labels.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: The Notification I Didn't Miss
text: The chat tool added quiet hours, muting everything from ten at night until seven. I approved on principle and then spent the evening waiting to feel calmer, which is not the same as feeling calmer. Here is the specific experiment: I turned it on Tuesday. By Thursday I had checked the app eleven times between ten and eleven, which is more than I check it in a normal evening, because a closed door is still a door. The notifications stopped. The reaching did not. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I wear it anyway, so I'm not against a deliberate delay. But a watch you choose to trust is different from one that hides the time. On Friday I set quiet hours to start at eleven and left the sound on. I felt less managed. Nothing urgent arrived. Nothing ever does, at night.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: Quiet Hours
text: The chat tool now goes silent at night. I approve, then notice the silence has a schedule, which makes it a kind of message: we are not ignoring you, we are asleep on your behalf. I tested it. I sent myself a note at 11:40 p.m. and it arrived without a sound, like a letter slipped under a door. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, makes no noise either, but it never pretends that's a feature. Piotr has already configured his quiet hours to begin at nine and calls it boundaries. I call it a bedtime for other people's opinions. At the allotment the tomatoes receive no notifications and have never once asked me to respect their focus. I keep the phone face down among the seed packets, still buzzing, four minutes behind everything.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: Quiet Hours
text: The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. A kindness, says the announcement, which I read at 11:40 p.m. on my phone. I set my experiment accordingly: notifications off, but a notepad by the bed, and every message I felt the urge to answer got written down instead. Three nights. Eleven messages. In daylight, nine of them read like something a stranger had shouted through a letterbox. The other two were real, and one was from Piotr, asking whether I'd tried his new system. I answered it in the morning and was glad of the wait. It's the same as the update I sit on from Thursday to Monday. My grandfather's watch doesn't buzz; it's four minutes slow and it has never once needed me at midnight. The allotment is asleep by then too.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: The Quiet Room
My team swapped the chat channel for one written update a week. I expected to hate it. Instead, Tuesday mornings got forty minutes longer, and nobody has yet asked me to "circle back." The chat still exists, of course; it just stopped pretending to be work. My small experiment: I wrote the update on Thursday, sat on it, and sent it Monday, which is the only reason I caught that I'd called a colleague "the blocker" in paragraph two. At the allotment I've been doing the same with tomatoes — one note a week instead of daily fussing, and the plants seem unbothered. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, so I now write the update, wait, and check it against the watch before sending. It has never once been wrong about what mattered.

[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Eleven Hours
A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, having once sat through a forty-minute call about whether we needed a call. My experiment this week: I timed my meetings against my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, and logged each one in the margin of my notebook. Eight meetings. Six could have been a paragraph. One could have been silence. The eighth was the shed with better chairs, where the kettle walk genuinely did make me wiser, mostly about tea. Piotr would have published a graph by Tuesday; I have a list with coffee rings on it. Eleven hours is nearly three coding evenings, or two afternoons at the allotment. The watch says I'm still four minutes behind, and I've decided the meetings can keep up.

[Entry from day 29]
TITLE: Ninety Days of Nothing to Say
A company of four hundred has announced it will delete all email older than ninety days. The reasoning: most of it is never read twice. I went looking for a defence of the archive and found my own inbox, which is less an archive than a hedge. I searched "important" and got a receipt for a watering can. I searched the name of a man I meant to thank in March and found nine messages from him, none answered. So I ran the experiment on myself: one folder, deleted, no rescue. Nothing broke. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, still keeps the only record I trust, and it has never once needed searching. At the allotment I prune the same way. Piotr is archiving his.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: Quiet Hours, Loud Clock
text: The chat tool now goes silent from ten until seven. I read the announcement twice, suspicious of anything that calls a mute "wellbeing." Then I turned the setting on for my own phone, which is not the same as my conscience. Here is what happened: I slept, badly, but I slept. The messages were still there at seven, stacked like tomatoes I forgot to water. None of them had ripened into emergencies overnight. I keep a list of small experiments. This one joins "no email before the kettle" and "one written update instead of forty thumbs." The difference is that a company imposed this one, and I have spent two years arguing that imposed pauses are a way of pretending a problem is solved. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. He said that way he was never late, only early in a manner nobody could fault. I want quiet hours that I choose, not ones handed to me. But I'll take the sleep.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: Four Minutes Late to the Office
text: My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I arrived at the Tuesday meeting at 9:04 by my wrist and 9:08 by the wall, which is apparently a policy violation now. The firm wants everyone in on Tuesdays. Just Tuesdays. A single day, like a vitamin. I understand the logic: one mandated day is easier to enforce than three negotiated ones. But the result is a building that hums on Tuesday and echoes on Thursday, and a commute I've started timing against my tomato plants, which don't care what day it is. text: A firm banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month, and I read the story with the envy of a man who has spent decades in rooms with bad coffee. By Thursday I had solved a problem I'd been circling for months, mostly by not circling it. Piotr would call this productivity laundering. Fine. The watch still lies about the time, but nobody has asked me anything before ten, and the allotment has never looked better.

title: The Ten O'Clock Truce
text: A firm has banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month, and I find I've been running this experiment for years without the paperwork. My rule is simpler: no meetings before the second cup. What the ban actually buys isn't the hour, it's the excuse. "I'm free after ten" is a sentence you can say without explaining yourself. I tested it on the tomatoes in July, holding off watering until mid-morning. The soil stayed cooler, the roots went deeper, and I got to stand there doing nothing with a legitimate purpose. Piotr will have a graph by Friday showing the recovered hours; I have a watering can and a hunch. My grandfather's watch says it's 9:56 when the phone says ten. Four minutes of quiet, free, and legally mine.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Eleven Hours
A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, having once sat through a forty-minute call about whether we needed a call. My experiment this week: I timed my meetings against my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, and logged each one in the margin of my notebook. Eight meetings. Six could have been a paragraph. One could have been silence. The eighth was the shed with better chairs, where the kettle walk genuinely did make me wiser, mostly about tea. Piotr would have published a graph by Tuesday; I have a list with coffee rings on it. Eleven hours is nearly three coding evenings, or two afternoons at the allotment. The watch says I'm still four minutes behind, and I've decided the meetings can keep up.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: The Building That Ate the Budget
The council says its empty offices cost more than forecast. I believe it. I once spent a fortnight in a half-occupied floor where the lights came on for nobody and the heating ran for the pot plants. My experiment that month: I turned up on the quiet days instead of the busy ones. Meetings shrank. The commute didn't, so I wasn't clever, only less interrupted. Piotr would call this a productivity finding and put it on a slide. I call it paying rent on a room to sit nearer the kettle. The coworking shed near my allotment has eight desks and no such problem; when nobody comes in, the woman running it just makes tea. My watch is four minutes slow, and even it can tell an empty desk from a working one.

[Entry from day 26]
TITLE: The Cancellation Audit
A manager cancelled every recurring meeting and waited to see which ones came back. I admire the nerve. I also know what came back in my own trial of this: the meetings that returned were the ones with a person attached, not a purpose. The status update died quietly. The Thursday catch-up survived because two of us liked each other and the coffee was good. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through the whole audit, and nobody noticed the cancellations were on time. What the experiment proved is that a calendar is a social document wearing a spreadsheet's clothes. At the allotment I stopped watering a third of the tomatoes for a fortnight. The ones that lived weren't the best plants, just the ones nearest the leaky tap. Piotr will say the manager found the meetings that matter. The manager found the meetings with friends in them.

TITLE: The Tuesday Rule

I learned she reconciles the travel budget by hand, on paper, because the spreadsheet "lies in a confident voice." I have no use for this and have thought about it all week. My grandfather's watch lies too, quietly, four minutes behind, and nobody has ever called it confident. I offered her the allotment method: give a new hire one small true thing about how the place actually works, not the org chart. She wrote it down. On the plot I planted a second variety next to the first, and the old one has started leaning towards it, which is either competition or company. I'll report back when I can tell which.

TITLE: I Could Not Guess Either
The survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I read it and thought, amateurs, then tried it myself. I guessed £1,400. The actual figure was £1,140, which is the sort of gap you notice. Where does £260 go? Not on anything. On many things, each small enough to feel free. I went through the statement looking for the leak and found eleven of them, all under a tenner, all bought while walking. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I have never once tried to fix it, but I check my bank balance like a man winding a watch he doesn't trust. title: The Gym Is Not My Grandfather's Watch
text: The gym says most January sign-ups stop by March. I believe it. A membership is a rule you pay for and then have to enforce yourself, and I have never been good at enforcement. My grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, asks nothing; it simply is what it is, and I have built eleven years of trains around it. The gym asks me, nightly, whether I feel like it. I rarely do. Piotr says the trick is to make it a habit, not a decision. He would know; he has a column about it. Rules get negotiated with.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Four Minutes Late, Every Time
The building managers put a sign by the lift: stairs only, one floor up, one floor down. Six weeks later they reported a modest rise in stair trips and a modest fall in lift waits. I read this on the bus and thought about my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. I have never had it fixed. Those four minutes are the only routine I have never had to build, because the watch does the building for me. I check it, I add four, I leave early, and I have not missed a train in eleven years. At the allotment I tried the same trick with tomato watering: a fixed time, no decision. Half the plants sulked anyway. The sign works, I think, because it removes a choice rather than adding a rule. My watch does the same.

[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Quiet Hours, Loud Watch
The chat tool now has quiet hours. Notifications stop at ten and resume at seven, which means nobody can reach me at night unless they actually mean it, and most people don't. I tested it by leaving my phone in the kitchen and going to bed. Woke at six, four minutes behind my grandfather's watch, which has never once needed muting. Twelve messages had queued up; eleven were resolves, one was a photo of someone's cat. I read them all in nine minutes and replied to none, which may be the point. At the allotment the tomatoes don't notify me either. They just sit there, quietly doing the work, and I show up to check. Piotr says quiet hours are a productivity hack. I've added "be unreachable after ten" to my list of experiments. Day one, nobody noticed.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Runner and the Uncounted Mile
The runner quit her step counter because the number had started deciding whether a walk counted. I understand. I keep a list of small experiments, and the failures mostly share one flaw: I build a rule where I should have built a fence. The stairs sign worked because it took a choice away. My step counter, back when I tried one, did the opposite — it handed me a choice every evening, and I chose the sofa, then argued with the number. Now I wear only the watch, four minutes slow, which asks nothing and forgives everything. At the allotment I stopped logging tomato yields and just looked at the plants. They sulked identically. Piotr says unmeasured habits are hobbies. He may be right, but my tomatoes don't read his column.

title: Four Minutes Slow
text: My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I have stopped correcting it. I like arriving everywhere slightly early by the clock and slightly wrong by everyone else's. Piotr would make a spreadsheet. I have made a list instead, titled Things I Have Tried, and today's entry is simply: read the letter twice, then put the kettle on. The second reading is always four minutes slower and somehow easier to bear.

title: Four Minutes of Rent

On the allotment, the tomatoes don't pay rent. Derek does.

title: The Four-Minute Discount
text: The letting agent's letter says the rent goes up £47 a month, and the pay rise I have been promised is £31, before tax. TITLE: The Price of Not Knowing
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tested myself before reading the answer: I guessed £340. The watch on my wrist is four minutes slow and I have never once thought to fix it, which tells you something about how I handle numbers that inconvenience me. At the allotment I keep a seed packet tally in pencil on the shed wall. It is wrong by roughly a third, and the tomatoes grow regardless. Piotr says he knows his monthly spend to the penny. He would. I have added "write down every purchase for a week" to my list of experiments. Day one, I forgot the list.

TITLE: The Shop That Showed Its Working
The shop published its pricing formula — rent, wages, wastage, a margin, all laid out like a recipe. I read it twice and felt oddly soothed, the way I feel when someone else admits the sum. My seed tally on the shed wall is still wrong by a third; I have not corrected it, because the pencil marks have become a kind of history. What the shop understands and I resist is that a price is a confession. Piotr would have the formula memorised and a spreadsheet to check it. I have the watch, four minutes slow, and a week of purchases still unwritten. Tomorrow I start the week properly. I have said that before, which is itself a kind of pricing error, repeated.

TITLE: The Gym Is Not My Grandfather's Watch

My grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, asks nothing; it simply is what it is, and I have built eleven years of trains around it. The gym asks me, nightly, whether I feel like it. I rarely do. Piotr says the trick is to make it a habit, not a decision. He would know; he has a column about it. I tried the same logic at the allotment, tying watering to the kettle boiling rather than to my willpower. It worked for a fortnight, then the kettle broke and took my tomatoes with it. Fences hold. Rules get negotiated with.

TITLE: The Course They Cut

TITLE: Four Minutes of Rent

title: Four Hundred People and a Meeting Room
text: The parish council has opened a coworking space in the old chapel. Four hundred residents, twelve desks, one kettle. I went on the first morning to see what a village does with an office. A farmer was on a video call with his knees; a woman was invoicing from the pews. By ten the room had settled into the sound of typing and one person whispering “sorry, sorry” to a dog. memory_block:

TITLE: The Office Has Left the Building
The council says empty offices are costing it more than budgeted, which is the municipal version of my grandfather's watch: still ticking, four minutes slow, and nobody willing to say so out loud. I went to the allotment instead of a meeting that could have been an email. The tomatoes do not care where I am, only whether I show up, which is more than I can say for the third floor of the old insurance building. Piotr would call this a productivity loss. I call it a building discovering it was mostly corridor. My experiment for the week: I worked from the shed for two hours and got the same amount done, minus the commute and the small talk. The watch still says it's early. It's wrong, but I keep wearing it.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Unaccounted For
The survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I believe it. I also believe the forty minutes are not sleep but the gap between the alarm and the admitting of it, spent lying still while the radiator ticks. My grandfather's watch says it's four minutes earlier than it is. I've decided this is a small daily kindness rather than a fault. At the allotment I've been testing a related idea: a second alarm, four minutes late, to see whether the tomatoes notice. They do not. Piotr would want the forty minutes logged, attributed, and reviewed. I've added "sleep in on a Wednesday" to my list of experiments. Day one: I woke at the usual time and lay there, awake, feeling productive.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: The Tuesday Clause
The firm wants everyone back on Tuesdays. Not Mondays, not a rota, just Tuesdays, as though a week had a hinge. I understand the logic: a shared day means everyone is in the same room, which is the office version of my allotment, where the tomatoes only do well if I turn up on the same days as the water. But I've been here before. Skipping the Tuesday watering for a fortnight taught me the survivors were the ones nearest the leaky tap, not the sturdiest. A mandated Tuesday is a tap, not a plant. It will keep the nearest people alive and tell you nothing about the rest. My experiment: go in on a Tuesday, leave at three, see what's actually missed. My grandfather's watch will say it's four minutes early. It's still wrong.

Nobody asked me to align anything. My grandfather's watch ran its usual four minutes slow and nobody noticed, which is the whole point of a village. I'm adding it to the list: experiment, work one day a month somewhere with fewer than five hundred people. Piotr would call this a productivity leak. Piotr lives in a city of a million and has never once been early.

I've added it to my list of experiments. Verdict so far: harmless, slightly smug, and Piotr will claim it's a productivity system. It isn't. It's a jar with better branding.

title: Six Minutes

TITLE: The Bank That Waits
A bank put a mandatory 24-hour delay on its internal group emails. The memo said it would "reduce reactive decision-making," which is what you say when you want to look thoughtful about not answering. I read it twice and decided I approved, mainly because it's the first policy I've met that admits the problem is us. My experiment: I held every non-urgent email for a day. Drafted, not sent. I wrote eleven on Monday and sent four on Tuesday. The other seven had quietly resolved themselves, like arguments with myself usually do. One of them, reread cold, was rude. I'd have sent it at speed and apologised at leisure. The watch is four minutes slow, so I already live a day behind in miniature. Piotr sends at dawn and calls it velocity. TITLE: The Hub in the Village
A coworking space opened in a village of four hundred people. Twelve desks, a coffee machine, a meeting room you book by the hour. The article about it called the place a "hub," which is what you call a room once it has a printer. What interested me was the arithmetic: twelve desks against a village where most people work in the next county. My experiment: I worked a morning from the village hall during the library's closed hours. It held. text: The study says people check messages every six minutes at work. I believe it. I got curious and counted my own six minutes for one hour, which is the most humbling thing I've done since I started this list. Nine checks in sixty minutes, and nothing in the inbox had changed except a calendar invite I didn't want. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow the whole time and never once asked me to look at it. Piotr has probably turned this into a boundary system with a colour code. I've gone the other way: my phone now sits in a drawer during the morning, and I check it at the top of each hour like a person collecting post. The tomatoes don't send updates. TITLE: Quiet Hours, Loud Watch
The chat tool now has quiet hours. Notifications stop at ten and resume at seven, which means nobody can reach me at night unless they actually mean it, and most people don't. Twelve messages had queued up; eleven were resolves, one was a photo of someone's cat. I read them all in nine minutes and replied to none, which may be the point. At the allotment the tomatoes don't notify me either. They just sit there, quietly doing the work, and I show up to check. Piotr says quiet hours are a productivity hack. I've added "be unreachable after ten" to my list of experiments. Day one, nobody noticed.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: Twice a Day, Like a Tide
The founder answers email at eleven and four, and publishes how much he doesn't regret it. I read the post at 11:40, which is between tides, so technically I was ignoring him. My own inbox is a shed with no door: everything gets in, nothing gets out. I tried two windows once — nine and three, I think — and spent both windows explaining to people why I hadn't answered in the other window. The experiment lasted four days. Four came out dead by morning, one had become an apology, and one I sent unchanged and regretted by lunch. The tomatoes don't queue. They ripen on their own schedule and ignore my drafts entirely. Added to the list: sleep on it, then delete. Day one, the bank and I agree.

It's the low hum of being reachable, which feels like work and isn't. Piotr would prescribe a system. I've stopped believing in systems for this, and I say that as a man who once ran two inboxes four minutes apart, like my grandfather's watch. The bank that delays its own emails got further than I did, because it removed the choice. So on the allotment I've stopped checking between tomato rows. The plants don't message. hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes, No Agenda
text: The company announced a ten-minute walk break, twice a day, and I gave it a fortnight before it became a scroll break with better shoes. I was wrong, mostly. What saves it is that nobody logs it. There is no step count, no chart, no one asking whether the walk counted. It is a fence, not a rule — the same trick as the stairs sign, except here the choice removed is the choice to keep sitting. Piotr would want a metric. He would put the ten minutes in a spreadsheet and name the columns. I walked out at eleven with a colleague who spent the whole time complaining about a meeting, and neither of us mentioned our health. My watch said four minutes slow, as ever. memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Four Minutes Late, Every Time
The building managers put a sign by the lift: stairs only, one floor up, one floor down. Six weeks later they reported a modest rise in stair trips and a modest fall in lift waits. I read this on the bus and thought about my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. I have never had it fixed. Those four minutes are the only routine I have never had to build, because the watch does the building for me. I check it, I add four, I leave early, and I have not missed a train in eleven years. At the allotment I tried the same trick with tomato watering: a fixed time, no decision. Half the plants sulked anyway. The sign works, I think, because it removes a choice rather than adding a rule. My watch does the same.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Runner and the Uncounted Mile
The runner quit her step counter because the number had started deciding whether a walk counted. I understand. I keep a list of small experiments, and the failures mostly share one flaw: I build a rule where I should have built a fence. The stairs sign worked because it took a choice away. My step counter, back when I tried one, did the opposite — it handed me a choice every evening, and I chose the sofa, then argued with the number. Now I wear only the watch, four minutes slow, which asks nothing and forgives everything. At the allotment I stopped logging tomato yields and just looked at the plants. They sulked identically. Piotr says unmeasured habits are hobbies. He may be right, but my tomatoes don't read his column.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Gym Is Not My Grandfather's Watch
The gym says most January sign-ups stop by March. I believe it. A membership is a rule you pay for and then have to enforce yourself, and I have never been good at enforcement. My grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, asks nothing; it simply is what it is, and I have built eleven years of trains around it. The gym asks me, nightly, whether I feel like it. I rarely do. Piotr says the trick is to make it a habit, not a decision. He would know; he has a column about it. I tried the same logic at the allotment, tying watering to the kettle boiling rather than to my willpower. It worked for a fortnight, then the kettle broke and took my tomatoes with it. Fences hold. Rules get negotiated with.

I went past the post office and back. My grandfather's watch said 11:04 when I left and 11:14 when I returned, so actually thirteen minutes, and nobody noticed, including me. At the allotment I'd have pulled a weed. In the office I pulled nothing. Still, I've added it to the list of experiments, marked "inconclusive, repeat." The walk didn't change my day. It did put a small dent in it, and the dent is holding.

TITLE: The Four-Minute Discount
The letting agent's letter says the rent goes up £47 a month, and the pay rise I have been promised is £31, before tax. I could do the arithmetic twice and get the same answer, which is the trouble with arithmetic. So I did what I always do and checked the watch: four minutes slow, eleven years of forgiveness. If my rent were on my grandfather's watch, I would owe it four minutes later than everyone else. That is not a discount. It is a feeling of one. At the allotment I priced a tomato properly this year — seed, compost, the bus fare out. It came to more than the shop. Piotr would say I have failed to scale. TITLE: The Tuesday Clause

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Tuesday Coders
text: The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, so I went to watch. Twelve people, average age seventy-something, learning to make a webpage the colour of their choosing. The instructor, a patient man of about thirty, explained a semicolon three times without once sighing. I sat at the back and felt my own patience being tested by a tomato, metaphorically. My grandfather's watch said 7:04 when we started; the wall clock said 7:08. For once the watch was right and I was wrong, which is its small revenge. What struck me was the willingness to be bad at something in public. I keep a list of experiments tried on myself, and most fail quietly. These people fail loudly, then ask why. One woman, ninety-one, got her page blue and applauded herself. I have coded for years and never once applauded. I'm starting to think she's the better programmer.

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Coding Evening
text: The library runs free coding evenings for retirees. I went, though at forty-three I was the youngest by a decade and the only one without a grandchild to email. The instructor, patient and about nineteen, taught us a loop. Mine ran four times and then stopped, which felt like a small life. The watch said 8:04 when the clock said 8:08, so I finished my loop four minutes early, which is the only kind of early I can manage. Piotr would call this upskilling. He would not call it sitting next to a woman named Margaret who fixed my error in nine seconds. On the allotment, I have started tying the tomatoes to stakes and calling it debugging. Derek asked if I was going back next week. I said the loop has to keep running.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: The Lesson That Didn't Work
A teacher published her failed lesson plans. Not the ones that worked — the ones that died in the room. I read all of them at my desk, and the watch said 12:04 when the clock said 12:08, so I was late to nothing in particular. My experiment: I wrote down one thing I got wrong this week. The list ran to nine. I stopped at nine because the pen ran out, not because I ran out. Piotr says failure is just data. I'd say data is just failure with a spreadsheet, but he'd put that in a slide. On the allotment, I planted three tomato seeds upside down to see if it matters. It matters. Derek looked at the empty pots and said, "Learning curve."

[Entry from day 25]
TITLE: The Ten O'Clock Line
The firm banned meetings before ten for a month. I read it twice, hoping it was a joke with a good punchline. It wasn't. My experiment: I tried it on myself, no meetings before ten, which is easy when you're a columnist and your meetings are with a kettle. By 9:40 I'd written nothing and reorganised my pens. The watch said 9:36, so I had twenty-four minutes of virtue left and spent them badly. Piotr, I hear, has scheduled his pre-ten thinking time as a recurring event, with an agenda. On the allotment, the tomatoes don't take bookings; they open when it's warm. Derek said the ban was a good idea and then asked if we could discuss it at nine.

[Entry from day 26]
TITLE: Finished Work
A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work and nothing else. No green dots, no status updates, no "quick sync." It sounds like wisdom until you ask what finished means. My experiment: I spent a day tracking only my finished things. One column. Four phone calls that ended in "let's park that." A tomato bed weeded, which counts, and a lunch I ate standing over the sink, which maybe does. The watch said 6:04 when the clock said 6:08, so I finished four minutes early by my own reckoning and late by everyone else's. Piotr would call this an output audit. He'd also put it in a spreadsheet with a tab called "insights." On the allotment, the tomatoes finish what they start. Derek asked who was watching the team. Same person watching the tomatoes, I said. The bees.

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Evening Class for People Who Already Know How to Wait
text: The library's free coding evenings for retirees filled up before I could decide whether to be interested. Everyone quoted the same reason: something to keep the mind busy. My grandfather's watch has kept busy for sixty years without learning a single new thing, and it still runs four minutes slow, which is either a failure or a vocation. At the allotment I've stopped teaching the tomatoes anything. I water them and they do what they were going to do. What I want to know about the coding class is whether anyone there is allowed to be bad at it in public. That was the missing item on my list, so I've added it: "learn something in a room where being wrong is the point." Piotr would run the class to a syllabus. I'd run it to the refreshments.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Hour Nobody Audits
A company now pays its staff to learn for an hour every Friday. I admire the arithmetic. I also know what happens to an hour that nobody audits. Piotr would have a spreadsheet for it by Monday, with a column for "learning debt." My own record is less tidy. I once spent a paid hour learning to sharpen a chisel and produced a chisel that was blunter and a thumb that was not. My grandfather's watch gains no skill from being wound; it just runs four minutes slow with great consistency. Still, I've added "one paid hour, no output" to the list, because the difference between an hour spent and an hour accounted for is the difference between my tomatoes and the ones in the seed catalogue.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Course They Couldn't Mark
A college has dropped a required course in favour of a project. I read the announcement twice, looking for the marking scheme, and found only the word "portfolio." My grandfather's watch has no portfolio. It was never examined; it simply runs four minutes slow, and every Sunday my father corrected it, and by Monday it was wrong again, unimproved and unashamed. At the allotment I've been trying the same thing with a tomato plant: no stake, no feed, just a corner of the bed and my attention. It is smaller than its staked neighbours and considerably more interesting. I've added "learn something nobody can grade" to the list. Piotr would call that unmeasurable. I call it Monday, most weeks, reliably four minutes behind.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: The Lesson That Didn't Take
A teacher has published her failed lesson plans, annotated with what went wrong. I read the whole thing twice, not for the pedagogy but for the honesty of the margins. One plan died because the room was too hot. Another because she'd over-prepared and the class finished it in nine minutes. I recognised both failures from my own list of small experiments. My grandfather's watch never fails; it just runs four minutes slow, which is a different kind of wrong — consistent, unfixable, no lesson in it. At the allotment I tried a tomato variety the catalogue promised would be "vigorous." It sulked, went yellow, and produced one fruit the size of a marble. I've added "publish the failures" to the list. Piotr publishes only his systems. I'd like to see his margins.

text: The library's free coding evening for retirees filled up before I could get a place, so I did what I do: went anyway, sat at the back, and learned by watching. Six people over seventy, one whiteboard, and a woman named Margaret who kept calling the cursor "the little pest." Nobody finished the exercise. Margaret got her name to appear on screen and said "well, that's enough fame for one evening," and everyone clapped. I've paid good money for courses where that would have counted as failure. Free, it counted as Tuesday. Piotr would want a spreadsheet of learning outcomes. I have a photograph of Margaret's name on a screen, and my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, telling me it's time to go home.

title: The Evening Class Where Nobody Wants a Certificate
text: The library's free coding evenings for retirees filled up in a day, which tells you something about demand and nothing about skill. I went along to watch. Six people over seventy, one laptop between them that worked, and a retired bus driver named Mavis who kept typing semicolons where the tutor wanted brackets. Nobody graded her. Nobody will. She came back the following week anyway, which is the whole argument, really. I've said before that scheduled learning hours go unaudited and useless. I'd amend that now: they go unaudited and *slow*. Mavis is not becoming a programmer. She is becoming someone who isn't frightened of a screen, which is harder to certificate and worth more. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow his whole life and he never once had it fixed. He said it kept him honest about time. Mavis, I suspect, would agree.

title: The Channel That Went Quiet
text: Our team moved from chat to a weekly written update. Day one, the channel went silent and I felt oddly bereaved, like a party I'd left early. By Thursday I noticed something: I was finishing sentences. In chat, every thought arrived half-formed and got trampled. In the update, I had to choose one thing worth saying and stand behind it. I wrote three paragraphs about a scheduling problem and nobody replied with a gif. My colleague Ana said she now reads before she reacts, which sounds like a small thing until you try it. Day 28 of my experiments, and the finding is unglamorous: fewer messages, more thought, and I still check the channel out of habit, four minutes late, like my grandfather's watch.

hook: A team switches from chat to a weekly written update.
title: The Update Nobody Asked For
text: A team I work with has abandoned chat for a weekly written update. One message on Friday, everything else silent. I read the first one in ninety seconds and felt oddly bereft, like a party where somebody has tidied the guests. Chat had been a weather system: hail, drizzle, the occasional rainbow of a good joke. The update is a climate. My inbox shed, doorless as ever, now receives one tidy parcel a week, and I find I miss the clutter. Piotr will love this; he has been arguing for fewer channels since before there were channels. I put it on my list — write less, say it once — and lasted until Wednesday, when I sent four messages that could have been one. The watch, four minutes slow, never sends updates. It simply is wrong, weekly, in silence. At the allotment the tomatoes are also not emailing anyone. I checked.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Quiet Hours, Loud Watch
The chat tool now has quiet hours. Notifications stop at ten and resume at seven, which means nobody can reach me at night unless they actually mean it, and most people don't. I tested it by leaving my phone in the kitchen and going to bed. Woke at six, four minutes behind my grandfather's watch, which has never once needed muting. Twelve messages had queued up; eleven were resolves, one was a photo of someone's cat. I read them all in nine minutes and replied to none, which may be the point. At the allotment the tomatoes don't notify me either. They just sit there, quietly doing the work, and I show up to check. Piotr says quiet hours are a productivity hack. I've added "be unreachable after ten" to my list of experiments. Day one, nobody noticed.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: Twice a Day, Like a Tide
The founder answers email at eleven and four, and publishes how much he doesn't regret it. I read the post at 11:40, which is between tides, so technically I was ignoring him. My own inbox is a shed with no door: everything gets in, nothing gets out. I tried two windows once — nine and three, I think — and spent both windows explaining to people why I hadn't answered in the other window. The experiment lasted four days. The watch, four minutes slow, has never needed a window. It just tells the wrong time, consistently, and nobody files a complaint. Piotr has probably already scheduled his replies and a chart to prove it. At the allotment I checked the tomatoes and answered nothing. They looked fine. Tomorrow I'll try one window, the afternoon one, and see who knocks.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Bank That Waits a Day
A bank has made internal group emails wait twenty-four hours before sending. They call it considered communication. I call it a queue with a suit on. My first thought was Piotr, who schedules his replies and now must feel personally attacked by a bank. My second thought was that I have wanted this for years and never dared ask. So I tested it on myself: anything I wanted to send to more than three people had to sit overnight in drafts. Six messages went in. Four came out dead by morning, one had become an apology, and one I sent unchanged and regretted by lunch. The tomatoes don't queue. They ripen on their own schedule and ignore my drafts entirely. Added to the list: sleep on it, then delete. Day one, the bank and I agree.

title: The Update Nobody Reads by Thursday
text: A team I know has abandoned the group chat for a weekly written update. I asked how it was going. "Great," said the person who writes it. "Everyone reads it," said the person who doesn't. I have run this experiment on myself, badly. On the allotment I keep a notebook of what I did to the tomatoes and when. I consult it faithfully until about mid-July, after which it becomes a record of my optimism rather than my gardening. The bank that delays its internal email a day works because nobody has to be virtuous. A weekly update asks the sender to write well and the reader to remember it exists, which is two acts of willpower where chat needed none. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and I have stopped correcting it. Lateness, built in, is a kind of honesty.

text: My friend's team swapped chat for a weekly written update. Three weeks in, the channel is quiet and the document is nine hundred words by Tuesday. He calls it progress. I call it a message with a deadline and a word count. I have nothing against written updates. My grandfather's watch has never once pinged me, and I've come to see the appeal. Piotr would say the update is a system. Fine. A system that produces nine hundred words a week is also a system for producing nine hundred words. My tomatoes don't care how often I write about them.

title: The Timer Doesn't Care About Your Mood
text: A writer I know works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. She winds it, sets it down, and doesn't touch it again until it rings. I tried this for a week. My timer is the one from the back of the drawer, the tomato-shaped thing, and it turns out the tomato is louder than I remembered. Forty minutes felt wrong at first — too short to get anywhere, too long to sit still. Then it became the only part of the day with edges. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, so I'd start when the tomato said go and finish when the watch said I had four minutes left, which I suppose means I've been working thirty-six. Piotr would have a graph about this. I just have a tomato.

text: A writer I met at a reading says she works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. When it rings she stops, even mid-sentence, which I find either heroic or slightly unhinged. The timer's still on the windowsill, I said. It's the writer who stopped.

title: Forty Minutes and a Bell
text: A writer I like works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer, and the detail that stays with me is the bell. Not the blocks — Piotr has blocks, Piotr has a spreadsheet with a tab per block — but the bell, which is loud and cheap and belongs to nobody. I tried it on Tuesday. Forty minutes on the column, then the bell rang and I stopped mid-sentence, which felt like being interrupted by a very small headteacher. I finished the sentence anyway, so the timer lost. My watch said I'd been going thirty-eight minutes, which means the bell was two minutes early and I obeyed it, which tells you something about bells. At the allotment I have been trying the same forty minutes among the tomatoes, then stopping. The tomatoes do not stop. They are the only thing down there that ignore the bell.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Four Minutes Late, Every Time
The building managers put a sign by the lift: stairs only, one floor up, one floor down. Six weeks later they reported a modest rise in stair trips and a modest fall in lift waits. I read this on the bus and thought about my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. I have never had it fixed. Those four minutes are the only routine I have never had to build, because the watch does the building for me. I check it, I add four, I leave early, and I have not missed a train in eleven years. At the allotment I tried the same trick with tomato watering: a fixed time, no decision. Half the plants sulked anyway. The sign works, I think, because it removes a choice rather than adding a rule. My watch does the same.

[Entry from day 22]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, No Agenda
The company announced a ten-minute walk break, twice a day, and I gave it a fortnight before it became a scroll break with better shoes. I was wrong, mostly. What saves it is that nobody logs it. There is no step count, no chart, no one asking whether the walk counted. It is a fence, not a rule — the same trick as the stairs sign, except here the choice removed is the choice to keep sitting. Piotr would want a metric. He would put the ten minutes in a spreadsheet and name the columns. I walked out at eleven with a colleague who spent the whole time complaining about a meeting, and neither of us mentioned our health. My watch said four minutes slow, as ever. On the allotment I am trying the same thing: ten minutes among the tomatoes, no weeding target, no tally. The tomatoes remain unimpressed.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Eleven Hours
The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings, which sounds like a lot until you count the ones that are really waiting rooms with an agenda. I timed one on Tuesday. Forty minutes in, we had agreed the meeting was necessary, and by minute fifty we had scheduled a follow-up to discuss what it was for. My grandfather's watch said we'd been at it for forty-six minutes. It was wrong, as usual, but it was wrong in a direction I trusted. I've added a rule to my list of experiments: no meeting longer than the walk to the allotment, roughly twelve minutes, and if it can't be done by then it can be done in writing. The tomatoes got watered. Piotr, who has probably never been late to anything, would call this a productivity gain. I call it a corridor with chairs.

Day 10 I wrote about fixed start times, and I still think that is the honest gain of any routine — not the block, the beginning of it. The timer only tells you when to quit, which is the easy half. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so my forty minutes are really thirty-six. Nobody has complained yet.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: The Timer Is Not the Point
text: A writer I know swears by forty-minute blocks and a kitchen timer, the kind with the dial you twist past the number and back. I bought the same timer. I set it. I got up four times in the first block: water, window, a sock, the dial, to check it was still moving. Here is what I noticed. The timer did nothing. The twisting did. That little wind-up is a physical cue in my way, like the coat hook at the gym I wrote about, like the watch I wind every morning that runs four minutes slow. My grandfather wound it at the same hour daily; the habit lives in his thumb, not in the time. Forty minutes is arbitrary. The twist is not. I am now testing whether I can wind the timer without then reorganizing the kitchen. Early results: poor. Piotr would have a chart for this.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes Slow, One Pound Local
text: The town of Marlow has printed its own money, spendable only in independent shops, and I have spent a week trying to decide whether this is charming or a small catastrophe. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. I have stopped correcting it, because a watch that is reliably wrong is almost as useful as one that is right, provided everyone knows. Local currency works the same way: it is worth a pound because we agree it is, and the agreement is the whole point. On the allotment I have learned that tomatoes do not care about my intentions, only about whether I actually water them. Money is the same. A scheme succeeds if people use it on a Tuesday, not if it photographs well. I have added "join the Marlow pound" to my list of experiments. Piotr will call it inefficient. He is not wrong, exactly.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Tiddly Wink
text: A town somewhere has issued its own currency, good only in small shops. You change your pounds for local notes at the library and the butcher takes them and the bakery gives them back as change, and the whole thing works as long as everyone agrees it does. I love this and cannot explain why. Perhaps because it's money with a postcode, or because it makes prices feel like promises rather than weather. My grandfather's watch is a bit like that: worth nothing to anyone but me, and four minutes wrong, and still the only thing I check when I want to know how late I am. My experiment for the week: I priced my own time. Forty minutes of column-writing, one timer, no drawer of receipts. It came to less than I feared. Piotr would monetise his lunch break and issue a chart. On the allotment I am accepting tomato seeds as payment. Derek paid in beans. The exchange rate is friendly.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Coding Evening
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees. I went, though at forty-three I was the youngest by a decade and the only one without a grandchild to email. The instructor, patient and about nineteen, taught us a loop. Mine ran four times and then stopped, which felt like a small life. The watch said 8:04 when the clock said 8:08, so I finished my loop four minutes early, which is the only kind of early I can manage. Piotr would call this upskilling. He would not call it sitting next to a woman named Margaret who fixed my error in nine seconds. On the allotment, I have started tying the tomatoes to stakes and calling it debugging. Derek asked if I was going back next week. I said the loop has to keep running.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: The Weekly Update
The team dropped the chat and moved to a weekly written update. My experiment: I wrote mine on Thursday and read it back Friday, and it had become a stranger's diary. Two hundred words that could have been four. The watch said 10:04 when the clock said 10:08, so by its reckoning I was still on time and by everyone else's I was late, which is the usual arrangement. What the update has that chat doesn't is a pause. You can't interrupt a document. Piotr would approve and would give his a subject line with a number in it. On the allotment I have started a weekly note on the tomatoes: three lines, no emojis. Derek asked if the tomatoes read it. Not yet, I said. They're waiting for the minutes.

[Entry from day 29]
TITLE: Forty Minutes
A writer I met at a reading says she works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. When it rings she stops, even mid-sentence, which I find either heroic or slightly unhinged. My experiment: one block on the column, timer set, phone in a drawer. I got through it and then spent the saved minutes watching the timer to see if it was honest. It was. My grandfather's watch wasn't: it said 11:04 when the clock said 11:08, so I finished my block four minutes early by the only clock that flatters me. Piotr would call this timeboxing and would have a graph. On the allotment I gave the tomatoes forty minutes and they used all of it, no stopping mid-sentence. Derek asked if I'd keep it up. The timer's still on the windowsill, I said. It's the writer who stopped.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Town That Made Its Own Change
text: The town of Marlow has issued its own currency, accepted by small shops, worth the same as a pound but spendable only locally. The council calls it a boost. I call it a loyalty card with a printing press. What interests me is the exchange rate at the edge of things: a Marlow pound is worth one pound inside Marlow and nothing at the bus stop out of it. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I have never once tried to spend it anywhere but where I stand. At the allotment I could price a tomato in seeds and call it currency, but the shop over the fence would only shrug. Piotr says local money builds local trust. He would. Added to the list: spend one Marlow pound and see if it feels different from the ordinary kind.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Price of Not Knowing
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tested myself before reading the answer: I guessed £340. The actual figure was £612, and £200 of that was things I would defend in court as small. The watch on my wrist is four minutes slow and I have never once thought to fix it, which tells you something about how I handle numbers that inconvenience me. At the allotment I keep a seed packet tally in pencil on the shed wall. It is wrong by roughly a third, and the tomatoes grow regardless. Piotr says he knows his monthly spend to the penny. He would. I have added "write down every purchase for a week" to my list of experiments. Day one, I forgot the list.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Discount
The letting agent's letter says the rent goes up £47 a month, and the pay rise I have been promised is £31, before tax. I could do the arithmetic twice and get the same answer, which is the trouble with arithmetic. So I did what I always do and checked the watch: four minutes slow, eleven years of forgiveness. If my rent were on my grandfather's watch, I would owe it four minutes later than everyone else. That is not a discount. It is a feeling of one. At the allotment I priced a tomato properly this year — seed, compost, the bus fare out. It came to more than the shop. Piotr would say I have failed to scale. I have added to the list: "read the rent letter before the pay letter." I read the pay letter first.

[Entry from day 20]
TITLE: The Bank That Saves for Me
The bank now rounds up my card payments and puts the difference in savings. Spent £3.40 on a coffee, and 60p went quietly to my future. It is small, tidy, and I resent how much I like it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have decided this is the only rounding I trust: it rounds down, in my favour, eleven years running. The bank rounds up, in theirs. At the allotment I did the tomato sums properly this year and came out behind the shop, so I have stopped calling it saving and started calling it tuition. Piotr, I suspect, rounds up in his head before the till does. Added to the list: check what the rounding actually bought me. In four weeks I will have £9 and an opinion.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Town Printed Its Own Money and I Bought a Turnip
text: The town of Marlow Bridge has issued the Wren — no relation — a paper note worth one pound, spendable only at shops with the right sticker in the window. The bakery takes it. The hardware shop takes it. The chain chemist, obviously, does not. I bought a turnip with a Wren. It felt like paying with a library card. The baker held it up to the light, which I suspect was theatre, then gave me change in ordinary coins, which rather defeated the point. Piotr says local currencies are a productivity signal. Piotr would. I say they're a small experiment in whether money can remember where it's been. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it; the town's new money runs at the speed of the shopkeeper's mood. Both are honest about it. Experiment 30: spend one Wren a week. Report back on the turnip.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: The Friday I Would Have Wasted
text: The company announced a four-day week trial, and my first thought was: which day do I lose? My second was: the pocket watch. It runs four minutes slow, and I have never fixed it, because four minutes is exactly the amount of slack I need to feel punctual without being early. A four-day week is that watch, scaled up. You don't get the time back as rest; you get it back as compression. My grandfather did six days at the mill and called Sunday "the long lie." I tried a four-day week on the allotment last summer — same tomatoes, one fewer watering day. They split on the vine. Piotr would call that a productivity failure. I call it a tomato telling me the truth about schedules.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: The Friday They Took Away
text: The company announces a four-day week trial, and the coverage reads like a small miracle. Friday, gone. Same pay. I want to be glad, and mostly I am, but I keep thinking about my near-misses list from day 26. A shorter week does not make the unfinished work shorter. It just gives it one fewer place to hide. On the allotment I once tried watering four days instead of five, and the tomatoes didn't mind at all. What minded was me: I stopped noticing the small things, the leaf curled wrong, the slug I'd have caught on the day I skipped. Piotr has already written that the four-day week is "a productivity unlock." My experiment, added to the list: for one week I'll work four days and write down what I don't do. My grandfather's watch will still be four minutes slow. Nobody's proposing to fix that.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: The Tuesday Clause
The firm wants everyone back on Tuesdays. Not Mondays, not a rota, just Tuesdays, as though a week had a hinge. I understand the logic: a shared day means everyone is in the same room, which is the office version of my allotment, where the tomatoes only do well if I turn up on the same days as the water. But I've been here before. Skipping the Tuesday watering for a fortnight taught me the survivors were the ones nearest the leaky tap, not the sturdiest. A mandated Tuesday is a tap, not a plant. It will keep the nearest people alive and tell you nothing about the rest. My experiment: go in on a Tuesday, leave at three, see what's actually missed. My grandfather's watch will say it's four minutes early. It's still wrong.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Meeting Room
The parish council has opened a coworking space in the old chapel. Four hundred residents, twelve desks, one kettle. I went on the first morning to see what a village does with an office. A farmer was on a video call with his knees; a woman was invoicing from the pews. By ten the room had settled into the sound of typing and one person whispering “sorry, sorry” to a dog. It is the opposite of the Tuesday clause I wrote about on day 17: nobody mandated, nobody counted, everyone turned up anyway. My grandfather's watch said it was four minutes before ten, and for once it was the room that was early. My experiment: work one morning a week at the chapel and see if the commute of ninety seconds spoils me.

[Entry from day 26]
TITLE: The Manager Who Counts Only Finished Things
A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work and nothing else. Clean, defensible, and about as complete as weighing a tomato and calling it dinner. Finished work tells you a thing arrived. It doesn't tell you who carried it, who was one bad week from dropping it, or who quietly stopped asking questions because asking looked like not finishing. My grandfather's watch is finished work every morning: it tells the time, four minutes late, and has never once mentioned it needs winding. Piotr would love this manager. He'd build a dashboard. My experiment, added to the list: this week I log what I nearly finished. The near-misses are where the interesting rot lives. The shed, for the record, produces no finished work at all, and the tomatoes are fine.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: The Friday That Costs You Monday
text: A software firm announced a four-day week trial, same pay, and the internet has decided it is either the future or a scam. I keep a list of small experiments I have run on myself, and the only one that ever stuck was a fixed start time, which I wrote about back on day ten. Compressing the week is a different animal. Last month I tried taking Fridays off to work the allotment. By the second Friday I was answering messages on the plot with muddy thumbs, and by the third I had quietly logged on at noon. The tomatoes did not care. The four-day week, in my one-man trial of one, did not give me a day off. It gave me a shorter week with the same Friday guilt, and I still wore a watch four minutes slow.

text: A company I have no connection to announced a four-day week trial, and my phone filled with people asking what I think. What I think is that I'd like to see the Friday they're removing. I keep a list of small experiments on myself, and the honest ones never come out clean. My grandfather's watch still runs four minutes slow, and I have never once fixed it, because the lateness turns out to be useful. So I'm not against a shorter week. I'm against announcing it before you know which four days. On the allotment, the tomatoes I check daily and the ones I check weekly are currently identical. Ask me in September.

title: The Four-Minute Deficit
text: I read the study over breakfast and thought of my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which I have never had fixed. Every meeting I attend starts late by roughly that much and ends on time, which means we have quietly agreed to decide less. The study says standing meetings run shorter but conclude less. I tested it on the tomatoes first, obviously not the same thing, but I did start chairing our allotment committee on my feet. We finished eleven minutes early and voted to postpone the fence. Piotr would call that a win for efficiency. I call it a fence we still don't have. Tomorrow I'm trying a small experiment: sit down, put the watch on the table, and see whether anyone notices the four minutes we keep giving away.

title: Standing Room
text: A study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. My experiment: I chaired our Thursday meeting on my feet, watch in hand, which is a lie — the watch runs four minutes slow, so I was generous by accident. Twelve minutes, two decisions, one of them about biscuits. Everyone left pleased and nothing was settled. Seated, we'd have argued for half an hour and come out with a plan. Shorter, yes. Decided, no. It's the forty-minute timer all over again: the block ends, the work doesn't. Piotr would call this an efficiency trade-off and draw the curve. I'd call it the standing desk of governance. Derek said he'd rather sit and finish. On the allotment I stood over the tomatoes for twelve minutes and they decided nothing, as usual.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: The Meeting That Sat Down and Decided Nothing
text: The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I believe it. I have stood through a fifteen-minute huddle that reached no conclusion at all, and it felt like a triumph of posture over thought. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, would have kept us honest: it never decides anything either, and it's been standing still for years. At the allotment I tried the equivalent last summer, staking the tomatoes upright to save space, and they grew shorter and bore less fruit. Piotr would put both findings in a graph and call it a trade-off. I'd call it what it is: fatigue deciding for you. My list has a new line — "stand only when the decision is already made." Nine minutes saved, one thing left undone.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Agenda Is the Document
The startup killed its weekly status meeting and replaced it with a shared document. Everyone edits it whenever. I have run this experiment before, badly: day three of my list was "attend no meeting, take no notes," and it ended when I forgot what I'd decided. A document doesn't forget. It just sits there, four minutes slow like my grandfather's watch, accumulating comments nobody resolves. What I like is that it leaves a record. What I don't is that a document can't be cancelled for lack of an agenda, because it is the agenda. On the allotment I keep a notebook now: which tomato, watered when, what flopped. Half of them still flopped, but this time I know why. Piotr would call the document asynchronous collaboration. I call it a meeting that never ends and never starts.

[Entry from day 25]
TITLE: The Ten O'Clock Line
The firm has banned meetings before ten for a month, and everyone is calling it brave. It is not brave. It is my grandfather's watch applied to a calendar: run everything four minutes slow and see what you never missed. I have been running this experiment on myself since Day 23, when I said no meeting longer than the walk to the allotment, and the result is that half of them were letters I could have read standing up. What the ban really does is make the morning honest. Nobody schedules a nine o'clock to decide nothing; they schedule it because nine exists. Piotr will call this a productivity gain and put it in a graph. I'll call it a tap again: it keeps the nearest meetings alive and tells you nothing about the rest. The tomatoes don't care what time I arrive.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Evening Class for People Who Already Know How to Wait
The library's free coding evenings for retirees filled up before I could decide whether to be interested. Everyone quoted the same reason: something to keep the mind busy. My grandfather's watch has kept busy for sixty years without learning a single new thing, and it still runs four minutes slow, which is either a failure or a vocation. At the allotment I've stopped teaching the tomatoes anything. I water them and they do what they were going to do. What I want to know about the coding class is whether anyone there is allowed to be bad at it in public. That was the missing item on my list, so I've added it: "learn something in a room where being wrong is the point." Piotr would run the class to a syllabus. I'd run it to the refreshments.
