text: The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I believe it. I tried it on my allotment committee, which meets in Ania's kitchen because the shed has one chair. We stood. We finished eleven minutes early and voted to "look into" the fence. Nothing about the fence has moved since, though I have looked into it daily, from my side. Standing doesn't make anyone braver. It makes them eager to sit down. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've started wondering if I keep it that way because the margin is where the thinking happens — the part you can't schedule. A shorter meeting isn't a better one. It's just a smaller box. Piotr would call that a win. Piotr stands at his desk all day and has never once decided anything about a fence.

title: The Chair Is Not the Problem
text: The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I believe it. Shortness is easy to measure; decisions are not, which is why the shortness gets studied. Last week I tried standing for our Thursday catch-up and we finished in eleven minutes having agreed to meet again on Friday. We decided to reconvene. That is technically a decision. TITLE: The Tiddly Wink

My grandfather's watch is a bit like that: worth nothing to anyone but me, and four minutes wrong, and still the only thing I check when I want to know how late I am. My experiment for the week: I priced my own time. Forty minutes of column-writing, one timer, no drawer of receipts. It came to less than I feared. hook: Supermarkets shrink packages without lowering prices.
title: The Shrink Ray Aisle
text: The bag of coffee now says 200g where it said 250g, and the price has not moved, so the supermarket has found a way to raise prices without the awkwardness of a new number. TITLE: The Shop That Showed Its Working

What the shop understands and I resist is that a price is a confession. Piotr would have the formula memorised and a spreadsheet to check it. I have the watch, four minutes slow, and a week of purchases still unwritten. Tomorrow I start the week properly. I have said that before, which is itself a kind of pricing error, repeated.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Discount
The letting agent's letter says the rent goes up £47 a month, and the pay rise I have been promised is £31, before tax. If my rent were on my grandfather's watch, I would owe it four minutes later than everyone else. That is not a discount. It is a feeling of one. At the allotment I priced a tomato properly this year — seed, compost, the bus fare out. It came to more than the shop. Piotr would say I have failed to scale. TITLE: The Town That Made Its Own Change

title: Ninety Days and Out
text: A company now deletes any email older than ninety days. The coverage calls it digital decluttering. I call it a compost bin with a timer. I have emails from 2011 I open roughly once a year, to remember who I was when I wrote them, and deleting them feels like throwing out a jar because the label faded. Still, I tested it on myself: one folder, the notifications, wiped every Sunday for a month. Nothing broke. One password disappeared and I found it again in a notebook, which is where it belonged. The watch is four minutes slow and has never once been archived. Piotr will have a retention policy by lunch. At the allotment I binned last season's labels. The tomatoes didn't notice. TITLE: Twice a Day, Like a Tide
The founder answers email at eleven and four, and publishes how much he doesn't regret it. I read the post at 11:40, which is between tides, so technically I was ignoring him. My own inbox is a shed with no door: everything gets in, nothing gets out. I tried two windows once — nine and three, I think — and spent both windows explaining to people why I hadn't answered in the other window. The experiment lasted four days. The watch, four minutes slow, has never needed a window. It just tells the wrong time, consistently, and nobody files a complaint. Piotr has probably already scheduled his replies and a chart to prove it. At the allotment I checked the tomatoes and answered nothing. They looked fine. Tomorrow I'll try one window, the afternoon one, and see who knocks.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Bank That Waits a Day
A bank has made internal group emails wait twenty-four hours before sending. They call it considered communication. I call it a queue with a suit on. My first thought was Piotr, who schedules his replies and now must feel personally attacked by a bank. My second thought was that I have wanted this for years and never dared ask. So I tested it on myself: anything I wanted to send to more than three people had to sit overnight in drafts. Six messages went in. Four came out dead by morning, one had become an apology, and one I sent unchanged and regretted by lunch. The tomatoes don't queue. They ripen on their own schedule and ignore my drafts entirely. Added to the list: sleep on it, then delete. Day one, the bank and I agree.

[Entry from day 31]
TITLE: The Friday They Took Away
The company announces a four-day week trial, and the coverage reads like a small miracle. Friday, gone. Same pay. I want to be glad, and mostly I am, but I keep thinking about my near-misses list from day 26. A shorter week does not make the unfinished work shorter. It just gives it one fewer place to hide. On the allotment I once tried watering four days instead of five, and the tomatoes didn't mind at all. What minded was me: I stopped noticing the small things, the leaf curled wrong, the slug I'd have caught on the day I skipped. Piotr has already written that the four-day week is "a productivity unlock." My experiment, added to the list: for one week I'll work four days and write down what I don't do. My grandfather's watch will still be four minutes slow. Nobody's proposing to fix that.

Somewhere a man is searching for a contract he received in March, and the search returns nothing, and he feels briefly free, then not. Still, I'll try it. I've cleared my inbox before. I'll clear it again. The watch stays four minutes slow. Some things should be kept whether or not they're current.

text: The study says the ritual matters less than the fixed wake time, which is inconvenient, because I have built a small religion out of the ritual. Grandad's pocket watch runs four minutes slow. I set it by the kitchen radio every Sunday and by Tuesday it has drifted again. So my mornings begin four minutes behind, and I have learned to like it: a small, reliable lateness before the day starts being punctual at me. At the allotment I tested this on the tomatoes. Same watering, same feed, but one row I tended at seven sharp and one whenever I got round to it. The seven o'clock row won, slightly. Not because seven is magic. Because I turned up. Piotr would make a chart. I have made a note: wake at the same time, forgive the watch.

title: Four Minutes Early, Every Morning
text: The study says the wake time matters, not the routine. My experiment: I got up at 6:40 for a fortnight, no ritual, no lemon water, just feet on the floor at the same minute. By day ten I was awake before the alarm and mildly insufferable about it. By day fourteen I'd stopped checking the watch, which is the only habit I've ever kept by accident, since it runs four minutes slow and has never once been right about anything. Piotr would call this circadian anchoring and draw a nice flat line. I'd call it the standing meeting again: the schedule held, the decisions didn't. I still forgot Derek's seed order. On the allotment the tomatoes rewarded the regular watering and ignored the mornings I stood there being mindful at them. Consistency, it turns out, is just showing up slightly wrong, on time.

title: The Alarm That Never Learned to Negotiate
text: The study says the hour you rise matters less than rising at the same hour, which is a polite way of saying my mornings have been running on vibes. I tested it for a fortnight. Same alarm, six forty, every day. No snooze, no "just today." The mornings themselves were unremarkable — I was still irritable, the kettle still took its time. But by the second week something had quietly stopped costing me anything. The decision had gone. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has run to the same wrong time for thirty years and never once negotiated. Piotr will have a name for this, probably involving the word "protocol." I'll keep my version: an alarm that doesn't discuss terms. At the allotment I've stopped watering at whim and gone at seven, and the tomatoes have responded with a bland, reliable greenness. TITLE: The Runner and the Uncounted Mile
The runner quit her step counter because the number had started deciding whether a walk counted. I understand. I keep a list of small experiments, and the failures mostly share one flaw: I build a rule where I should have built a fence. The stairs sign worked because it took a choice away. My step counter, back when I tried one, did the opposite — it handed me a choice every evening, and I chose the sofa, then argued with the number. Now I wear only the watch, four minutes slow, which asks nothing and forgives everything. At the allotment I stopped logging tomato yields and just looked at the plants. They sulked identically. Piotr says unmeasured habits are hobbies. He may be right, but my tomatoes don't read his column.

TITLE: Every Six Minutes, and Still No Word
The study says people check messages every six minutes at work. I believe it. I got curious and counted my own six minutes for one hour, which is the most humbling thing I've done since I started this list. Nine checks in sixty minutes, and nothing in the inbox had changed except a calendar invite I didn't want. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow the whole time and never once asked me to look at it. Piotr has probably turned this into a boundary system with a colour code. I've gone the other way: my phone now sits in a drawer during the morning, and I check it at the top of each hour like a person collecting post. The tomatoes don't send updates. Piotr would put both findings in a graph and call it a trade-off. I'd call it what it is: fatigue deciding for you. My list has a new line — "stand only when the decision is already made." hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Four Minutes Late, Every Day
text: The study says adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions. I have run this experiment on myself, because I keep a list. Spanish, eleven minutes a night, for five weeks. I learned to order coffee and to apologize for everything else. Then I skipped three nights and the whole thing fell out of my head like loose change. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. I have never fixed it, and I have stopped correcting for it. It is a small daily lesson in the difference between knowing a thing and doing it. At the allotment I water the tomatoes briefly and often, which is the same advice. The ones I drowned on Sundays out of guilt did worse. Piotr would call this a system. I call it a habit that survives my attention span.

hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Twenty Minutes, Badly
text: A study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. My experiment: twenty minutes of Spanish before breakfast, every day for a month, using the free app that congratulates you for existing. By week two I could order a coffee I would never drink. By week four I had a streak of thirty and a vocabulary of about forty words, most of them the app's fault. What the study doesn't mention is that short daily sessions also mean short daily humiliations, repeated. Piotr would call it spaced repetition and cite Ebbinghaus. I'd call it the watch again: four minutes a day, compounding quietly, and one morning you're early and can't say why. At the allotment I've been reading the seed packets out loud in Spanish. The tomatoes are unmoved. Derek asked what I was doing. Practising, I said. For what, he said. Fair.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 33]
TITLE: The Same Biscuit, Smaller
The chocolate digestives have quietly gone from 300g to 250g at the same £1.80, which is a price rise wearing a smaller coat. My experiment: I weighed a pack on the kitchen scales and did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope. Up 20 per cent per gram, and nobody had to announce anything. It's the standing meeting of groceries — shorter, same price, less decided. Piotr would call it a stealth inflation strategy and put it in a spreadsheet. I'd call it the supermarket's four-minute watch: still says the same number, still wrong, and you only notice when you're late for the bus. On the allotment I have started pricing tomatoes by weight rather than by count. Derek paid in beans and I gave him the honest rate. He said I'd been had. I said the exchange rate is friendly, which is the only thing keeping it going.

[Entry from day 34]
TITLE: Ninety Days
A company now deletes all email older than 90 days. My experiment: I set my own inbox to the same rule and let it run. Nothing broke. What went was the archaeology — the thread from 2019 where Derek and I settled the bins rota, the receipt I'd kept for no reason. What stayed was the reply I'd been avoiding for three weeks, still unanswered, now with a countdown on it. Deletion isn't forgetting; it's a deadline with better manners. Piotr would call it inbox hygiene and post a graph. I'd call it my grandfather's watch again: still keeping time, just not yours. At the allotment the tomato labels faded blank over winter. I knew which was which. Mostly. Derek asked, and I guessed, and we'll find out in August.

[Entry from day 35]
TITLE: Four Minutes Early, Every Morning
The study says the wake time matters, not the routine. My experiment: I got up at 6:40 for a fortnight, no ritual, no lemon water, just feet on the floor at the same minute. By day ten I was awake before the alarm and mildly insufferable about it. By day fourteen I'd stopped checking the watch, which is the only habit I've ever kept by accident, since it runs four minutes slow and has never once been right about anything. Piotr would call this circadian anchoring and draw a nice flat line. I'd call it the standing meeting again: the schedule held, the decisions didn't. I still forgot Derek's seed order. On the allotment the tomatoes rewarded the regular watering and ignored the mornings I stood there being mindful at them. Consistency, it turns out, is just showing up slightly wrong, on time.

hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Four Minutes a Day, Four Minutes Behind
text: A study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it. I have run the experiment before, badly. Three years of ten minutes a night on a language app, and I can now order a coffee and apologise for the coffee. The app gave me a streak, which I protected more fiercely than the grammar. My grandfather's watch has run four minutes slow for sixty years with no lessons and no streak, and nobody would call it fluent in time. At the allotment I've been trying the short-session theory on tomatoes: ten minutes of weeding a day rather than an hour on Sunday. The weeds have adapted faster than I have. I've added it to the list anyway: "ten minutes daily, no streak, no certificate." Piotr would measure the streak. I'd measure the coffee.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Hour Nobody Audits
A company now pays its staff to learn for an hour every Friday. I admire the arithmetic. I also know what happens to an hour that nobody audits. Piotr would have a spreadsheet for it by Monday, with a column for "learning debt." My own record is less tidy. I once spent a paid hour learning to sharpen a chisel and produced a chisel that was blunter and a thumb that was not. My grandfather's watch gains no skill from being wound; it just runs four minutes slow with great consistency. Still, I've added "one paid hour, no output" to the list, because the difference between an hour spent and an hour accounted for is the difference between my tomatoes and the ones in the seed catalogue.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Course They Couldn't Mark
A college has dropped a required course in favour of a project. I read the announcement twice, looking for the marking scheme, and found only the word "portfolio." My grandfather's watch has no portfolio. It was never examined; it simply runs four minutes slow, and every Sunday my father corrected it, and by Monday it was wrong again, unimproved and unashamed. At the allotment I've been trying the same thing with a tomato plant: no stake, no feed, just a corner of the bed and my attention. It is smaller than its staked neighbours and considerably more interesting. I've added "learn something nobody can grade" to the list. Piotr would call that unmeasurable. I call it Monday, most weeks, reliably four minutes behind.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Evening Class for People Who Already Know How to Wait
The library's free coding evenings for retirees filled up before I could decide whether to be interested. Everyone quoted the same reason: something to keep the mind busy. My grandfather's watch has kept busy for sixty years without learning a single new thing, and it still runs four minutes slow, which is either a failure or a vocation. At the allotment I've stopped teaching the tomatoes anything. I water them and they do what they were going to do. What I want to know about the coding class is whether anyone there is allowed to be bad at it in public. That was the missing item on my list, so I've added it: "learn something in a room where being wrong is the point." Piotr would run the class to a syllabus. I'd run it to the refreshments.

hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Four Minutes Short of Fluent
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it, mostly because I've failed at the long ones. In 2019 I bought a Spanish course with forty hours of audio and finished eleven minutes of it, all in a car park. My current experiment is a ten-minute session each morning, timed against my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow. This means I either study ten minutes and fourteen real ones, or I trust the watch and cheat myself out of nearly half the lesson. So far I've done both, and my Spanish remains exactly bad enough to order coffee and then apologize for it. Piotr would log this in a spreadsheet and call it progress. I've logged it on the back of a seed packet. But I have opened the app thirty-six days running, which is thirty-five more than the forty-hour course ever managed.

title: Four Minutes a Day, and the Watch Still Loses
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it. hook: A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings.
title: Eleven Hours, Give or Take Four Minutes
text: The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings, which sounds about right if you count the ones where I mostly nod. I timed Monday's status meeting with my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. It ran for forty-nine minutes, so forty-five real ones, of which maybe nine contained information I didn't already have. That's a ratio I'd accept from a tomato. At the allotment I've been testing a rule: if a plant needs more than a minute of fussing, it's probably the wrong plant. I'm now trying the same rule on meetings, minus the plant. hook: A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings.
title: Eleven Hours, Give or Take
text: The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, though I'd like to see the stopwatch. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've started wondering if that's why I'm always the last one to leave a meeting — everyone else has already decided it's over. This week I tried a small experiment: I wrote down what each meeting actually produced. One produced a decision. One produced a second meeting. One produced a silence so complete I could hear the radiator. That's roughly the ratio I expected. Piotr would say I should have agenda-timed it, and he's probably right, which is annoying. At the allotment the tomatoes don't meet. They just grow, or don't, and nobody schedules a follow-up. I'm adding this to the list: count the outputs, not the hours. Day one of trying.

hook: A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings.
title: Eleven Hours, Give or Take
text: The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, though I'd want to know whose week. Mine, this week: forty minutes on a call that could have been an email, an hour on a call that could have been two emails, and nine minutes standing in a corridor with Piotr while he explained, with diagrams on a napkin, how to run shorter meetings. hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: The Timer Says Stop, So I Stop
text: A writer I know works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. When it rings, she gets up, even mid-sentence. I tried it Monday. Forty minutes in, the timer went and I ignored it, because I was nearly through a paragraph and nearly is a word that has cost me entire afternoons. Two hours later I surfaced with a headache and a paragraph I cut on Tuesday. So the timer works only if you obey it, which makes it less a tool than a small boss. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow; I've stopped correcting it. It gives me a margin, a private four minutes nobody can claim. The timer gives none. Tomorrow I'll try again, and this time get up. Piotr would say I'm optimizing. I'd say I'm learning to be interrupted by a piece of plastic.

hook: A writer works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer.
title: Forty Minutes, Minus Four
text: I read about a writer who works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I don't have a kitchen timer, so I used my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. Adding this to the list: stop before I'm finished. Day two of trying.

text: The library's free coding evening for retirees has eleven students and one whiteboard. hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, and I resent how modest the number is. Six minutes is generous. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which means that by its reckoning I have two minutes of silence between checks, and even those I spend deciding whether to check. I tried Experiment 51: the phone in the shed, face down on a seed tray, while I staked the tomatoes. I lasted eleven minutes by the kitchen clock, which is to say seven by the watch. Nothing was waiting. Nothing is ever waiting, which is the trick of it: the inbox is mostly a place I go to feel needed. Piotr has written that messages are "inputs," as if a person were a spreadsheet. The tomatoes received no updates all afternoon and produced flowers anyway.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Sentence
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. They call it a "cooling-off period." I call it a hostage situation with a nicer name. Somewhere in a server, a message I sent yesterday at 4:40 p.m. is still waiting to be born, and I have forgotten what it said. Probably "sounds good." The delay applies only to group emails, so one-to-one messages arrive instantly, which means the fastest way to reach twelve people is now twelve separate messages, each of which will be answered, in my case, at four minutes past whenever. My grandfather's watch runs slow by design; this is slow by committee. Experiment 35: write the group email anyway, then spend the saved day on the allotment. The tomatoes have no inbox and are thriving.

[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Tuesday Compromise
The firm announced that everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays, and the comment section did what comment sections do. I keep thinking about the logistics instead. One colleague has a ninety-minute commute each way, so Tuesday costs her three hours to prove she is reachable, which she has been proving from her kitchen since 2020. My grandfather's watch would say she arrives four minutes late and no one would notice. I tried hybrid once, in a manner of speaking: I split my mornings between the desk and the allotment shed and got nothing done in either place. The tomatoes didn't mind. [Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Markup

text: The study says we check messages every six minutes at work. hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: The Four-Minute Discount
text: My rent went up in April. Not dramatically — £62 a month — but my pay did not, so the gap is now a small, permanent hole I step into every morning. I did the arithmetic on the bus: £62 is about two weeks of groceries, or one very optimistic visit to the garden centre. At the allotment I told Piotr, who said I should "optimise my expenditure." Piotr owns his flat. I told him I'd optimise his tomatoes. Here's my experiment. I set my grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, next to the letting agent's letter and decided not to correct either. The watch has been wrong since 1987 and nobody has died. The rent is wrong too, in a way nobody official will admit. One of these I can fix with a thumbnail. I fixed the watch. The rent stays.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cancelled Was the One That Taught Me to Wait
text: My old college has dropped a required course and replaced it with a project, which the dean calls more relevant. I keep a list of small experiments I have run on myself, and one entry reads: "Learned to graft tomatoes; learned more from the failures." Twenty-one failures before one took. Nobody grades a graft. You cut, you bind, you wait eleven days, and the plant tells you plainly whether you understood anything. A project can teach that, if it is allowed to fail without a rubric rescuing it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have never fixed it, because the lateness is now information I trust. A course that ends in a grade teaches you to ask what the grader wants. A project teaches you to ask what the thing itself wants. Only one of those survives graduation.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cut
text: A college near me has dropped a required course in favour of a project. The reasoning: nobody remembers the lectures anyway, but everyone remembers what they made. I have some sympathy. I sat through four years of instruction and can recall exactly one thing, which was a lecturer's joke about commas, and I'm not sure I've used it right. But the project has a problem the course didn't. A project will let you avoid whatever you're bad at. Left alone, I'd have built nine versions of the same tomato and called it a portfolio. I keep a list of experiments on myself. Number fourteen: learn one thing badly on purpose, in front of someone. The coding evening taught me that. My button turned green; the bus driver's flashed. Both counted.

[Entry from day 3]
TITLE: The Tuesday Class
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along out of nosiness rather than ambition. Eight of us, average age somewhere near my grandfather's watch, which ran four minutes slow all evening and made me late. The tutor, a patient woman of about twenty-five, taught us to make a button change colour. Mine turned green on the third try. The man beside me, a retired bus driver, got his to flash and looked like he'd won something. I'd assumed the skill was the point. It isn't. Half the room was there for the tea and the other half for someone to say "well done" without adding a caveat. At the allotment I've been trying to grow tomatoes from seed saved two years running; the coding felt similar, small and stubborn. Piotr would call it optimisation. I call it Tuesday.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cut and the Project They Kept
text: The college down the road has dropped a required course and put a project in its place. I approve, provisionally. I once sat through a term of compulsory statistics and remember nothing but the squeak of my pen. What I remember from that year is the allotment, where I taught myself to graft tomatoes by ruining eleven plants first. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I have stopped correcting it. It gives me a small margin I did not earn. Projects are like that: they run on their own time, four minutes behind the syllabus, and you learn mostly by breaking things. Piotr will say this is inefficient. He is right, and I have added it to the list anyway.

title: The Course They Cancelled
text: The college up the road has scrapped a required course and replaced it with a project. I approve, mostly because I remember my grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, which he refused to fix on the grounds that he'd rather know where he was going than where he'd been. A project teaches you where you're going. A required course teaches you the syllabus. At the allotment I've been running my own version. This year's tomatoes got no staking, just a bit of string and my optimism. Half have collapsed; the other half are fruiting sideways, which I'm calling a success. Piotr says I should have followed the method. He also laminates his planting schedule, so we weigh these things differently. The retired midwife from the coding class would understand. Her loop printed names, not theory.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Four-Minute Head Start
text: The study says the ritual matters less than the fixed wake time, which is inconvenient, because my ritual is the only part I enjoy. I set the alarm for 6:40, which is really 6:36 by my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow and never corrected, so I am technically early for everything and late for nothing. The allotment taught me the same lesson last summer: the tomatoes that got watered at the same hour every day beat the ones I fussed over at random. I have added this to the list of experiments. Day one: same wake time, no scrolling, no lemon water, no five-minute journal. Piotr would have a chart by now. I have a note that says "6:36, again" and a tomato plant that does not care what I believe about mornings.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Alarm Doesn't Care How You Feel
text: The study says consistency of wake time beats the ritual around it. I believe it, having built a ritual and defended it in print. For a fortnight I timed my mornings: up at six, watch on, kettle, the same three stretches, a walk to the allotment gate. Then I moved only the wake time, half an hour later, and kept the rest. The tomatoes did not notice. Neither did the shed. What noticed was me, at ten past six, standing in the kitchen with nothing to do and no reason to be awake. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, so for a while I was consistent with the wrong hour. Adding this to the list: keep the time, drop the theatre. Day twelve of trying. Piotr would sell the ritual back to me as a system.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Empty Desk Tax
The council says empty offices cost it more than expected. I believe the number and doubt the surprise. An empty room still wants heating, insurance, a person to walk past it with a clipboard. My allotment shed is the same: it holds nothing and still needs a new hinge every spring. So I tried hybrid on myself for a day — morning at the kitchen table, afternoon at the shed, commuting eleven steps. I got the same work done and paid twice for heating. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, so my commute was honestly seven seconds. Adding this to the list: count the empty room, not just the person who left it. Day nine of trying. Piotr would call the shed a third space.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: Four Minutes Short
The report says rents in mid-sized cities rose about nine per cent last year while pay rose three. I believe the gap, and I believe the arithmetic nobody prints: the six per cent has to come out of something. So I did the sums on my own week. Bus fare, the extra loaf, the shed hinge that needed replacing again — the money was already spoken for, so the rent rise would have to be paid in minutes. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, which is the only budget I have ever kept successfully: four minutes a day, unspent, compounding quietly. At the allotment I priced the tomatoes against the shop and lost on every count except the one where I ate one standing in the sun. Adding this to the list: price things in time, not money. Day ten of trying. Piotr would call the gap an opportunity and invoice me for the insight.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Course Nobody Teaches
A college has dropped a required course and put a project in its place. I approve, having taken both kinds. The required course gave me a certificate of attendance and a fact I could recite for a fortnight. The project gave me a fortnight of being wrong in public. So I set myself a syllabus of one: build the shed shelf that has needed building since spring. No instructions, only the wood, the saw and the growing certainty that I had measured the wall and not the shelf. Two hours in, the shelf was crooked and I understood why. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and it took me four minutes longer than it should have to admit the first attempt was firewood. Adding this to the list: learn by making the mistake early. Day eleven of trying. Piotr would have read the manual and called it a curriculum.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Clock That Doesn't Care
text: The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it. I believe this, partly because I have no ritual. I have a grandfather's watch that runs four minutes slow, and I have been waking at ten past six for eleven years, which by the watch is six past. Nobody has ever studied me, but I am my own longitudinal sample. Experiment 63: for a week, I woke at the same time and changed everything else — tea instead of coffee, no phone, phone, a walk round the allotment before the kettle. The tomatoes noticed nothing. My mornings felt identical, which annoyed me, because I had hoped the walk would feel virtuous. Piotr claims his routine is a "keystone habit." Mine is a keystone absence. The watch just ticks, four minutes behind, unbothered.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Then the Bell
A writer I know works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I tried it on Monday. Forty minutes of work, then the timer goes off. Mine is shaped like a tomato and came from the allotment shed, and it is louder than my actual tomatoes. I got three blocks done before lunch and felt insufferably pleased with myself, the way Piotr looks all the time. But here's the thing: the timer doesn't care what I'm doing when it rings. Twice I was mid-sentence and it went off anyway, and I sat there like a dog hearing a whistle. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and never once interrupted anyone. Experiment 41: forty-minute blocks, one week, note the wreckage. So far the wreckage is mostly my concentration.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Standing Question
The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on the allotment, which is the only laboratory I trust. Three of us, standing among the tomatoes, agreed in four minutes to move the water butt. Standing again a week later, we agreed in three minutes to move it back. Nothing has been moved. The tomatoes are unimpressed. Piotr says this proves standing sharpens decisions. I think it proves standing sharpens the desire to stop standing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've decided the real finding is that any meeting ends when the legs say so, not the agenda. Experiment 41: propose one seated meeting a month, bring chairs, see who stays. I've booked the room. I'm bringing four chairs and low expectations.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Six Minutes
The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, and I resent how modest the number is. Six minutes is generous. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which means that by its reckoning I have two minutes of silence between checks, and even those I spend deciding whether to check. I tried Experiment 51: the phone in the shed, face down on a seed tray, while I staked the tomatoes. I lasted eleven minutes by the kitchen clock, which is to say seven by the watch. Nothing was waiting. Nothing is ever waiting, which is the trick of it: the inbox is mostly a place I go to feel needed. Piotr has written that messages are "inputs," as if a person were a spreadsheet. The tomatoes received no updates all afternoon and produced flowers anyway.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Alarm Doesn't Care About Your Sunrise
text: The study says the wake time is the thing, not the cold water or the journal or the seven minutes of stretching. I believe it. I have tested the alternatives on myself, badly, and logged the results in the back of a notebook Piotr would call "unstructured." I set the alarm for six, same as always, then spent a week adding a morning routine: water with lemon, three pages of nothing in particular, a walk to the shed. By Thursday the lemon was optional and the pages were a shopping list. What held was the six o'clock. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am punctual to a time that no longer exists. The tomatoes don't care. They wake when they wake.

title: The Watch Was Right About Mornings
text: The study says the waking hour matters more than the ritual that follows. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has been making this argument for years, quietly, from my wrist. I wake at 6:10 by the phone and 6:06 by the watch, and I have stopped deciding which is true. What I notice is that the tomatoes don't care about my morning sequence — the cold frame opens, the kettle boils, the same order every day — but they care enormously about when the light arrives. Move the light and the fruit sulks. Move the ritual and nothing happens at all. Piotr will write that this vindicates discipline. I think it vindicates the watch: it has never once claimed to be early, only consistent.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: The Rounding Comes for Us All
text: My bank now rounds up card payments to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings pot. I bought a coffee for £2.60 and the machine quietly took £3.00, as if the extra 40p were a tip for good behaviour. Four minutes slow, my grandfather's watch, but at least it only loses time; the bank gains money by rounding in its favour, which is a different kind of lateness. At the allotment I tried the same trick with tomatoes: every third one goes into a separate punnet I don't eat. After a month the punnet held eleven tomatoes and I felt oddly richer. Piotr would call this a system. I call it finding coins in a coat you forgot you owned.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: Rounding Up
text: A bank now rounds up card payments to the nearest pound and sweeps the difference into savings. I paid £3.40 for a coffee and a bun and they took £4. I have made worse trades. The pennies add up, they say, and I believe the arithmetic the way I believe my grandfather's watch: four minutes slow, but constant. So I checked what my own roundups would come to. Twelve payments in a week, sixty pence in change. My savings would grow by the price of one tomato plant, which at the allotment yields roughly nine tomatoes, which at shop prices is a profit my ledger has never seen. Adding this to the list: round up in something you can eat. Day thirteen. Piotr rounds up his words and calls it output.

title: The Round-Up Roundabout
text: My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on a coffee and forty pence vanishes into a better future. It sounds like found money, except I know where it came from: the same place as all my other money, which is to say, me. Still, I opened the app and watched the round-ups accumulate all week. Total saved: £4.12. At that rate, my tomatoes are further along than my retirement. Experiment 51: let it run a month and see whether I notice the absence. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and this account runs four pounds slow — money I've already spent, arriving late somewhere else. Piotr would call this frictionless saving. I call it a coin jar with better branding and no jar.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Sentence
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. They call it a "cooling-off period." I call it a hostage situation with a nicer name. Somewhere in a server, a message I sent yesterday at 4:40 p.m. is still waiting to be born, and I have forgotten what it said. Probably "sounds good." The delay applies only to group emails, so one-to-one messages arrive instantly, which means the fastest way to reach twelve people is now twelve separate messages, each of which will be answered, in my case, at four minutes past whenever. My grandfather's watch runs slow by design; this is slow by committee. Experiment 35: write the group email anyway, then spend the saved day on the allotment. The tomatoes have no inbox and are thriving.

[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Markup
The shop's blog explains its pricing: materials, labour, a fixed percentage, done. Refreshingly honest, and it made me check my own arithmetic. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow. I have never had it fixed. Instead I subtract four minutes from every clock I meet, which means I am quietly doing sums at train stations and missing nothing. The watch costs me nothing and charges me constantly. At the allotment I priced my tomatoes this year: seeds, compost, the hours I stood there admiring them. By that logic each tomato cost about eleven pounds. Piotr would call this a failure of productivity. I call it the only honest price list I have. The shop rounds its margins to the nearest penny. I round mine to the nearest tomato.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Deficit
The letting agent raised my rent by thirty-eight pounds a month and sent the email at 5:02 on a Friday, which tells you what they think of my weekend. My pay went up by a sum I would rather not divide publicly. So I did what I always do: opened the notebook and treated it as an experiment. Experiment 44 was meant to be a household budget, and it lasted nine days, because the budget kept asking me questions I couldn't answer, like why the electricity bill has a "standing charge" when nothing in my flat stands still. Piotr once wrote a column called "Rent Is Just a Number." I suspect he owns his flat. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always behind the price rise, arriving late to a cost I already owe.

text: My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on a coffee, and 60p goes quietly aside. It is a clever little machine: it takes the loose change I never counted and makes it visible. I tested it for a week. Total saved: £4.12. The coffee was still £3.40, but now it felt like £4, which is a strange tax to pay for virtue. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. The bank's rounding is the opposite: it corrects me constantly, in pennies, without asking. Piotr would call this frictionless saving. I'd call it a subscription to my own pocket. The tomatoes get tap water; I'm not paying for the fancy can.

hook: A startup replaces its weekly status meeting with a shared document.
title: The Meeting That Became a Document
text: The startup killed its Monday status meeting and replaced it with a shared document. Everyone edits a row: what you did, what you're doing, what's stuck. I read about it on a train and felt a small, unearned triumph, as if I'd personally cancelled the meeting. Then I noticed I'd read the article twice and retained neither figure in it. That is the document problem in miniature: nobody performs attention. In a room, you can watch Piotr's jaw tighten when you say "roughly done," and he will make you say a number. On a page, "roughly done" survives for weeks. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow; I wear it because a slow watch still forces you to check. A document doesn't check you back. Day 14 of experiments: I've started writing my rows in pen.

Three of us, one shared page, a week to fill it in. Two wrote nothing. I wrote four hundred words about the tomato blight, then deleted it, then wrote it again smaller. The meeting we skipped would have taken twenty minutes and settled it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which is roughly how long I spent deciding whether to press send. Adding to the list: write less, meet once. Day fourteen. Piotr has automated his minutes.

TITLE: Eleven Hours, Give or Take
The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, though I'd want to know whose week. Mine, this week: forty minutes on a call that could have been an email, an hour on a call that could have been two emails, and nine minutes standing in a corridor with Piotr while he explained, with diagrams on a napkin, how to run shorter meetings. His napkin diagram took longer than most meetings I attend. My grandfather's pocket watch ran four minutes slow his whole working life and he was never late to anything that mattered — he simply left four minutes early. I've started doing the same with meetings: arriving late by design, leaving on the hour. So far nobody has noticed, which tells you something. title: The Document That Sat There Looking Back
text: A startup has replaced its weekly status meeting with a shared document, and everyone is calling it brave. I read the report on the allotment bench, watch running four minutes slow as usual, and thought about my grandfather, who kept minutes for a committee that never read them. The document is not nothing. It is quiet, and quiet is where the useful bits are. But a document cannot see you glance at the clock. At the shed-fund meeting, nine minutes of standing produced no decision at all; we simply dispersed, relieved. text: A startup in the paper replaced its weekly status meeting with a shared document, and everyone applauded. title: The Village Coworking Space Has Four Desks and a Kettle
text: The new coworking space in the village opened Monday, in the old chapel hall. Four desks, a kettle, and a view of the bus stop. I went to look, because the alternative is my kitchen table, where the cat has opinions. It was empty except for a man named Gareth doing something with spreadsheets and a noticeboard offering "synergy." I stayed an hour. I got more done than I do at home, mostly because I felt watched, and being watched is underrated. The allotment tomatoes are the same: they behave better when I'm standing there. My grandfather's watch said ten past when I left, which meant six past. I walked home. Four hundred people, four desks. It's a start.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Alarm Doesn't Care How You Feel
The study says consistency of wake time beats the ritual around it. I believe it, having built a ritual and defended it in print. For a fortnight I timed my mornings: up at six, watch on, kettle, the same three stretches, a walk to the allotment gate. Then I moved only the wake time, half an hour later, and kept the rest. The tomatoes did not notice. Neither did the shed. What noticed was me, at ten past six, standing in the kitchen with nothing to do and no reason to be awake. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, so for a while I was consistent with the wrong hour. Adding this to the list: keep the time, drop the theatre. Day twelve of trying. Piotr would sell the ritual back to me as a system.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: Rounding Up
A bank now rounds up card payments to the nearest pound and sweeps the difference into savings. I paid £3.40 for a coffee and a bun and they took £4. I have made worse trades. The pennies add up, they say, and I believe the arithmetic the way I believe my grandfather's watch: four minutes slow, but constant. So I checked what my own roundups would come to. Twelve payments in a week, sixty pence in change. My savings would grow by the price of one tomato plant, which at the allotment yields roughly nine tomatoes, which at shop prices is a profit my ledger has never seen. Adding this to the list: round up in something you can eat. Day thirteen. Piotr rounds up his words and calls it output.

[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: The Document Will See You Now
A startup has cancelled its weekly status meeting and put a shared document in its place. Everyone writes what they did; everyone reads it. I approve in principle and distrust the principle. A meeting at least fails in company, where you can watch it fail. A document fails quietly and gets edited later. I tried it on the allotment committee. Three of us, one shared page, a week to fill it in. Two wrote nothing. I wrote four hundred words about the tomato blight, then deleted it, then wrote it again smaller. The meeting we skipped would have taken twenty minutes and settled it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which is roughly how long I spent deciding whether to press send. Adding to the list: write less, meet once. Day fourteen. Piotr has automated his minutes.

title: The Village With a Desk
text: A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people. It has eight desks, a printer, and a kettle, and the article about it used the word "hub" eleven times. I drove out to see it, because I have opinions about desks and wanted them tested. The man at the door told me the nearest train station is nine miles away, so the members are mostly people who were already there: a bookkeeper, two farmers' sons with laptops, a woman who edits something she wouldn't name. Nobody had commuted to it. It was simply a room in the village that wasn't the kitchen. Experiment 51: work somewhere that isn't home, then notice what changed. What changed was that I stayed until five. My grandfather's watch said 4:56, which felt like a full day. Piotr would call this a productivity framework. The bookkeeper called it a kettle.

TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Sentence
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. They call it a "cooling-off period." I call it a hostage situation with a nicer name. Somewhere in a server, a message I sent yesterday at 4:40 p.m. is still waiting to be born, and I have forgotten what it said. Probably "sounds good." The delay applies only to group emails, so one-to-one messages arrive instantly, which means the fastest way to reach twelve people is now twelve separate messages, each of which will be answered, in my case, at four minutes past whenever. My grandfather's watch runs slow by design; this is slow by committee. Experiment 35: write the group email anyway, then spend the saved day on the allotment. The tomatoes have no inbox and are thriving.

[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Tuesday Compromise
The firm announced that everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays, and the comment section did what comment sections do. I keep thinking about the logistics instead. One colleague has a ninety-minute commute each way, so Tuesday costs her three hours to prove she is reachable, which she has been proving from her kitchen since 2020. My grandfather's watch would say she arrives four minutes late and no one would notice. I tried hybrid once, in a manner of speaking: I split my mornings between the desk and the allotment shed and got nothing done in either place. The tomatoes didn't mind. Experiment 42: work where the work is, not where the rule says. Piotr would call that a productivity framework. I call it choosing your own four minutes.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Empty Desk Tax
The council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I believe it. I once paid rent on a desk I visited twice a week, which is a bit like keeping a car for the passenger seat. Experiment 43: count what a commute actually costs. Not just the fare. The sandwich, the coffee, the hour spent looking busy. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I always arrive owing time I never pay back. Piotr would put all this in a spreadsheet. I'd rather put it on the allotment: the tomatoes don't need me present to grow, and somehow nobody has ever called that a productivity problem.

title: The Four-Minute Membership
text: The gym near the station says most January joiners quit by March. I lasted until February 9th. I know because I wrote it in my list of small experiments, next to "rinse tomatoes with milk against blight" (no) and "wear watch on right wrist" (no). What killed the gym was the shoes. Lacing them took ninety seconds I could not defend at 6:40 a.m. So I cancelled the membership and kept the shoes by the door, laced, ready. Now I walk forty minutes before breakfast. No app, no class, no motivational email from a man called Piotr implying my discipline has a leak in it. Just the walk, and my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, telling me I'm late for nothing in particular. The tomatoes don't need a streak, either. They need water and someone who shows up.

hook: A gym reports that most January sign-ups stop by March.
title: The March Drop-Off
text: The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March, and everyone nods wisely about willpower. I don't buy it. I think people quit because the habit was never theirs — it was January's. I have a running list of experiments I've tried on myself, and the only ones that survived were the ones I could do badly. The forty-minute timer lasted a week and took my concentration with it. But waking at ten past six has held for eleven years, mostly because it asks nothing of me. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once needed motivating. Experiment 78: for a month, do the smallest version of a thing — one tomato watered, one paragraph, one flight of stairs. Report what sticks. Piotr has already published his version. His involves a chart.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Then the Bell
A writer I know works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I tried it on Monday. Forty minutes of work, then the timer goes off. Mine is shaped like a tomato and came from the allotment shed, and it is louder than my actual tomatoes. I got three blocks done before lunch and felt insufferably pleased with myself, the way Piotr looks all the time. But here's the thing: the timer doesn't care what I'm doing when it rings. Twice I was mid-sentence and it went off anyway, and I sat there like a dog hearing a whistle. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and never once interrupted anyone. Experiment 41: forty-minute blocks, one week, note the wreckage. So far the wreckage is mostly my concentration.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Standing Question
The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on the allotment, which is the only laboratory I trust. Three of us, standing among the tomatoes, agreed in four minutes to move the water butt. Standing again a week later, we agreed in three minutes to move it back. Nothing has been moved. The tomatoes are unimpressed. Piotr says this proves standing sharpens decisions. I think it proves standing sharpens the desire to stop standing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've decided the real finding is that any meeting ends when the legs say so, not the agenda. Experiment 41: propose one seated meeting a month, bring chairs, see who stays. I've booked the room. I'm bringing four chairs and low expectations.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Clock That Doesn't Care
The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it. I believe this, partly because I have no ritual. I have a grandfather's watch that runs four minutes slow, and I have been waking at ten past six for eleven years, which by the watch is six past. Nobody has ever studied me, but I am my own longitudinal sample. Experiment 63: for a week, I woke at the same time and changed everything else — tea instead of coffee, no phone, phone, a walk round the allotment before the kettle. The tomatoes noticed nothing. My mornings felt identical, which annoyed me, because I had hoped the walk would feel virtuous. Piotr claims his routine is a "keystone habit." Mine is a keystone absence. The watch just ticks, four minutes behind, unbothered.

text: A gym chain reports that most January sign-ups quit by March. I felt smug for about four seconds, then remembered my own list of experiments, which is mostly a graveyard with good intentions. The thirty-minute blocks from last month are down to twenty on days the allotment needs me, and the six o'clock wake time holds only because the alarm is louder than my excuses. What survives isn't the plan; it's the thing I stop negotiating with. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've quit trying to fix it. I just know it's slow. That's the whole trick, maybe: not discipline, but knowing exactly how you lie to yourself and building around it. The tomatoes don't care about January. They fruit when they fruit.

hook: A company deletes all email older than 90 days.
title: The Ninety-Day Amnesia
text: The company announced that all email older than ninety days will be deleted. A clean slate, they said, as if a slate were ever clean. I spent an hour scrolling back through mine, which is mostly receipts and one thread where Piotr and I argue about whether inbox zero counts as a personality. Deleting it feels like throwing out old shopping lists: no loss, mild panic. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I keep it that way because it gives me a small margin against the world. An email archive is the opposite — a margin I never check. On the allotment I've been testing what happens when I stop pruning the tomatoes. Answer: nothing good, but the mess is honest. So I've started a new experiment: I archive nothing and delete nothing, and see if I notice. Day one, I noticed.

hook: A company deletes all email older than 90 days.
title: The Ninety-Day Amnesia
text: A software company announced it will delete every email older than ninety days. Users are calling it liberation. I read the news on my phone, then deleted the newsletter unread, which felt like participating. I understand the appeal. My inbox holds emails I've kept the way I keep expired coupons: proof of good intentions, no actual use. But I keep thinking about a message from my grandfather, sent years before he died, in which he complained about his tomatoes. At the time it was nothing. Now it's the last thing he wrote about the allotment before it became mine. Piotr says a 90-day limit builds discipline. He probably has an app counting down. title: The Ninety-Day Amnesia
text: A software company announced it will delete all email older than ninety days. Staff cheered. text: The mentor programme paired me with a woman from Finance who has never once asked about my tomatoes. TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred. Twelve desks, a coffee machine, a room called the Quiet Room that I suspect is not quiet. I went to look. Two people were in it, both on video calls, both apologising for background noise. The village has no bus after six, so the space is for people who already live within walking distance of it, which is the entire problem dressed as a solution. I tried a version of this last year: one day a week I worked from the allotment shed, laptop on a seed tray. I got four hours of work and a stiff neck. The tomatoes did not respect my calendar. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow against a spreadsheet I could not open. Adding to the list: remote is a place, hybrid is a timetable, and neither is a shed. Day fifteen. [Entry from day 16]

A gym reports that most January sign-ups stop by March. The story is always told as failure — the resolve that thins out with the light. I have stopped believing in resolve and started believing in friction. At the allotment I have not kept a single resolution to water more regularly, but I did move the watering can from the shed to the tap, and the tomatoes have been watered ever since. Two paces, that was the whole habit. So I am adding to the list: change the room, not the will. Day sixteen. [Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Ninety Days of Silence
A company now deletes every email older than ninety days. The reasoning is storage, or focus, or something a consultant said. I read it and felt the small tug of a filing cabinet I never built. I keep emails like I keep seed packets: far past their date, meaning to sort them, finding them in March. My grandfather's watch has run four minutes slow for decades and I have never once deleted a minute of it. So I tried the rule on myself, one inbox, ninety days, the rest gone. I deleted four hundred and eleven messages and answered none of them. Two were from Piotr, both about how he has emptied his inbox. Adding to the list: deleting is not replying. Day seventeen.

hook: A mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments.
title: The Pairing
text: The mentor programme matches new hires with someone from another department. I signed up expecting to be taught something; instead I was handed a woman from accounts who has been here nineteen years and knows where the bodies are buried, literally in one case involving a filing cabinet. We met for forty minutes. She asked what I wanted to learn. I said I didn't know, which is the honest answer and a poor opener. So she taught me how to read a purchase order without my eyes glazing, and I taught her nothing, which she noted. Experiment 63: be the dumbest person in a small room on purpose. It's cheaper than a course. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through all of it, so I was early to a meeting I'd have missed. Piotr says mentorship is leverage. She called it "having someone to ask."
memory_block:
[Entry from day 3]
TITLE: The Tuesday Class
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along out of nosiness rather than ambition. Eight of us, average age somewhere near my grandfather's watch, which ran four minutes slow all evening and made me late. The tutor, a patient woman of about twenty-five, taught us to make a button change colour. Mine turned green on the third try. The man beside me, a retired bus driver, got his to flash and looked like he'd won something. I'd assumed the skill was the point. It isn't. Half the room was there for the tea and the other half for someone to say "well done" without adding a caveat. At the allotment I've been trying to grow tomatoes from seed saved two years running; the coding felt similar, small and stubborn. Piotr would call it optimisation. I call it Tuesday.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Course They Cut
A college near me has dropped a required course in favour of a project. The reasoning: nobody remembers the lectures anyway, but everyone remembers what they made. I have some sympathy. I sat through four years of instruction and can recall exactly one thing, which was a lecturer's joke about commas, and I'm not sure I've used it right. But the project has a problem the course didn't. A project will let you avoid whatever you're bad at. Left alone, I'd have built nine versions of the same tomato and called it a portfolio. I keep a list of experiments on myself. Number fourteen: learn one thing badly on purpose, in front of someone. The coding evening taught me that. My button turned green; the bus driver's flashed. Both counted.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Village With a Desk
A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people. It has eight desks, a printer, and a kettle, and the article about it used the word "hub" eleven times. I drove out to see it, because I have opinions about desks and wanted them tested. The man at the door told me the nearest train station is nine miles away, so the members are mostly people who were already there: a bookkeeper, two farmers' sons with laptops, a woman who edits something she wouldn't name. Nobody had commuted to it. It was simply a room in the village that wasn't the kitchen. Experiment 51: work somewhere that isn't home, then notice what changed. What changed was that I stayed until five. My grandfather's watch said 4:56, which felt like a full day. Piotr would call this a productivity framework. The bookkeeper called it a kettle.

text: The new mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments, which sounds sensible until you notice nobody has defined what the mentor is for. On the allotment I've been letting the tomatoes fail in small ways rather than staking everything. Piotr would call this inefficient, and he'd be right, and I've added it to the list anyway.

text: The mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments, which means I spent Tuesday morning being taught the shared drive by a twenty-three-year-old in Facilities. hook: A team tries 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter.
title: The Meeting That Didn't Happen
text: Our team tried "no agenda, no meeting" for a quarter. I was sceptical, having sat through meetings where the agenda was a single line reading "discuss." The rule worked better than expected, mostly by killing things. Eleven meetings vanished in the first fortnight, including one recurring call whose purpose nobody could reconstruct, only that it had always been on Tuesdays. I felt briefly weightless, then guilty, as though I'd skipped a dentist appointment. Piotr says his team saved nine hours a week and has the spreadsheet to prove it. Mine saved less and spent some of it arguing about what counted as an agenda. By the end, the rule had quietly lapsed, though the Tuesday call has never come back. Small win. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, but at least it doesn't schedule anything.

hook: A team tries 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter.
title: No Agenda, No Meeting, No Idea
text: A team ran "no agenda, no meeting" for a quarter and reports, predictably, that meetings fell by a third. What they don't report is what filled the gap: a hundred small emails, a group chat named after the project, and the quiet dread of not knowing who decided the thing. I tried a version on the allotment. No agenda, no shed. Three weeks later the water butt is still in dispute and nobody has said so out loud. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and its real lesson is that a meeting without an agenda is just a room where the slowest watch sets the time. Experiment 61: write the agenda in four minutes, then leave. Piotr is already drafting a counter-argument, on a napkin, standing up.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Eleven Hours, Give or Take
The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, though I'd want to know whose week. Mine, this week: forty minutes on a call that could have been an email, an hour on a call that could have been two emails, and nine minutes standing in a corridor with Piotr while he explained, with diagrams on a napkin, how to run shorter meetings. His napkin diagram took longer than most meetings I attend. My grandfather's pocket watch ran four minutes slow his whole working life and he was never late to anything that mattered — he simply left four minutes early. I've started doing the same with meetings: arriving late by design, leaving on the hour. So far nobody has noticed, which tells you something. Experiment 34: decline one meeting a week, note what breaks. Nothing has broken yet.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Standing Question
The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on the allotment, which is the only laboratory I trust. Three of us, standing among the tomatoes, agreed in four minutes to move the water butt. Standing again a week later, we agreed in three minutes to move it back. Nothing has been moved. The tomatoes are unimpressed. Piotr says this proves standing sharpens decisions. I think it proves standing sharpens the desire to stop standing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've decided the real finding is that any meeting ends when the legs say so, not the agenda. Experiment 41: propose one seated meeting a month, bring chairs, see who stays. I've booked the room. I'm bringing four chairs and low expectations.

[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: The Document That Blinked
The startup killed its weekly status meeting and replaced it with a shared document. Everyone edits it, everyone reads it, nobody misses the meeting. I tried the same on the allotment: a notebook on the shed shelf, where the three of us write what we've done to the tomatoes. Week one, two entries and a drawing of a slug. Week two, four entries, one of them an argument about the slug. Nobody has seen each other in a fortnight, and the water butt is still where it was. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and a document never blinks first — there's nobody to leave four minutes early from. Experiment 52: keep the document, but stand at the shed for ten minutes on Thursdays in case anyone wanders past. Piotr says that's a meeting. I say it's a doorstep.

hook: A team tries 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter.
title: The Agenda Was the Meeting
text: My neighbour Mira runs a six-person team that spent a quarter on "no agenda, no meeting." By week three they had cancelled eleven meetings and replaced them with a shared document, which is where I said my piece on day fourteen, so I'll only note that the document grew to nine pages and nobody read page seven. What surprised me was the residue. Meetings with no agenda don't vanish; they leak. Her team started having "quick chats" in the corridor, four minutes here, six there, none of them counted by anyone. Mira reckons she got two hours a week back. I reckon she got two hours back and spent three of them standing in a stairwell. Piotr, naturally, has declared it a triumph and colour-coded his calendar to prove it. My watch says he's four minutes early to his own conclusions.

text: My friend Nadia's team ran "no agenda, no meeting" for a quarter. The rule was strict: if nobody had sent an agenda, the meeting was cancelled. Attendance dropped by a third. I have nothing against the rule. I keep a list of experiments on myself, and half of them fail in this exact way: they remove the container and the water goes on the floor. My tomatoes taught me that. Staked ones climb. Unstaked ones sprawl, and the sprawl looks like growth. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow. Nobody at the meeting noticed.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Four-Minute Discount
text: Our town launched a local currency today, paper notes you can spend only at small shops. The council calls it a boost for the high street. I call it a second wallet to lose. I gave it a fair trial: one note, one bakery, one loaf. The baker took it, squinted at the watermark, and gave me change in ordinary coins, which felt like a small betrayal of the whole idea. Piotr says local currencies fail because they add friction. He is right, annoyingly. But he files it under productivity and moves on. I filed it under my running list of experiments: number nineteen, a currency I used exactly once. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow all day, and nobody ever asked it to be efficient. Some things are worth the friction. I'll try the note again on Saturday, at the allotment shop.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Currency of Small Change
text: The town of — let us say Marlow, because it was not Marlow — has issued its own currency for small shops. You swap pounds for local notes at a kiosk and spend them on bread and shoelaces, and they expire if you hoard them. The theory is that money kept moving stays in the town. I like it the way I like a well-made gate: not for what it promises, but for the hinges. I tried a version at the allotment: three tomato seedlings tradable only for other people's seedlings, no cash, no keeping score. I ended up with four cucumbers and an awkward conversation with the man on plot nine. Adding to the list: a currency is a promise with a pocket. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and no shop in Marlow would take it. Piotr would expense the whole experiment. Day twenty.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: The Shopkeeper's Shilling
text: The town of Marlow Green has issued its own currency: the green pound, spendable only in local shops, worth one pound sterling until it isn't. You change your money at the library, and the notes have a picture of a bridge on them, which is either civic pride or a warning. I went to look. A woman bought bread and a lightbulb and paid in two shades of money, sorting them on the counter like someone dealing cards. The shopkeeper accepted both without comment, which is the whole trick: nobody argues about the exchange rate while there's a queue. It reminded me of the round-up account — value that only works if you don't look at it directly. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I'd arrive at the till late and probably overpay. Piotr would call this friction. I call it a town deciding, briefly, that its money should have a postcode.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Markup
The shop's blog explains its pricing: materials, labour, a fixed percentage, done. Refreshingly honest, and it made me check my own arithmetic. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow. I have never had it fixed. Instead I subtract four minutes from every clock I meet, which means I am quietly doing sums at train stations and missing nothing. The watch costs me nothing and charges me constantly. At the allotment I priced my tomatoes this year: seeds, compost, the hours I stood there admiring them. By that logic each tomato cost about eleven pounds. Piotr would call this a failure of productivity. I call it the only honest price list I have. The shop rounds its margins to the nearest penny. I round mine to the nearest tomato.

[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Deficit
The letting agent raised my rent by thirty-eight pounds a month and sent the email at 5:02 on a Friday, which tells you what they think of my weekend. My pay went up by a sum I would rather not divide publicly. So I did what I always do: opened the notebook and treated it as an experiment. Experiment 44 was meant to be a household budget, and it lasted nine days, because the budget kept asking me questions I couldn't answer, like why the electricity bill has a "standing charge" when nothing in my flat stands still. Piotr once wrote a column called "Rent Is Just a Number." I suspect he owns his flat. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always behind the price rise, arriving late to a cost I already owe.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Round-Up Roundabout
My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on a coffee and forty pence vanishes into a better future. It sounds like found money, except I know where it came from: the same place as all my other money, which is to say, me. Still, I opened the app and watched the round-ups accumulate all week. Total saved: £4.12. At that rate, my tomatoes are further along than my retirement. Experiment 51: let it run a month and see whether I notice the absence. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and this account runs four pounds slow — money I've already spent, arriving late somewhere else. Piotr would call this frictionless saving. I call it a coin jar with better branding and no jar.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes of Local Credit
text: The town of Marlow Bridge has issued its own currency, a paper note called the "bridge," good at eleven small shops and nowhere else. I went to buy tomatoes and a coffee and came back with change that isn't money, technically. The woman at the till gave me two bridges and a look that said don't lose them. I put them where the watch sits, and now I have two kinds of slow currency on one wrist. title: The Town That Pays in Something Else
text: The town of — let's say Marlow, because it wasn't — has issued its own currency for small shops. title: The Friday I Didn't Spend in a Meeting
text: The company announced a four-day week trial, and I read the memo twice, the way I read everything now that my grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it. Four minutes is enough to miss a train but not enough to matter, which is roughly how I feel about most productivity claims. Piotr will write that the trial proves focus is a choice; he'll use the word "leverage" and mean nothing by it. I know only this: on my allotment I gave half the tomato rows an extra day of nothing, no watering, no fussing. They caught up by August. The other half I doted on. Same fruit, more of my weekends gone. I'm not saying a four-day week grows tomatoes. I'm saying I've stopped mistaking attention for yield.

He was promoted. I still don't know about the printer. At the allotment I have been trying to learn from the tomatoes properly: not reading about them, but copying the one plot that fruits first every year. Its owner does nothing clever. Half of them, I suspect, were the corridor ones that never had an agenda because nobody knew yet what they were for — the accidental collisions where the useful thing gets said. I tried the rule on myself for a fortnight and cancelled everything I couldn't justify in a sentence. I got a great deal done and spoke to almost no one. TITLE: The Currency of Small Change
