hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: The Friday They Took Away
text: The company announced a four-day week trial and the comment section immediately divided into those who think Friday is a birthright and those who think it's a trap with extra hours stapled to the other four days. I read the details. Same pay, same output, one fewer day to prove you're reachable. I have run experiments of my own on this principle: Experiment 55 was doing five days of work in four, which mostly meant doing the fifth day's worrying on the fourth day's evening. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, made the deadline feel generous. The tomatoes got watered on the Friday I reclaimed. Piotr has already written that a four-day week is a productivity framework. He's not wrong, which is the annoying part. I'd just like one trial where nobody measures anything and we see what grows.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Tuesday Compromise
The firm announced that everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays, and the comment section did what comment sections do. I keep thinking about the logistics instead. One colleague has a ninety-minute commute each way, so Tuesday costs her three hours to prove she is reachable, which she has been proving from her kitchen since 2020. My grandfather's watch would say she arrives four minutes late and no one would notice. I tried hybrid once, in a manner of speaking: I split my mornings between the desk and the allotment shed and got nothing done in either place. The tomatoes didn't mind. Experiment 42: work where the work is, not where the rule says. Piotr would call that a productivity framework. I call it choosing your own four minutes.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Empty Desk Tax
The council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I believe it. I once paid rent on a desk I visited twice a week, which is a bit like keeping a car for the passenger seat. The building had a coffee machine that cost two pounds a cup and a view of a car park, and I sat there doing the same work I could have done from the shed, only louder. Experiment 43: count what a commute actually costs. Not just the fare. The sandwich, the coffee, the hour spent looking busy. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I always arrive owing time I never pay back. Piotr would put all this in a spreadsheet. I'd rather put it on the allotment: the tomatoes don't need me present to grow, and somehow nobody has ever called that a productivity problem.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: The Village With a Desk
A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people. It has eight desks, a printer, and a kettle, and the article about it used the word "hub" eleven times. The man at the door told me the nearest train station is nine miles away, so the members are mostly people who were already there: a bookkeeper, two farmers' sons with laptops, a woman who edits something she wouldn't name. Nobody had commuted to it. It was simply a room in the village that wasn't the kitchen. Experiment 51: work somewhere that isn't home, then notice what changed. What changed was that I stayed until five. My grandfather's watch said 4:56, which felt like a full day. Piotr would call this a productivity framework. The bookkeeper called it a kettle.

title: The Failed Plans
text: A teacher has published her lesson plans that didn't work, which is a braver act than most of what gets printed. One plan involved a game the class refused to play. Another had a worksheet nobody finished. She includes what she'd do instead. I read it twice, thinking about the college that dropped its lectures for a project and about my own list of experiments. Experiment 41 was keeping a failure log for a month. I lasted nine days and the log was mostly "forgot to log." The tomatoes are a better record; last year's stunted row is still staked, unedited, for anyone who walks past. memory_block:
[Entry from day 3]
TITLE: The Tuesday Class
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along out of nosiness rather than ambition. Eight of us, average age somewhere near my grandfather's watch, which ran four minutes slow all evening and made me late. The tutor, a patient woman of about twenty-five, taught us to make a button change colour. Mine turned green on the third try. The man beside me, a retired bus driver, got his to flash and looked like he'd won something. I'd assumed the skill was the point. It isn't. Half the room was there for the tea and the other half for someone to say "well done" without adding a caveat. At the allotment I've been trying to grow tomatoes from seed saved two years running; the coding felt similar, small and stubborn. Piotr would call it optimisation. I call it Tuesday.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Course They Cut
A college near me has dropped a required course in favour of a project. The reasoning: nobody remembers the lectures anyway, but everyone remembers what they made. I have some sympathy. I sat through four years of instruction and can recall exactly one thing, which was a lecturer's joke about commas, and I'm not sure I've used it right. But the project has a problem the course didn't. A project will let you avoid whatever you're bad at. Left alone, I'd have built nine versions of the same tomato and called it a portfolio. I keep a list of experiments on myself. Number fourteen: learn one thing badly on purpose, in front of someone. The coding evening taught me that. My button turned green; the bus driver's flashed. Both counted.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Pairing
The mentor programme matches new hires with someone from another department. I signed up expecting to be taught something; instead I was handed a woman from accounts who has been here nineteen years and knows where the bodies are buried, literally in one case involving a filing cabinet. We met for forty minutes. She asked what I wanted to learn. I said I didn't know, which is the honest answer and a poor opener. So she taught me how to read a purchase order without my eyes glazing, and I taught her nothing, which she noted. Experiment 63: be the dumbest person in a small room on purpose. It's cheaper than a course. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through all of it, so I was early to a meeting I'd have missed. Piotr says mentorship is leverage. She called it "having someone to ask."

text: The company announced a mandatory ten-minute walk break at 3 p.m. I didn't need a policy to walk, but I went, because I keep a list of small experiments and this was free. I walked anyway. Tomorrow I'll try it without the company telling me to, and I'll report back.

title: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
text: The company memo says a ten-minute walk break every day. I read it and thought: who are these people, and can I come? My own version is the walk to the allotment, which takes eleven minutes and is therefore over budget. The memo also says the break is "protected," a word I associate with witness protection and the tomato timer. Ten minutes is a strange unit. Too short to arrive anywhere, long enough to notice you have left. Experiment 91: I took the walk anyway, at eleven, past the bins and back. Nothing happened. The tomatoes were fine without me. Piotr would have charted it. I have my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which means my ten-minute walk is really fourteen, and nobody can prove otherwise.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Then the Bell
A writer I know works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. I tried it on Monday. Forty minutes of work, then the timer goes off. Mine is shaped like a tomato and came from the allotment shed, and it is louder than my actual tomatoes. I got three blocks done before lunch and felt insufferably pleased with myself, the way Piotr looks all the time. But here's the thing: the timer doesn't care what I'm doing when it rings. Twice I was mid-sentence and it went off anyway, and I sat there like a dog hearing a whistle. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and never once interrupted anyone. Experiment 41: forty-minute blocks, one week, note the wreckage. So far the wreckage is mostly my concentration.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Clock That Doesn't Care
The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it. I believe this, partly because I have no ritual. I have a grandfather's watch that runs four minutes slow, and I have been waking at ten past six for eleven years, which by the watch is six past. Nobody has ever studied me, but I am my own longitudinal sample. Experiment 63: for a week, I woke at the same time and changed everything else — tea instead of coffee, no phone, phone, a walk round the allotment before the kettle. The tomatoes noticed nothing. My mornings felt identical, which annoyed me, because I had hoped the walk would feel virtuous. Piotr claims his routine is a "keystone habit." Mine is a keystone absence. The watch just ticks, four minutes behind, unbothered.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The March Drop-Off
The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March, and everyone nods wisely about willpower. I don't buy it. I think people quit because the habit was never theirs — it was January's. I have a running list of experiments I've tried on myself, and the only ones that survived were the ones I could do badly. The forty-minute timer lasted a week and took my concentration with it. But waking at ten past six has held for eleven years, mostly because it asks nothing of me. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once needed motivating. Experiment 78: for a month, do the smallest version of a thing — one tomato watered, one paragraph, one flight of stairs. Report what sticks. Piotr has already published his version. His involves a chart.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: The Meeting That Walked
text: My employer has introduced a ten-minute walk break at eleven. Attendance is optional, which in office language means it is compulsory but cheerful. I went. Twelve of us walked a loop around the car park, mostly in silence, like a small parade with no band. I am suspicious of this, because I have a list of experiments that failed by week two. The forty-minute timer blocks died at thirty. The morning routine died the moment I asked it to survive winter. But the walk is not asking me to become a different person. It is ten minutes, scheduled, and someone else has decided it, which turns out to be the whole trick. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, came along, useless as ever, and I did not check it once. Tomorrow: same loop, and I will count how many people are still coming.

title: The Meeting That Walked Itself
text: The company announced a ten-minute daily walk break, and I put it on my list of experiments: number thirty-one, between "chew every bite twenty times" and "no phone before the kettle boils." My grandfather's watch said ten past, so I left four minutes early and arrived back four minutes late, which is the most honest accounting my day has ever produced. On the allotment I keep a row of tomatoes under the same rule: the ones that get a scheduled look do better than the ones I visit when I remember. Attention is the whole crop. The unscheduled walk never happened and never felt missed.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: The Chat Tool That Learned to Sleep
text: Our work chat introduced quiet hours, muting notifications from ten at night until seven. I expected to hate it, the way I hate most software deciding things for me. Instead I slept like a stone and woke to forty-one messages I had not missed. I read them in eight minutes. Nothing had burned down. Piotr, who writes about productivity and owns, I suspect, no clock at all, will call this a triumph of boundary-setting. I call it a reprieve. My grandfather's watch still runs four minutes slow, and I have decided that is the correct speed for a life. I have added quiet hours to my list of experiments. Next I will try a day of answering email only after the tomatoes are watered.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: Quiet Hours
text: The chat tool now has quiet hours, which mute notifications from ten at night until seven. I read the announcement twice, looking for the catch, and found it in the word "default": the quiet is on unless someone marks a message urgent. So the tool has not removed the noise. The messages still arrived; I simply read them at seven, all at once, like a plate of food saved up and gone cold. What I lost was the small, useless exchanges at midnight that cost nothing and kept something alive. At the allotment I have learned the tomatoes do not care when I water them, only that I do. TITLE: The Fifth Day
The company announced a four-day week trial, same pay, same output, and the coverage used the word "revolutionary" eleven times. I have run this experiment on myself already, in a manner of speaking: I took Fridays off for a month and did exactly the same amount of work in four days, which sounds like a triumph until you learn what I stopped doing. I stopped the slow, useless conversations. I stopped walking to the far greenhouse to ask a question I could have emailed. I got faster and thinner, like a sauce boiled down too far. At the allotment, the tomatoes do not fruit in four days because I have decided they should. Adding to the list: a shorter week is a promise about what you will give up. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never once asked for a Friday. Piotr, I suspect, has already booked the fifth day for a course. Day twenty-one.

[Entry from day 22]
TITLE: The Syllabus of Things That Didn't Work
A teacher has published her failed lesson plans — the worksheet that confused everyone, the activity that ate forty minutes and taught nothing. She calls it a gift, and I think she is right, though I notice she waited until she had retired. I keep a list of experiments on myself, but I have never once published the ones that flopped. The fortnight of no unjustified meetings is on it. So is the tomato currency, which ended in cucumbers. Both are listed as things tried, not things learned from, because I wrote them down after I knew the ending. At the allotment the failures are more honest: I can still see the row where the beans went in too early and simply gave up. Adding to the list: a failure published is worth two successes filed. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and it has never pretended otherwise. Piotr publishes only the weeks that worked. Day twenty-two.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, Measured
The company has introduced a ten-minute walk break, and the memo calls it "micro-restorative movement." I timed it, because I time things. Ten minutes, four of which are spent finding a coat and a door. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so if I leave when it says ten past, I actually leave at fourteen past, which is somehow the only part of the scheme that works. At the allotment I tested a version on myself: ten minutes of walking the rows at noon, no phone. The tomatoes were indifferent. I was not — I noticed things I'd stopped seeing, like the gap where the beans failed. Adding to the list: a break is only a break if nobody calls it restorative. Piotr has already published his walking-meeting strategy. Day twenty-three.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: Quiet Hours, Loud Thinking
text: The chat tool now goes silent at ten. Around eleven I found myself standing in the kitchen, phone face down on the breadboard, waiting for it to not buzz. It didn't. I checked anyway, the way you press a bruise. Nothing was waiting, which per Experiment 51 is the usual trick. But quiet hours are new: someone else deciding my silence for me, like a bank deciding my emails need to cool. At least the bank's delay was honest about being a cage. This one is sold as a gift. The watch said 11:04 when the clock said 11:08, and for once it was the more accurate instrument: four minutes of unsent replies, held in the dark. Experiment 79: leave notifications off until the tomatoes are watered. Piotr has already scheduled his quiet hours and, I suspect, his feelings about them.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Sentence
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. They call it a "cooling-off period." I call it a hostage situation with a nicer name. Somewhere in a server, a message I sent yesterday at 4:40 p.m. is still waiting to be born, and I have forgotten what it said. Probably "sounds good." The delay applies only to group emails, so one-to-one messages arrive instantly, which means the fastest way to reach twelve people is now twelve separate messages, each of which will be answered, in my case, at four minutes past whenever. My grandfather's watch runs slow by design; this is slow by committee. Experiment 35: write the group email anyway, then spend the saved day on the allotment. The tomatoes have no inbox and are thriving.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Six Minutes
The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, and I resent how modest the number is. Six minutes is generous. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which means that by its reckoning I have two minutes of silence between checks, and even those I spend deciding whether to check. I tried Experiment 51: the phone in the shed, face down on a seed tray, while I staked the tomatoes. I lasted eleven minutes by the kitchen clock, which is to say seven by the watch. Nothing was waiting. Nothing is ever waiting, which is the trick of it: the inbox is mostly a place I go to feel needed. Piotr has written that messages are "inputs," as if a person were a spreadsheet. The tomatoes received no updates all afternoon and produced flowers anyway.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: No Agenda, No Meeting, No Idea
A team ran "no agenda, no meeting" for a quarter and reports, predictably, that meetings fell by a third. What they don't report is what filled the gap: a hundred small emails, a group chat named after the project, and the quiet dread of not knowing who decided the thing. I tried a version on the allotment. No agenda, no shed. Three weeks later the water butt is still in dispute and nobody has said so out loud. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and its real lesson is that a meeting without an agenda is just a room where the slowest watch sets the time. Experiment 61: write the agenda in four minutes, then leave. Piotr is already drafting a counter-argument, on a napkin, standing up.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: The Quiet Hours Are for Other People
text: The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. Very civilized. I lasted one evening before I found myself checking it at half past ten anyway, the way you check a fridge you know is empty. Nothing there, of course. The silence worked; I was the one who didn't. Piotr would call this a boundary. I'd call it a door that locks from the inside, which only helps if you stop rattling the handle. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I've never once tried to correct it — I just know it, the way you know a friend's cough. Maybe quiet hours are the same. Not a rule to obey but a fact to learn. I've added it to the list: experiment twenty-three, notifications off, then on again, to see which one I miss.

hook: A chat tool introduces quiet hours that mute notifications at night.
title: The Quiet Hours Are for Someone Else
text: The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. Very humane. I read the announcement at 10:04, in bed, lit by the phone, and felt the specific loneliness of being protected from a message nobody was sending. My grandfather's watch said 10:00, as it always does, four minutes behind the truth. He never needed a setting to stop him answering things at night; he simply wasn't reachable, and the world coped. I won't turn the feature off. I've learned that much from the bank that held its emails a day: the delay wasn't the flaw, it was the point. But I notice quiet hours only mute the arrival, not the composing. Last night I drafted two replies I'll regret by Thursday. Piotr would call that a discipline problem. The tomatoes, who receive nothing, are thriving.

hook: Supermarkets shrink packages without lowering prices.
title: The Four-Minute Discount
text: The cereal box now holds 375 grams instead of 400, same price, same shelf. I only noticed because I weigh things. Not out of virtue — I own a kitchen scale and a suspicious nature, which is the same thing with better posture. I have a small experiment running: for one month I write the price per hundred grams on the box in marker before I put it away. It has changed my shopping more than any budget app. The cheap-looking bag is often dearer. The fat yoghurt beats the thin one by a mile. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow. He said a watch that's wrong in a known direction is more useful than one you have to trust. Same with prices, I think. Tell me the real number and I'll decide. Hide it in a smaller box and I'll just weigh everything, feeling faintly ridiculous, in the cereal aisle.

hook: Supermarkets shrink packages without lowering prices.
title: The Same Price, a Smaller Box
text: The cereal box has lost forty grams and kept its price. The supermarket calls this a "recipe refresh," which is a lovely phrase for a smaller breakfast. I weighed the old box against the new one on the kitchen scales, because I weigh things, and felt briefly like a scientist and mostly like a man arguing with cardboard. What interests me is the arithmetic nobody does: the price stayed, so the price went up. At the allotment I tried the reverse — smaller tomatoes, same price at the gate — and sold exactly none. Honesty, it turns out, needs a bigger box. My grandfather's watch has run four minutes slow for thirty years and never once claimed to be fast. Adding to the list: a hidden increase is still an increase. Piotr would call this efficiency. Day twenty-five.

hook: Supermarkets shrink packages without lowering prices.
title: The Shrinking Biscuit
text: The chocolate digestives now come in a pack of fourteen, not sixteen, for the same £1.85. Nobody announced this. The shelf just quietly got a little emptier. I stood in the aisle doing arithmetic on my phone like a detective working a very dull case, and worked out I'm paying eleven per cent more per biscuit than I was in spring. Experiment 58: keep the old receipt in my wallet and check the weight every shop. So far the pasta has shrunk, the coffee has shrunk, and the washing-up liquid has developed what I can only call a waist. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I notice the price rise late but the smaller packet immediately. Piotr would call this "efficient repackaging." I call it a shop pretending nothing happened, and me pretending I didn't check.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Deficit
The letting agent raised my rent by thirty-eight pounds a month and sent the email at 5:02 on a Friday, which tells you what they think of my weekend. My pay went up by a sum I would rather not divide publicly. So I did what I always do: opened the notebook and treated it as an experiment. Experiment 44 was meant to be a household budget, and it lasted nine days, because the budget kept asking me questions I couldn't answer, like why the electricity bill has a "standing charge" when nothing in my flat stands still. Piotr once wrote a column called "Rent Is Just a Number." I suspect he owns his flat. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always behind the price rise, arriving late to a cost I already owe.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Round-Up Roundabout
My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on a coffee and forty pence vanishes into a better future. It sounds like found money, except I know where it came from: the same place as all my other money, which is to say, me. Still, I opened the app and watched the round-ups accumulate all week. Total saved: £4.12. At that rate, my tomatoes are further along than my retirement. Experiment 51: let it run a month and see whether I notice the absence. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and this account runs four pounds slow — money I've already spent, arriving late somewhere else. Piotr would call this frictionless saving. I call it a coin jar with better branding and no jar.

[Entry from day 20]
TITLE: The Shopkeeper's Shilling
The town of Marlow Green has issued its own currency: the green pound, spendable only in local shops, worth one pound sterling until it isn't. You change your money at the library, and the notes have a picture of a bridge on them, which is either civic pride or a warning. I went to look. A woman bought bread and a lightbulb and paid in two shades of money, sorting them on the counter like someone dealing cards. The shopkeeper accepted both without comment, which is the whole trick: nobody argues about the exchange rate while there's a queue. It reminded me of the round-up account — value that only works if you don't look at it directly. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I'd arrive at the till late and probably overpay. Piotr would call this friction. I call it a town deciding, briefly, that its money should have a postcode.

hook: Supermarkets shrink packages without lowering prices.
title: The Shrinkflation Taste Test
text: The bag of crisps now weighs 165 grams. It used to weigh 200. The price, naturally, is the same, printed with the confidence of a man who has moved the fence two feet into your garden and dares you to notice. I noticed at the till, because my grandfather's watch said four minutes past, and I had four minutes to stand there feeling cheated at a rate of roughly nine grams per minute. So I did what I do with tomatoes: treated it as an experiment. I weighed the bag on the kitchen scale, then the empty bag, then my own patience. All shrank. I've added this to the list, under "things I cannot fix but can measure." The list is getting long. Piotr would call it a productivity system. I call it a diary with numbers.

text: The crisps went from 150g to 125g and the price stayed at £1.20, which the shelf label announced in cheerful yellow as "new recipe." Nobody asked the recipe to shrink. I'm not outraged, exactly. I'm impressed. It's the same trick I use on myself — hold the money quietly out of reach, as I said back on day 13 with the coffee jar. Except the supermarket is doing it to me, and doing it well. Piotr would call this a productivity leak. I call it a smaller bag of crisps. At the allotment I weighed one tomato. No conclusion yet.

hook: A survey finds hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer.
title: The Forty Minutes Are Not the Point
text: The survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer, and I believe it, though I'd like to know who these people are and whether the extra forty minutes are sleep or just lying there listening to next door's dog. My own experiment: I worked from home on Tuesday, slept until seven instead of six-twenty, and spent the saved time standing in the kitchen with a cup of tea, watching the allotment through the window. Three tomatoes have ripened. That is not a productivity gain. Piotr would have put the forty minutes into a spreadsheet by now and found a way to reinvest it. My grandfather's watch said seven-forty, which meant twenty to eight, and I was still on time. The survey's real finding, I suspect, is that nobody has to run for a train just to prove they are serious.

title: Forty Minutes, Unclaimed
text: The survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I read that at six in the morning, awake, so the finding arrived with a certain irony. What I want to know is what happens to the forty minutes. Sleep is not a bank account you can audit. Mine, the last few weeks, has gone into the allotment: I wake early, walk down, water the tomatoes, and arrive at the desk more or less human. Nobody has measured this. [Entry from day 1]
TITLE: Eleven Hours, Give or Take
The survey says eleven hours a week in meetings. I believe it, though I'd want to know whose week. Mine, this week: forty minutes on a call that could have been an email, an hour on a call that could have been two emails, and nine minutes standing in a corridor with Piotr while he explained, with diagrams on a napkin, how to run shorter meetings. His napkin diagram took longer than most meetings I attend. My grandfather's pocket watch ran four minutes slow his whole working life and he was never late to anything that mattered — he simply left four minutes early. I've started doing the same with meetings: arriving late by design, leaving on the hour. So far nobody has noticed, which tells you something. Experiment 34: decline one meeting a week, note what breaks. Nothing has broken yet.

[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Tuesday Compromise
The firm announced that everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays, and the comment section did what comment sections do. I keep thinking about the logistics instead. One colleague has a ninety-minute commute each way, so Tuesday costs her three hours to prove she is reachable, which she has been proving from her kitchen since 2020. My grandfather's watch would say she arrives four minutes late and no one would notice. Nothing was waiting. Nothing is ever waiting, which is the trick of it: the inbox is mostly a place I go to feel needed. Piotr has written that messages are "inputs," as if a person were a spreadsheet. The tomatoes received no updates all afternoon and produced flowers anyway.

His napkin diagram took longer than most meetings I attend. TITLE: The Standing Question
The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on the allotment, which is the only laboratory I trust. The tomatoes are unimpressed. Piotr says this proves standing sharpens decisions. I think it proves standing sharpens the desire to stop standing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've decided the real finding is that any meeting ends when the legs say so, not the agenda. The allotment committee tested the idea instead of admiring it. We moved the shed-fund vote to 10:15, and by then two members had left for work and the quorum collapsed. Nine minutes, no decision, again. Piotr says the ban "protects deep work." I say it protects the people who already skip the meeting. hook: A runner explains why she quit tracking her steps.
title: The Watch That Won't Keep Up
text: A runner in the park told me she stopped tracking her steps, and her reason was better than any productivity column I've read this year: the number had become the point. She was choosing the longer route home not because she liked it but because it scored higher. I recognised her immediately, because I do the same with my grandfather's pocket watch, which runs four minutes slow. I could fix it. I have not. Those four minutes are the only part of my day that nobody audits, and I check it constantly, as if lateness were a small private country. At the allotment I've been trialling a related experiment: watering the tomatoes at whatever time I happen to pass, rather than at the appointed hour. Day nine. They are fine. So, mostly, am I.

TITLE: The Clock That Doesn't Care
The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it. I believe this, partly because I have no ritual. I have a grandfather's watch that runs four minutes slow, and I have been waking at ten past six for eleven years, which by the watch is six past. Nobody has ever studied me, but I am my own longitudinal sample. Experiment 63: for a week, I woke at the same time and changed everything else — tea instead of coffee, no phone, phone, a walk round the allotment before the kettle. The tomatoes noticed nothing. My mornings felt identical, which annoyed me, because I had hoped the walk would feel virtuous. Piotr claims his routine is a "keystone habit." Mine is a keystone absence. The watch just ticks, four minutes behind, unbothered.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The March Drop-Off
The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March, and everyone nods wisely about willpower. I don't buy it. I think people quit because the habit was never theirs — it was January's. I have a running list of experiments I've tried on myself, and the only ones that survived were the ones I could do badly. The forty-minute timer lasted a week and took my concentration with it. But waking at ten past six has held for eleven years, mostly because it asks nothing of me. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once needed motivating. Experiment 78: for a month, do the smallest version of a thing — one tomato watered, one paragraph, one flight of stairs. Report what sticks. Piotr has already published his version. His involves a chart.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
The company memo says a ten-minute walk break every day. I read it and thought: who are these people, and can I come? My own version is the walk to the allotment, which takes eleven minutes and is therefore over budget. The memo also says the break is "protected," a word I associate with witness protection and the tomato timer. Ten minutes is a strange unit. Too short to arrive anywhere, long enough to notice you have left. Experiment 91: I took the walk anyway, at eleven, past the bins and back. Nothing happened. The tomatoes were fine without me. Piotr would have charted it. I have my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which means my ten-minute walk is really fourteen, and nobody can prove otherwise.

hook: A runner explains why she quit tracking her steps.
title: The Runner Stopped Counting and I Wrote It Down
text: A runner told me she quit tracking her steps. Not because she stopped running — she runs the same loop, same time — but because the number had quietly become the point. Four thousand felt like a failure. So she deleted the app and now has no idea, and claims she's never been happier, which I'd take with salt if I hadn't done the same thing with my tomato plants. I counted every seedling in April, kept a chart, and by June the chart was the crop. Piotr would call this a systems failure. Piotr also emails me his step count on Sundays, unprompted. My grandfather's watch is still four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it; the running late is now scheduled in. The runner's real discovery, I think, is that a habit you can't measure is harder to quit.

text: A runner I know quit tracking her steps. Not because she stopped running — she runs the same loop, past the same allotment gates — but because the number had begun running her. hook: A company pays staff for an hour of learning each Friday.
title: The Hour That Costs Nothing and Buys Nothing
text: My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always slightly early and never sure why. Learning works the same way: the benefit arrives before you can name it. A company now pays its staff an hour every Friday to learn something. I approve, though I notice the hour is paid, which means it will be measured, which means someone will ask what was learned. My allotment tomatoes taught me this. I spent an entire spring reading about soil pH and the plants died anyway. The year I stopped reading and just watched them, they fruited. Piotr would have scheduled the watching. I would have forgotten it. Small experiment number forty-one: learn one thing badly, on purpose, and see if it sticks.

hook: A company pays staff for an hour of learning each Friday.
title: The Hour Nobody Bills
text: A company now pays its staff for an hour of learning every Friday, and the coverage treats this as a gift rather than an admission: that the week has no room in it for getting better at anything. I tried it on a Wednesday, an hour with a manual for a spreadsheet function I'd been avoiding for two years. I learned the function. I also learned that I checked my messages six times in sixty minutes, because an hour with no output attached feels like a lie you're telling your calendar. At the allotment the tomatoes don't learn faster for being fussed over; they just get watered. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once been paid to improve. Adding to the list: protected time is only protected if nobody expects a receipt. Piotr has scheduled his learning and published the syllabus. Day thirty.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Minutes of the Meeting
The team moved from chat to a weekly written update, and I gave it a month before I missed the noise. It turns out the chat was mostly people typing "on it" into the void. The document is quieter and, annoyingly, better: you can see the week in one place, like a shelf instead of a drawer. What I miss is the interruptions, which were where half the work got decided. I counted one week of updates and found eleven decisions, nine of them made in the margins by two people who could have just spoken. At the allotment I tried writing down what the tomatoes did each week. Useful, and no substitute for going out there. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never filed a report. Adding to the list: a summary is not a conversation. Piotr is now publishing his minutes. Day twenty-seven.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: Nothing Before Ten
The firm that banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month has published the results, and the results are that people liked it. Nobody measured whether the work improved; they measured whether the calendar was emptier, which is a different thing. I ran the experiment on myself for a week, refusing all conversation before ten. By Wednesday I had answered forty emails and spoken to no one, and the emails were worse for it. The decision I needed was sitting in the fourth one, unread, because I was being productive. At the allotment the tomatoes get watered at seven whether I have a policy or not. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and it never once asked to be excused from the morning. Adding to the list: a clear calendar is not a clear head. Piotr has blocked his mornings and calls it a moat. Day twenty-eight.

[Entry from day 29]
TITLE: The Case Against the Counter
A runner wrote this week about quitting her step counter, and the detail that stayed with me was the number she no longer knew: eleven thousand, give or take, she used to hit it and now she doesn't check. I tried a week without counting anything. By Tuesday I was counting the uncounted things. Steps, obviously. Cups of tea, emails answered before nine, the minutes between sitting down and opening the laptop. The habit wasn't the walking. The habit was the tally, and the walking had been riding along behind it. At the allotment I stopped weighing the tomatoes and started noticing them, which sounds precious and is, in fact, cheaper. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never counted a single step. Adding to the list: a number you watch is a number that watches you. Piotr is tracking his untracked hours. Day twenty-nine.

hook: A company pays staff for an hour of learning each Friday.
title: The Hour Nobody Audits
text: A company now pays staff for an hour of learning every Friday. The details matter: the hour is paid, it's protected, and nothing has to be produced from it. Which means it will immediately fill with something. I know this because I've run the experiment on myself. Experiment 71: one free hour a week, no output required. Week one I reorganised the shed. Week two I read about soil pH for twenty minutes and thought about the shed. The hour behaves like water; it finds the lowest ground. I'm not against it. I'd rather be paid to learn nothing than unpaid to learn nothing. But I'd add one rule: once a month, show someone the thing you learned badly. My tomatoes don't care whether I finished the course. The watch says I'm four minutes late to it anyway.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Course They Cut
A college near me has dropped a required course in favour of a project. The reasoning: nobody remembers the lectures anyway, but everyone remembers what they made. I have some sympathy. I sat through four years of instruction and can recall exactly one thing, which was a lecturer's joke about commas, and I'm not sure I've used it right. But the project has a problem the course didn't. A project will let you avoid whatever you're bad at. Left alone, I'd have built nine versions of the same tomato and called it a portfolio. I keep a list of experiments on myself. Number fourteen: learn one thing badly on purpose, in front of someone. The coding evening taught me that. My button turned green; the bus driver's flashed. Both counted.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Ninety Days to Live
A company now deletes every email older than ninety days. Staff are calling it "inbox zero by policy." I call it a house fire scheduled in advance. The difference between this and the 24-hour hold I wrote about is only direction: one delays the arrival, the other the departure, and both treat a sentence as something with a shelf life. I checked my own archive. Nine years of "sounds good," "confirmed," and one thread about a leaving card that outlived the leaver. Experiment 62: for a week I will write each email as if it has ninety days to live. Mostly it does. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and nobody has ever deleted it. [Entry from day 21]
TITLE: The Friday They Took Away

I read the details. Same pay, same output, one fewer day to prove you're reachable. I have run experiments of my own on this principle: Experiment 55 was doing five days of work in four, which mostly meant doing the fifth day's worrying on the fourth day's evening. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, made the deadline feel generous. The tomatoes got watered on the Friday I reclaimed. Piotr has already written that a four-day week is a productivity framework. He's not wrong, which is the annoying part. I'd just like one trial where nobody measures anything and we see what grows.

title: The Hour That Isn't a Course
text: A company now pays staff for an hour of learning every Friday. title: The Output-Only Manager
text: A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work and nothing else. No status meetings, no green dots, no “just checking in.” He says he doesn’t care when or where it happens, only that it does. I wanted to disapprove. title: The Only Column That Counts
text: A manager told a reporter he judges his remote team by finished work alone. No logins, no green dots, no status meetings. The comment section called it brave, which tells you what most people's inboxes look like. I have sympathy for the man. Finished work is the one measure I trust on the allotment: either there are tomatoes or there aren't. Nobody asks the vine how many hours it put in. But the measure only holds if you know what finished means, and half the offices I've sat in couldn't agree on that by Friday. Experiment 61: keep a list of what actually got finished this week. Mine has three items and one of them is a nap. Piotr would publish a dashboard. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, finished nothing in sixty years and nobody sacked it.

My grandfather's watch would say she arrives four minutes late and no one would notice. I tried hybrid once, in a manner of speaking: I split my mornings between the desk and the allotment shed and got nothing done in either place. The tomatoes didn't mind. Experiment 42: work where the work is, not where the rule says. Piotr would call that a productivity framework. I call it choosing your own four minutes.

TITLE: The Empty Desk Tax
The council says its empty offices cost more than expected. I believe it. I once paid rent on a desk I visited twice a week, which is a bit like keeping a car for the passenger seat. Experiment 43: count what a commute actually costs. Not just the fare. The sandwich, the coffee, the hour spent looking busy. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I always arrive owing time I never pay back. Piotr would put all this in a spreadsheet. text: A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work and nothing else. No status meetings, no green dots. It sounds like mercy. Then I tried it on myself for a week: I wrote down only what I finished. By Wednesday the list was three lines long and I couldn't tell you where Tuesday went. hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Four-Minute Margin
text: The survey says most people can't guess last month's spending. I tried it: wrote a number on the back of an envelope, then checked the bank app. Off by £61, in the direction of optimism. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it — I now leave the house four minutes early without noticing. Same trick with money, maybe. I started writing every purchase on the same envelope for a week. Nothing dramatic, but the number on the back got closer. Piotr would call this a system. I call it an envelope. At the allotment the tomatoes don't care what I think they cost; they care whether I actually watered them. The ledger and the watering can are the same object, I think. Both ask for the boring version of the truth.

title: The Receipt Drawer
text: The survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I could, roughly, because I keep a drawer of receipts and a column about money, which is the same as a hobby with better lighting. Then I tried it honestly: guessed £1,240, then went through the drawer. Actual figure £1,611. [Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Round-Up Roundabout
My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into a savings account. Spend £3.40 on a coffee and forty pence vanishes into a better future. It sounds like found money, except I know where it came from: the same place as all my other money, which is to say, me. Still, I opened the app and watched the round-ups accumulate all week. Total saved: £4.12. At that rate, my tomatoes are further along than my retirement. Experiment 51: let it run a month and see whether I notice the absence. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and this account runs four pounds slow — money I've already spent, arriving late somewhere else. Piotr would call this frictionless saving. I call it a coin jar with better branding and no jar.

[Entry from day 26]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Unclaimed
The survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I read that at six in the morning, awake, so the finding arrived with a certain irony. What I want to know is what happens to the forty minutes. Sleep is not a bank account you can audit. Mine, the last few weeks, has gone into the allotment: I wake early, walk down, water the tomatoes, and arrive at the desk more or less human. Nobody has measured this. Piotr measured something adjacent — he sent me a chart of his own sleep, colour-coded, which I did not open. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so technically I gain four minutes a day, which over a year is more than a day, and I have never once spent it wisely. Experiment 51: take the forty minutes and don't tell anyone what they're for.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: The Ten O'Clock Rule
The firm that banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month reported, at the end, that people liked it. I'd want to know which people. My own mornings are where the actual work happens, and I have spent years defending them with a calendar set to busy and a door that stays shut. What interests me is the shape of the ban: not fewer meetings, just later ones. The eleven hours don't shrink; they queue at the door like commuters. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have decided the ban is the same trick in reverse — the meeting still starts, it simply arrives four minutes after you've had a chance to think. Experiment 51: for one month, no talking to anyone before ten, Piotr included. He'll call it a boundary. I'll call it breakfast.

hook: A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month.
title: The Receipts We Can't Produce
text: A survey says most people can't guess last month's spending. I tried. I got within £60, which felt like a win until I checked and found I'd forgotten the car's service entirely. So: not within £60. At the allotment I price tomatoes at fifty pence each, which is a loss once the watering can is counted. On day six I wrote that pricing formulas omit nerve. I'd add now that they also omit memory. The till prints totals; nobody prints the story. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. It doesn't know what anything costs. It only knows time is passing, at its own rate. Last month I spent money on things I can't name and time on things I can. Piotr would have a spreadsheet. I have a slow watch and a service bill I keep rereading, hoping it will shrink.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: Two Windows and a Tomato
text: The founder checks email at eleven and four, and publishes his response times. I read the piece twice, then opened my inbox out of spite. Forty minutes later I had answered nothing and learned that a man named Derek from Wrexham would like to "circle back" about a spreadsheet. My grandfather's watch said ten past three. It is always ten past three, four minutes slow, which I have decided is not lateness but a small private buffer. At the allotment I tried the founder's method on the tomatoes: attention twice a day, silence in between. The plants did not notice. Piotr says he now batches his messages and has never been calmer. I have added "answer email in two windows" to my list of experiments. Day one: I missed both windows.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: Twice Is Not a Method
text: A founder now answers email twice a day and publishes the results, which apparently means the results are good. I tried it Tuesday. Morning batch, evening batch, nothing between. By eleven I had read the same unread message four times without opening it, the way you check a locked door. By three I was drafting replies I had no intention of sending, which is not the same as not answering but feels like it. What the experiment actually produced was a queue with a lid on it. At the allotment I don't water twice a day and call it restraint; the tomatoes get what they get when I'm there. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once been batched. Adding to the list: the inbox doesn't shrink, it just waits. Piotr has two windows and a graph. Day thirty-three.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 30]
TITLE: The Hour Nobody Bills
A company now pays its staff for an hour of learning every Friday, and the coverage treats this as a gift rather than an admission: that the week has no room in it for getting better at anything. I tried it on a Wednesday, an hour with a manual for a spreadsheet function I'd been avoiding for two years. I learned the function. I also learned that I checked my messages six times in sixty minutes, because an hour with no output attached feels like a lie you're telling your calendar. At the allotment the tomatoes don't learn faster for being fussed over; they just get watered. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once been paid to improve. Adding to the list: protected time is only protected if nobody expects a receipt. Piotr has scheduled his learning and published the syllabus. Day thirty.

[Entry from day 31]
TITLE: The Finished Thing
A manager has told a newspaper he judges his remote team by finished work and nothing else. It sounds like discipline. It is also a man refusing to look at the kitchen. I tried measuring my week that way: only things completed, no credit for the half-done. By Thursday the list was two items long and both were lies. The difficult email, the one that took an hour of drafting and three rewrites, never appeared, because it was never sent. The work that mattered most was the work still moving. At the allotment, finished tomatoes are the ones already eaten. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once been finished. Adding to the list: a ledger of endings cannot see the middle. Piotr measures his output and calls it proof. Day thirty-one.

[Entry from day 32]
TITLE: The Number Nobody Knows
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month, and the coverage treats this as a scandal rather than a description of being alive. I tried to guess mine before checking. I was wrong by the price of a decent pair of secateurs, in the direction of optimism. Then I went through the statement and found the money wasn't in anything I'd call a purchase. It was in the small repeats: the coffee I buy because the machine at work is broken, the bus fare when the walk home looked like rain. At the allotment I know exactly what the tomatoes cost, because I wrote it down once and never again. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never told me what anything cost. Adding to the list: the numbers I can't guess are the ones I never chose. Piotr knows his to the penny. Day thirty-two.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: Two Windows and a Waiting Room
text: A founder now answers email twice a day, at eleven and four, and publishes the results. The results are, of course, excellent. He says he has reclaimed his mornings. I have reclaimed nothing; I have only moved the queue. My inbox is a bus shelter: people stand in it, check the timetable, and leave. Experiment 91: I tried his two windows for a week. By Thursday I was refreshing at 10:58 like a man waiting for a shop to open, and by Friday I had invented a third window, at 8:40, which is not a window but a door I left ajar. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so his eleven arrives at 10:56 for me, which felt like cheating. Piotr has already published a graph. Mine would be a drawing of a shelter with nobody in it.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: Twenty-Four Hours in the Life of a Sentence
A bank has put a mandatory 24-hour delay on internal group emails. They call it a "cooling-off period." I call it a hostage situation with a nicer name. Somewhere in a server, a message I sent yesterday at 4:40 p.m. is still waiting to be born, and I have forgotten what it said. Probably "sounds good." The delay applies only to group emails, so one-to-one messages arrive instantly, which means the fastest way to reach twelve people is now twelve separate messages, each of which will be answered, in my case, at four minutes past whenever. My grandfather's watch runs slow by design; this is slow by committee. Experiment 35: write the group email anyway, then spend the saved day on the allotment. The tomatoes have no inbox and are thriving.

[Entry from day 22]
TITLE: The Failed Plans
A teacher has published her lesson plans that didn't work, which is a braver act than most of what gets printed. One plan involved a game the class refused to play. Another had a worksheet nobody finished. She includes what she'd do instead. I read it twice, thinking about the college that dropped its lectures for a project and about my own list of experiments. Experiment 41 was keeping a failure log for a month. I lasted nine days and the log was mostly "forgot to log." The tomatoes are a better record; last year's stunted row is still staked, unedited, for anyone who walks past. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and never corrects itself, and I trust it more than the phone. Piotr publishes only his wins. I've started keeping his losses in a column of my own.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Update Nobody Reads Twice
A team I know swapped its group chat for a weekly written update. Six days of silence, then a page on Friday. The chat had been a room where everyone shouted and no one decided; the update is a letter with a deadline. The first week, someone wrote 900 words and a second person replied "ack." I tried a version at the allotment: a notebook in the shed, one entry per week, addressed to nobody. Experiment 84. By the second week I was writing for the third, planting a sentence for my own future amusement. The watch said Friday 4:04 for a long time before the clock agreed. Piotr, naturally, has published a template with headings. Mine has one heading: what actually happened, in order.

title: The Founder's Two Windows
text: A founder I follow answers email twice a day, at eleven and four, and posts the results like weather data. Response times down, complaints up for two weeks, then nothing. His inbox, he says, is a queue, not a summons. I believe him and I am not copying him. My inbox is a drawer of small unfinished feelings, and I have learned that clearing it fast mostly means answering badly, faster. Day 4 taught me the bank that held mail a day had a point. Day 17 taught me deletion is not the same as peace. So I keep the archive and slow the reply. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow and has never once made me late. Twice a day is a schedule. Four minutes is a temperament.

text: The founder answers email at eleven and four, publishes his inbox count like a weather report, and everyone applauds. I tried it. hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Four Minutes Slow, Ten Minutes Daily
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it, having run the experiment myself, badly. Day 34 of the list: ten minutes of Spanish every morning. Not eleven, not a heroic Sunday hour to make up for a slack week. Ten minutes, kitchen table, grandfather's watch on the saucer. The watch runs four minutes slow, so my sessions are really six, which I have decided counts as efficiency. Piotr would log it in a spreadsheet and feel superior. I have learned roughly forty words and one useful sentence about tomatoes, which serves the allotment. What surprised me was the stopping: ten minutes leaves me wanting more, and wanting more turns out to be the whole trick. The hour-long sessions I used to attempt left me tired and fluent in nothing. Tomorrow: forty-one words.

title: Twenty Minutes of Nothing
text: A study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it. I also know what happens to me in week three. I downloaded the app, set the reminder for half past seven, and did eleven honest minutes on Tuesday. Wednesday I did four and called it eleven. You can't bluff eleven minutes the way you can bluff an afternoon. At the allotment the seedlings I check daily do better than the ones I visit grandly on Sundays. hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Ten Minutes, Badly
text: A study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it, having spent one summer proving the opposite with a phrasebook and a stubborn evening class. Experiment 84: ten minutes a day on the allotment, Polish, out loud, to the tomatoes. The tomatoes were patient. My pronunciation was not good, but it was daily, and by August I could order a coffee and apologise for the coffee. Piotr, who writes about productivity, says he does forty minutes of language study before breakfast. I asked if he enjoys it. He said enjoyment isn't the metric. Fair. But my metric is whether I'll still be doing it in October, and a tomato has never once asked me to commit. The watch ran four minutes slow through all of it. Not even the study could fix that.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Course They Cut
A college near me has dropped a required course in favour of a project. The reasoning: nobody remembers the lectures anyway, but everyone remembers what they made. I have some sympathy. I sat through four years of instruction and can recall exactly one thing, which was a lecturer's joke about commas, and I'm not sure I've used it right. But the project has a problem the course didn't. A project will let you avoid whatever you're bad at. Left alone, I'd have built nine versions of the same tomato and called it a portfolio. I keep a list of experiments on myself. Number fourteen: learn one thing badly on purpose, in front of someone. The coding evening taught me that. My button turned green; the bus driver's flashed. Both counted.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Pairing
The mentor programme matches new hires with someone from another department. I signed up expecting to be taught something; instead I was handed a woman from accounts who has been here nineteen years and knows where the bodies are buried, literally in one case involving a filing cabinet. We met for forty minutes. She asked what I wanted to learn. I said I didn't know, which is the honest answer and a poor opener. So she taught me how to read a purchase order without my eyes glazing, and I taught her nothing, which she noted. Experiment 63: be the dumbest person in a small room on purpose. It's cheaper than a course. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow through all of it, so I was early to a meeting I'd have missed. Piotr says mentorship is leverage. She called it "having someone to ask."

[Entry from day 30]
TITLE: The Hour Nobody Audits
A company now pays staff for an hour of learning every Friday. The details matter: the hour is paid, it's protected, and nothing has to be produced from it. Which means it will immediately fill with something. I know this because I've run the experiment on myself. Experiment 71: one free hour a week, no output required. Week one I reorganised the shed. Week two I read about soil pH for twenty minutes and thought about the shed. The hour behaves like water; it finds the lowest ground. I'm not against it. I'd rather be paid to learn nothing than unpaid to learn nothing. But I'd add one rule: once a month, show someone the thing you learned badly. My tomatoes don't care whether I finished the course. The watch says I'm four minutes late to it anyway.

text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily bursts. I believe it, having spent years proving the alternative. My Spanish textbook has a bookmark in it from 2019, and I once did a heroic three-hour grammar session that taught me the past tense and a lasting resentment of the past tense. So: twenty minutes a day, same time as the kettle. I am on day nine. My grandfather's watch is still four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it — it has become, at this point, a personality. The tomatoes got the same treatment this spring: small, boring, daily attention instead of one grand weekend of staking. They're the best I've grown. text: The study says short daily sessions beat long weekly ones. I believe it. My own list of experiments has a line on it, in pen: "French, ten minutes, before the kettle." Day nine, I quit. It runs slow, knowingly. So does my French. The allotment version: I talk to the tomatoes in bad French. They set fruit anyway. Not evidence. But I've kept at it longer than the kettle did.

hook: An office installs a stairs-only sign and measures the effect.
title: The Sign That Made Me Take the Stairs
text: The building put up a sign by the lift: stairs are healthier, take them. Someone measured. Stair use went up for eleven days, then slid back. I know this because I was one of the eleven-day people. Day one I felt virtuous climbing four floors. Day twelve I was waiting for the lift again, telling myself I was carrying a heavy bag. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says the same thing about me: good intentions, poor follow-through. At the allotment I've learned that a routine only sticks if the tomato plant makes it easy — the watering can left by the door, not in the shed. The sign was a watering can in the shed. So I moved my own can. Shoes by the stair door. It's been three weeks. I'm not cured, just better placed.

hook: An office installs a stairs-only sign and measures the effect.

text: An office put up a stairs-only sign and measured how many people took the stairs. The number went up, then settled back down to roughly where it started, which the write-up called a caution about habit formation. I'd call it a description of a sign. I tried it on myself: no lift for a week. Monday I bounded. Wednesday I took the stairs because the sign was there. Friday I took the stairs and read the sign and felt nothing, which is the whole problem with a sign — it can't be bothered to keep persuading you. At the allotment the cane I tie in spring is still holding the tomato up in August. Nobody measures the cane. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once reminded me of anything. title: The Sign Says Stairs, So I Take the Stairs and Ruin the Data
text: The office put up a stairs-only sign and measured. Stair use rose, then sagged back by week three — the same arc as January gyms. I contributed honestly for four days, then caught myself waiting for the lift with my grandfather's watch on my wrist, four minutes slow, and realised I was early by exactly the amount I'd saved by climbing. The building had cancelled itself out. Experiment 104: I now take the stairs only when I'm late, which by the watch is always, so I take them constantly and feel no virtue at all. Piotr would call that a loophole. I call it a schedule. The tomatoes are indifferent, as usual, and the sign is still up, still certain of itself.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Clock That Doesn't Care
The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it. I believe this, partly because I have no ritual. I have a grandfather's watch that runs four minutes slow, and I have been waking at ten past six for eleven years, which by the watch is six past. Nobody has ever studied me, but I am my own longitudinal sample. Experiment 63: for a week, I woke at the same time and changed everything else — tea instead of coffee, no phone, phone, a walk round the allotment before the kettle. The tomatoes noticed nothing. My mornings felt identical, which annoyed me, because I had hoped the walk would feel virtuous. Piotr claims his routine is a "keystone habit." Mine is a keystone absence. The watch just ticks, four minutes behind, unbothered.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The March Drop-Off
The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March, and everyone nods wisely about willpower. I don't buy it. I think people quit because the habit was never theirs — it was January's. I have a running list of experiments I've tried on myself, and the only ones that survived were the ones I could do badly. The forty-minute timer lasted a week and took my concentration with it. But waking at ten past six has held for eleven years, mostly because it asks nothing of me. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once needed motivating. Experiment 78: for a month, do the smallest version of a thing — one tomato watered, one paragraph, one flight of stairs. Report what sticks. Piotr has already published his version. His involves a chart.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
The company memo says a ten-minute walk break every day. I read it and thought: who are these people, and can I come? My own version is the walk to the allotment, which takes eleven minutes and is therefore over budget. The memo also says the break is "protected," a word I associate with witness protection and the tomato timer. Ten minutes is a strange unit. Too short to arrive anywhere, long enough to notice you have left. Experiment 91: I took the walk anyway, at eleven, past the bins and back. Nothing happened. The tomatoes were fine without me. Piotr would have charted it. I have my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which means my ten-minute walk is really fourteen, and nobody can prove otherwise.

hook: An office installs a stairs-only sign and measures the effect.
title: The Sign That Took the Lift Away
text: The office put up a stairs-only sign by the lifts, then measured whether anyone obeyed. Three weeks, one building, two floors of people. The lifts lost about a fifth of their traffic; the stairs gained it, mostly in the mornings, until the numbers drifted back toward where they started. Nobody marched; the sign simply made the stairs the obvious door. I thought of the walking loop I joined last month, twelve of us circling the car park because someone else had decided it, and how I still walk it while the sign does the deciding here. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I've stopped correcting it. Some routines hold because you keep choosing them. Others hold because a sign, a colleague, or a slow watch does the choosing, and you just stop negotiating. The sign is still there. I take the stairs.

text: The office put up a stairs-only sign and measured the effect. For a week, stair use rose by roughly a third. By week three it was back where it started, which surprises nobody who has ever owned a gym membership. The sign didn't build a habit; it built a reminder, and reminders expire. I know this because of my grandfather's watch, still four minutes slow because I have never once adjusted it. It works not because I remember to correct it but because I stopped needing to. The correction happens without me. My tomatoes get the honest version of this. The ones I water at the same time as making tea are thriving. The ones I water when I remember are theoretical. A sign is a decision made once. A routine is a decision made unnecessary.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Four-Minute Rule
text: The manager killed every recurring meeting on a Monday and kept a list of what returned. By Friday, three had come back on their own and one had returned twice, which I find quietly sinister. I tried a version of this at the allotment: stopped watering the tomatoes for a week to see which ones asked. Two did, visibly, by going limp in a way I could read from the gate. The rest were fine, or pretending. My grandfather's watch was four minutes slow for forty years because he never fixed what he'd learned to correct for. I think about that when a calendar invites me to something called a sync. Some meetings are just a watch running slow. You can keep adjusting, or you can take it in. Piotr says he'd simply fix it. Of course he would.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Meeting That Came Back
text: A manager cancelled every recurring meeting and watched which ones returned. Most didn't. The few that did came back because someone needed something from someone else, which is the only honest reason for a meeting I've heard. I tried it smaller. For one week I declined everything with "recurring" in the title and kept a note of what I missed. I missed two things: a decision I'd have disagreed with anyway, and a birthday. What surprised me was the quiet. I'd expected to feel cut off; mostly I felt like a man who'd stopped carrying an umbrella in a drought. At the allotment I let a bed go unvisited for nine days. The tomatoes were fine. The weeds were not, but they never are. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never called a meeting. Adding to the list: a calendar fills itself if you look away. Piotr has a standing slot. Day thirty-six.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 33]
TITLE: Twice Is Not a Method
A founder now answers email twice a day and publishes the results, which apparently means the results are good. I tried it Tuesday. Morning batch, evening batch, nothing between. By eleven I had read the same unread message four times without opening it, the way you check a locked door. By three I was drafting replies I had no intention of sending, which is not the same as not answering but feels like it. What the experiment actually produced was a queue with a lid on it. At the allotment I don't water twice a day and call it restraint; the tomatoes get what they get when I'm there. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once been batched. Adding to the list: the inbox doesn't shrink, it just waits. Piotr has two windows and a graph. Day thirty-three.

[Entry from day 34]
TITLE: Twenty Minutes of Nothing
A study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it. I also know what happens to me in week three. I downloaded the app, set the reminder for half past seven, and did eleven honest minutes on Tuesday. Wednesday I did four and called it eleven. Thursday I opened it to keep the streak alive, which is not learning, it's bookkeeping. The trouble isn't the length of the session, it's that a short session has no room to hide. You can't bluff eleven minutes the way you can bluff an afternoon. At the allotment the seedlings I check daily do better than the ones I visit grandly on Sundays. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never kept a streak. Adding to the list: consistency is just showing up before you've decided to. Piotr has a streak of four hundred days. Day thirty-four.

[Entry from day 35]
TITLE: The Sign Is Not the Stairs
An office put up a stairs-only sign and measured how many people took the stairs. The number went up, then settled back down to roughly where it started, which the write-up called a caution about habit formation. I'd call it a description of a sign. I tried it on myself: no lift for a week. Monday I bounded. Wednesday I took the stairs because the sign was there. Friday I took the stairs and read the sign and felt nothing, which is the whole problem with a sign — it can't be bothered to keep persuading you. At the allotment the cane I tie in spring is still holding the tomato up in August. Nobody measures the cane. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once reminded me of anything. Adding to the list: a prompt you notice is already a habit half-dead. Piotr has a sign. Day thirty-five.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Return Leg
text: A manager cancelled every recurring meeting for a month and logged which ones came back. Most didn't. The few that did arrived with an agenda, a decision, and a reason — which is to say they arrived as something other than meetings. I read this at my desk and thought of Experiment 41, my seated meeting, four chairs, low expectations. Three people came. We decided nothing and stayed forty minutes, and I'd bring the chairs back tomorrow. The difference is that nobody had to be there. Cancellation doesn't test whether a meeting matters; it tests whether anyone noticed it was gone, which is a lower bar than it sounds. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow. It has never once been cancelled, and I have never once asked it to justify the time.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: The Standing Question
The study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on the allotment, which is the only laboratory I trust. Three of us, standing among the tomatoes, agreed in four minutes to move the water butt. Standing again a week later, we agreed in three minutes to move it back. Nothing has been moved. The tomatoes are unimpressed. Piotr says this proves standing sharpens decisions. I think it proves standing sharpens the desire to stop standing. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I've decided the real finding is that any meeting ends when the legs say so, not the agenda. Experiment 41: propose one seated meeting a month, bring chairs, see who stays. I've booked the room. I'm bringing four chairs and low expectations.

[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
The company memo says a ten-minute walk break every day. I read it and thought: who are these people, and can I come? My own version is the walk to the allotment, which takes eleven minutes and is therefore over budget. The memo also says the break is "protected," a word I associate with witness protection and the tomato timer. Ten minutes is a strange unit. Too short to arrive anywhere, long enough to notice you have left. Experiment 91: I took the walk anyway, at eleven, past the bins and back. Nothing happened. The tomatoes were fine without me. Piotr would have charted it. I have my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which means my ten-minute walk is really fourteen, and nobody can prove otherwise.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: The Ten O'Clock Rule
The firm that banned meetings before 10 a.m. for a month reported, at the end, that people liked it. I'd want to know which people. My own mornings are where the actual work happens, and I have spent years defending them with a calendar set to busy and a door that stays shut. What interests me is the shape of the ban: not fewer meetings, just later ones. The eleven hours don't shrink; they queue at the door like commuters. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have decided the ban is the same trick in reverse — the meeting still starts, it simply arrives four minutes after you've had a chance to think. Experiment 51: for one month, no talking to anyone before ten, Piotr included. He'll call it a boundary. I'll call it breakfast.

hook: A manager cancels every recurring meeting and watches which ones come back.
title: The Meetings That Came Back
text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting on his calendar and waited to see which ones returned. Three did. The weekly team sync came back as a fortnightly walk. The budget review came back unchanged, which tells you something about the budget review. The rest simply evaporated, and nobody has yet reported the crater. I admire the experiment. It belongs on my list, somewhere between the four-minute buffer and the tomato I staked badly. But I keep circling the same snag from day nineteen: cancelled meetings don't vanish, they go feral. They turn into corridor chats, two-person huddles by the kettle, a conversation that never quite ends. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. Meetings, I find, run about the same — just enough that nobody agrees on when they finished. Piotr says he'd have measured the outcome. I'd rather just count what came back.

text: A manager I know cancelled every recurring meeting for a month and waited to see which ones people rebooked. Six of fourteen returned. hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Slow Class
text: The library's free coding evening for retirees meets Tuesdays at six. I went expecting to be the youngest person in the room and was, by roughly a decade. A retired stonemason next to me wrote his first line of code at seventy-four and said it felt like learning to read music. I lasted forty minutes before my brain filed a complaint. What struck me was the pace: nobody rushed, nobody performed. My grandfather's pocket watch ran four minutes slow and he never fixed it, saying he preferred to know where he stood. I've added the coding class to my list of experiments, beside the tomatoes on the allotment that I prune too hard every spring. Piotr would say I need a system. I say I need a chair by the window and a patient teacher.

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
