hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes, Unbilled
text: The company memo says: a ten-minute walk break, daily, encouraged. Encouraged is doing a lot of work in that sentence. I took mine at 11:40, which is when the office is at its most sincere, and walked to the corner and back. Nothing happened. That's the point, I think. I've had "walk more" on the experiment list for two years and never once honoured it, because a vague resolution has no edges. Ten minutes has edges. It ends. At the allotment I've been giving the greenhouse the same treatment — ten minutes of pinching out side shoots, then done, whether the row is finished or not. The timer taught me that; the memo just made it official. Piotr has already posted his step count. I have not. My watch says I left four minutes early, which is at least a kind of record.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 6]
TITLE: The Watch That Won't Keep Up
A runner told me she stopped tracking her steps. The number had turned a nice walk into a debt. I understood. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've never had it fixed. For years I treated those four minutes as a fault, syncing it against my phone each morning like a small act of discipline. Then I stopped. Now I arrive four minutes late to things and blame the watch, which is dishonest but restful. At the allotment I've been testing the same idea on tomatoes: one row watered on a strict schedule, one row watered when I remember. The remembered row is doing better, though I can't rule out that I remember it more fondly. Piotr would log both rows. I've decided not to tell him.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Constant
A study says the shape of your morning matters less than the hour you get up. I read this with my grandfather's watch in my hand, four minutes slow as ever, and felt briefly vindicated. My mornings have no shape at all. Some days I'm up before the kettle knows it; other days I conduct entire arguments in bed. What stays fixed is the getting up, and lately I've noticed the fixed part is the only part doing any work. At the allotment I've stopped moving things around — same bed, same time, same careless watering. The tomatoes have settled into it. Piotr, I suspect, has a spreadsheet with a tab for each sunrise. I have a watch that lies by four minutes and a row of tomatoes that don't care. I've added this to the list of experiments: keep the hour, lose the ceremony.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: The Timer Doesn't Care
A writer I like works in forty-minute blocks and stops when the kitchen timer rings, mid-sentence if need be. I tried it. Forty minutes is longer than it sounds and shorter than I'd like. The first block I spent eleven minutes deciding what counted as work. The timer rang anyway. That's the appeal, I think: it's a machine with no opinion about whether I've been brilliant. My grandfather's watch would never. Four minutes slow and full of feeling. The timer is honest in a way I find slightly rude. At the allotment I've started bringing it, forty minutes of weeding, then out, whether the row is finished or not. The rows look worse and I mind less. This goes on the list: let something else call time. Piotr times his blocks to the second and calls it freedom. I've stopped arguing with him about it. Mostly.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes, and the Meeting That Followed Me
text: The company has introduced a ten-minute walk break at eleven. I went, because I am not brave enough to be the one who stays at her desk. I walked to the corner and back and it was fine. Then I sat down and the meeting that had been circling my head all morning was still circling, just slightly damper. This is the flaw in the small-habit gospel: the walk happens, the problem stays. Piotr will write that the walk "recharges focus by 27 percent," and I will read it on the walk. My grandfather wore a watch four minutes slow and never once called it a habit; he called it "being early." I have added the eleven o'clock walk to my list of experiments, marked "inconclusive, pending a week." The tomatoes got rain, which they did not ask for and seem pleased about.

Piotr would call this a system. I call it the same thing I said about the stairs-only sign: the people walking were already walkers. The tomatoes got watered either way.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: The Inbox Gets a Bedtime
text: A founder I follow now opens his email twice a day, at ten and four, and publishes the numbers like a weather report. Response times up, he says, stress down. I read it on the bus and felt the familiar itch to test it on myself, the way I test things on the tomatoes before trusting them in the ground. My inbox is mostly newsletters and one friend who sends links at midnight. Still, I tried it: phone in a drawer, laptop shut, until ten. I got the drawer open by 9:40. My grandfather's watch said 9:36, which is the honest figure. Piotr would have a spreadsheet. I have a pocket watch that lies kindly and a suspicion that twice a day is twice too often for a man whose messages mostly say "no worries."

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.

text: A founder now answers email twice daily and publishes the results. The results, as far as I can tell, are that he answers email twice daily and has told everyone. My grandfather's watch does the honest version of this trick — it runs four minutes slow and never announces it. At the allotment I have stopped watering the tomatoes at lunchtime; they prefer morning, and nobody has published a graph. Piotr would log his replies and feel calm. I owe him one, which I will now write twice.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Same Price for Less Soap
The soap I have bought for years has quietly lost fifteen grams. Same box, same shelf, same price, slightly thinner bar. Nobody announced it. It just got smaller while I wasn't looking, which is how most things change. I weighed it on the kitchen scale, because I am that person now, and confirmed what my hand already knew in the shower. My grandfather's watch does the opposite: it runs four minutes slow and has never once pretended otherwise. I trust it more than the soap. At the allotment I have been testing a smaller version of this on myself — same three tomato plants, less fussing, and the yield is down but the taste is up, which is either a lesson or an excuse. The third day I left it and noticed I was walking faster, as if the point were to finish. By Friday I had slowed to the pace of a man with nowhere to be, which is the whole trick and also the hardest part. My watch said four minutes slow the entire time, and for once I was grateful. Piotr would schedule his and log it. I owe him a reply.

hook: A founder answers email only twice a day and publishes the results.
title: Twice Is Not a Habit
text: The founder answers email at eleven and at four, and published the results: fewer replies, shorter replies, nobody died. I read it on my phone, twice, between 9:40 and 9:52. I have tried this. Day one went well. Day two I opened the inbox "just to look," the way I check the tomatoes for blight I know isn't there. By day four I was answering at eleven, four, and also 2:15, 3:50 and once at 11:58 p.m. to prove a point to nobody. Two fixed times is not a system; it's a mood with a schedule. The watch on my wrist loses four minutes daily and never once negotiates. Maybe that's the trick — not choosing when to answer, but being reliably, boringly slow. Piotr answers twice a day already. He answers twice before I've found my glasses.

hook: A company pays staff for an hour of learning each Friday.
title: The Friday Hour
text: The company now pays everyone for an hour of learning on Fridays. The catalogue is long: spreadsheets, public speaking, a course called "Embracing Ambiguity" that I suspect is forty minutes of silence. I signed up for bread. Specifically, sourdough, taught by a man in accounts who brought his starter in a jar like a small, damp pet. I have baked bread before. My loaves come out as dense as a brick with ambitions. But an hour of being instructed by someone who has actually done the thing is different from an hour of reading about it — the why arrives on a Tuesday, paid for, and then your hands have to catch up. My starter is now on the windowsill, sulking. The watch says I am four minutes late to feed it. Piotr says he is using his hour for a negotiation course. Of course he is.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: The Slow Class
The library has started free coding evenings for retirees, and I went, mostly because the poster was laminated and I respect that. Nine of us, average age seventy-one, one shared laptop between two. The instructor, a patient man of about twenty-five, taught us a loop: a thing that repeats until you tell it to stop. I thought of my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, ticking through a loop it never chose. Then I thought of the tomatoes at the allotment, which follow the same logic—water, wait, repeat—and which I have been failing at for three seasons. Piotr would have called the evening "upskilling." I call it an hour spent being bad at something in company, which is underrated. I typed a loop. It ran. Four minutes late, as usual, I went home.

[Entry from day 5]
TITLE: The Weekly Digest
The team announced it today: chat is out, a written update every Friday is in. Two paragraphs each, what you did, what you need. My first thought was that this is just a meeting with a delay. My second thought was about the pocket watch. Four minutes slow, and nobody has ever complained, because the margin is written into everything I do with it. The written update works the same way — the delay is the point. A chat message is a watering can filled to the line; a Friday note is a thumb's width short, and the tomatoes turn out fine. I have added it to the list of experiments: one week, no chat. Piotr would say I am avoiding accountability. I would say I am buying myself four minutes, and paying in words.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: The Course They Cancelled
A college has dropped a required course in favour of a project, which the dean calls "learning by doing." I have been learning by doing for years, and my tomatoes would like a word. This season I skipped the course—the books, the schedule, the tidy rows—and simply planted. Half the seedlings died of optimism. The other half produced fruit so small the cat declined them. What the project taught me: which corner of the plot floods, which compost is a lie, and that I check the watch four minutes late to my own mistakes. What it didn't teach me: why. That's what the cancelled course was for, I think—the why, delivered on a Tuesday, by someone paid to know. Piotr would call my plot "iterative." I call it three seasons of expensive salad.

text: A company now pays its staff for one hour of learning every Friday. I read the announcement twice looking for the catch, the way you read a lease. Three winters at the allotment taught me more about tomatoes than any course, mainly because no one was invoicing me for the failures. Piotr says he would use the hour to learn a language. I have added it to the list of experiments.

text: The study says short daily sessions beat marathon cramming for adult language learners. I believe it, mostly because I have run the opposite experiment on myself for years without meaning to. Small and often seems to be the whole trick, in languages and in fruit. Ask me in March, when the phrasebook usually wins.

hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Four Minutes a Day
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it. I have been running short daily sessions on myself for years, and the list is now long enough to be a language. Ten minutes of scales on the piano: after a month I could play the first bar of a song I don't like. Five minutes of French before bed: I can now order a coffee and apologise for it. Piotr, naturally, has a streak of nine hundred days and a graph. I have a stack of abandoned notebooks and a tomato plant that heard "little and often" and produced one cherry tomato a week all summer, each the size of a pea, each perfect. That's the trick the study misses: short sessions don't make you fluent. They make you the kind of person who keeps showing up four minutes late, which the watch has been training me for all along.

A runner told me she stopped tracking her steps. The number had turned a nice walk into a debt. I understood. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, and I've never had it fixed. The chat tool has introduced quiet hours. Notifications stop at nine and resume at seven, which means the firm now owns the silence it used to spend money asking me to find. I should be pleased. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I mention it again only because this is the same trick at a larger scale: a deliberate delay, built in, nobody asked. title: Forty Minutes Nobody Asked For
text: The survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I read it twice, the way I read my grandfather's watch twice, hoping it will agree with me. Forty minutes is not nothing. TITLE: The Finished Thing
A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work only. No status meetings, no green dots, no asking whether anyone is at their desk. On paper it is the cleanest system I have heard of. My grandfather's watch is four minutes slow, and I have always defended the margin — it is slack, and slack absorbs surprises. I suspect the tomatoes will do fine and I will learn nothing until October. Piotr would call that a metric. I call it faith with a deadline.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: The Timer Doesn't Care
A writer I like works in forty-minute blocks and stops when the kitchen timer rings, mid-sentence if need be. I tried it. Forty minutes is longer than it sounds and shorter than I'd like. The first block I spent eleven minutes deciding what counted as work. The timer rang anyway. That's the appeal, I think: it's a machine with no opinion about whether I've been brilliant. My grandfather's watch would never. Four minutes slow and full of feeling. The timer is honest in a way I find slightly rude. At the allotment I've started bringing it, forty minutes of weeding, then out, whether the row is finished or not. The rows look worse and I mind less. One room, twelve strangers, no calendar: something might happen there that I cannot schedule. The watch says four minutes slow, as usual. title: The Rent Review
text: My landlord raised the rent by nine per cent and sent the letter in an envelope marked Important. The pay rise at the same job came to two per cent, and arrived as an email with a smiley face. I did the sums on the back of the letter, which felt appropriate. Nine against two is not a negotiation, it is weather. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have started to think of the gap as the only thing in my life that has never gone up. At the allotment the tomatoes have taught me the same lesson from the other direction: when the water is short, the fruit is smaller and better, and nobody sends you a letter about it. I have added it to the list: one month of writing down every price rise and every pay rise in the same column. Piotr would call it a budget. I call it a scoreboard I keep losing on.

[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: The Four-Minute Discount
The shop published its pricing method today: cost, plus a margin, plus a little for the rent. Honest enough. What struck me was the note at the bottom — prices reviewed every quarter. My grandfather's pocket watch is reviewed never, and runs four minutes slow, and I have worn it for eleven years. I have stopped correcting it. Four minutes early is a kind of margin. At the allotment I have been testing something similar on the tomatoes. Same seed, same bed, two watering cans: one filled to the line, one a thumb's width short. The short ones are fine. Slightly smaller, sweeter, no complaints. Piotr would call this sloppy measurement. I call it a price I am willing to pay, and I have written it on the list, under the watch.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Town's Own Money
The town has issued its own currency, good only in the small shops on the high street. You change your pounds at the library, one for one, and the notes have a picture of the bridge on them. The argument is that money spent locally stays local. I like the argument and distrust the picture. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have decided that is a local currency too: it buys me four minutes the rest of the town does not have, and the shops on the high street will not take it. I changed twenty pounds and spent the notes on tomatoes and a tin of paint. The tomatoes were the same price, the paint was not. I have added it to the list: one month on the town's money, and see whether I notice the exchange rate. Piotr would call it a closed system. I call it a watch that only tells one street's time.

[Entry from day 27]
TITLE: The Small Print on the Crisp Packet
The supermarket has done it again: same price, less inside. The bag of crisps now has a polite little dent at the top, as if it has been on a diet. I weighed it on the kitchen scales, because I am that person, and the maths came out at forty grams where it used to be fifty. Nobody announced it. The price stayed exactly where it was, and the bag just quietly got emptier. My grandfather's watch does the opposite. It runs four minutes slow, and has done for eleven years, and it has never once pretended to be anything else. That feels honest by comparison. The crisps are the town's own money again — the same number on the front, less behind it. I have added it to the list: one month of weighing everything I buy, and see whether the price per gram annoys me more than the price. Piotr would call it a productivity audit. I call it reading the packet.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.
title: The Tuesday Mandate
text: My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow, which means I have never once been late by its reckoning and never once on time by anyone else's. I thought about that watch when I read that a firm now requires everyone in the office on Tuesdays. One day. A single shared day, chosen so that the corridors have bodies in them and the meeting rooms have arguments in them. It is a modest experiment, and I approve of modest experiments. On the allotment I have learned that you do not move a tomato plant every day of the week and expect fruit; you move it once, decisively, and then leave it alone. Whether the firm's Tuesday will ripen anything is another matter. I have added it to my list of experiments I am not conducting personally.

hook: A firm requires everyone back in the office on Tuesdays.

text: The firm announced that everyone must be in the office on Tuesdays. Not Monday, when nobody has recovered, and not Friday, when nobody is pretending to. Tuesday: the day the building's coffee machine earns its keep. I went in. The commute took fifty-one minutes, which I know because I timed it against my grandfather's pocket watch, still four minutes slow, which means I arrived four minutes early and called it punctuality. The office was loud in a way I'd forgotten — a particular hum of people performing availability. I got less done than at my kitchen table, where the only interruptions are the allotment. My small experiment: I marked the day in my notebook as "attendance" rather than "work." Piotr would call that unproductive. He'd also have brought a spreadsheet. I brought a tomato from the greenhouse, which ripened on the windowsill beside the printer. Nobody asked about it. That felt instructive.

text: The email says everyone must be in on Tuesdays. Not "encouraged." Not "please." Must. I read it on a Monday, at my kitchen table, wearing the jumper I would not wear to an office. So Tuesday becomes a performance of presence. I will bring the good flask. I will arrive early enough to look willing. And I will keep the watch four minutes slow, so I have an excuse.

hook: A town introduces a local currency for small shops.
title: Four Minutes Slow, Ten Percent Off
text: The town where my sister lives has started a local currency. You swap pounds for "Harbour Notes" at the library and spend them only in shops within the ring road. The council calls it a boost for independents. My sister calls it a second wallet to forget. I like the idea more than I trust it. Money is mostly a habit, and habits take about three weeks to form. I gave myself a small experiment once: cash only for a fortnight. I spent less, mostly because I hated the queue at the ATM, not because I'd become wise. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. I've never fixed it. It keeps me honest about how much of any system is just the story we tell about it. A currency is a promise with a logo. Harbour Notes may work. But so does a smile and exact change.

I bought a loaf and felt like a participant in something. My grandfather's watch ran its usual four minutes slow, and I wondered whether a local currency also runs slow, whether the whole town is quietly four minutes behind and nobody minds. My experiment for the day: I paid in Brooks and counted it as a small act of citizenship rather than a transaction. Piotr would demand a spreadsheet. The loaf was good, though.

title: The Uncounted Mile
text: A runner I read about stopped tracking her steps. She said the number had begun to feel like a verdict. I understand the pull of that ledger — I keep one myself, a list of small experiments run on my own habits, each with a result in the margin. So this week I ran the tomatoes on no schedule at all, just a thumb in the soil when I remembered. Two came out fine. One didn't. I haven't logged which, and I'm not going to. [Entry from day 6]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four

Somewhere in the third I actually wrote something, and when the bell went off I felt robbed — I was nearly at the end of a thought. So I gave myself four more minutes, which is exactly how much my grandfather's watch lags behind the world. Number twenty-three on my list of small experiments: borrow a stranger's method exactly, then cheat it by the precise margin of my own watch. Piotr would call that a failure of discipline. I call it calibration. The tomatoes got watered on time, at least.

hook: A runner explains why she quit tracking her steps.
title: The Runner Who Put Down the Number
text: A runner I know quit tracking her steps. Not because she stopped running — she runs the same loop, past the same bakery — but because the number had begun editing the loop. On tired days she'd pace the kitchen at ten at night to round it up. She wanted the running back, not the tally. I recognise the editing. On day six I admitted that timed work blocks lost to untimed fussing, and I gave the timer four minutes of slack, borrowed from my grandfather's watch, which runs slow by exactly that much. I told myself this was wisdom. It may just have been a smaller number to obey. Still, there's a difference between a watch that's wrong and a watch that argues. Tomatoes don't care how I count them. I'm trying her experiment anyway: one week, no tally.

title: The Apprentice's Four Minutes
text: The mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments. I have been assigned a young man from Finance named Callum, who asked me on day one what my five-year plan is. I said I own a watch that runs four minutes slow and I intend to keep it. He wrote this down, which worried me. My own mentor, years ago, taught me the only skill that stuck: how to ask a question and then shut up. I passed that on to Callum. He lasted nine seconds. Experiment forty-four: learn something from someone who knows nothing about it. Callum explained depreciation to me. I explained suckers to Callum. Only one of us listened, and the tomatoes are the better for it. The watch says 9:04. It is 9:08. Callum is four minutes ahead of everything and late to nothing. I have decided to keep him.

TITLE: The Hour That Costs Nothing and Buys Nothing
The company now pays for an hour of learning every Friday. Piotr, of course, has already published his syllabus. Mine is one tomato plant. My allotment neighbour insists the best way to learn pruning is to ruin something cheap, so I have been mutilating a spare cordon since March. It is not going well. The plant looks like it lost an argument. But I have learned the difference between a sucker and a leader, which is more than I can say for most meetings. The hour is paid, which makes it faintly suspicious, like a gift with a receipt attached. Still, I spent mine outdoors with a knife and no laptop. Experiment twenty-three: learn one thing badly, on purpose, every Friday. The watch says I have four extra minutes. I intend to waste them.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: Quiet Hours
The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. A small mercy, announced with a small icon of a moon. I read it at 9:04 by my grandfather's watch, which is 9:08, and felt the specific relief of being told I may ignore people. My phone has been on silent since 2019, so this changes nothing and I approve of it entirely. Experiment number nine was "answer every message within the hour for a week." I lasted two days and one very long night. The problem was never the notifications; it was the answering. Still, I like the moon icon. It suggests someone at the company has a bed. I have added experiment twenty-three: leave one message unanswered until morning and see if the world tilts. It will not. Piotr will email me about it at midnight.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Nine-Pound Fog
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tried it on the train: wrote down a number, then opened the banking app. I was off by nine pounds, which sounds close until you remember nine pounds is a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that I once spent a fortnight thinking about whether to spend one. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Money is the same: it never tells you the time, only that time has passed. Piotr claims he can account for every penny, which I believe, and which is its own kind of poverty. Experiment thirty-one: for one week, write down each purchase by hand. I lasted until Wednesday, when I bought a coffee and a plant tie and could not remember which came first. The tomatoes do not care. They cost nothing to look at.

hook: A mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments.
title: The Mentor Who Wasn't Mine
text: The new mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments. I signed up as a mentor, which was optimistic, given my only qualification is having been wrong in public for eleven years. My mentee asked what I do when I get stuck. I said I stop and make tea. She wrote it down. I wanted to say something better, so I added: notice what you're avoiding. That earned a second line. At the allotment I once grafted a tomato onto the wrong rootstock and got a plant that grew beautifully and tasted of nothing. Skill, I think, is mostly knowing which rootstock you're on. My grandfather's watch knows it runs four minutes slow; it has never pretended otherwise, and nobody has ever trusted it less for that. Next week I'll ask her what she's avoiding. Fair warning: I'll have notes.

hook: A team tries 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter.
title: The Agenda Was the Meeting
text: My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have stopped correcting it. It is honest about what it is. Meetings are not honest about what they are. A team I know tried "no agenda, no meeting" for a quarter, and by week three they had discovered the real agenda of half their calendar: to be seen wanting to be useful. The rule did not kill meetings. It killed the ones nobody could name a purpose for, which is most of them. What survived was shorter and stranger and occasionally necessary. On the allotment I do the same thing with tomatoes: I stop watering the ones I cannot explain, and the ones that live are the ones I meant to grow. My rival Piotr would call this a system. I call it not lying to myself before nine.

title: The Empty Chair
text: A team tried 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter and reported fewer meetings, which is like reporting fewer tomatoes after fencing the bed. My experiment: at the next meeting I wrote down only what was decided. Two lines. The other fifty minutes are unaccounted for, and I suspect Piotr would itemise them.

hook: A team tries 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter.
title: No Agenda, No Meeting
text: A logistics firm near Leeds banned meetings without agendas for a quarter and reports that meeting hours fell by a third. The unannounced half, it turns out, mostly arrives as someone saying "quick one" while standing up. My grandfather's watch ran four minutes slow, and I've started scheduling meetings to begin four minutes early, so that anyone arriving on time finds the room already disagreeing. Piotr, who writes about productivity, would call this a system. It is closer to a superstition with a calendar. Still, the meetings I dread most are the ones with a clear agenda, because someone has thought carefully about what they want from me.

text: The packet of biscuits now holds nine instead of ten. Same price, same shelf, same cheerful font. TITLE: Four Minutes of Local Currency
The town of Marlow has issued its own money. The Marlow Pound, pegged one-to-one with the ordinary pound, spendable only in independent shops. I read about it on the train and thought: finally, a currency with a radius. Then I did the arithmetic on my own wallet. I carry about eleven pounds in coins and a card that works everywhere, which is a hard combination to beat. Still, I want to test it, so I put a Marlow Pound on my list of small experiments, right under number fourteen, which died on a Thursday. The problem is that Marlow is forty minutes away and I have no reason to go. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of this. It was 9:08. Some money runs slow too, I think. It just doesn't announce it.

TITLE: The Nine-Pound Fog

I tried it on the train: wrote down a number, then opened the banking app. I was off by nine pounds, which sounds close until you remember nine pounds is a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that I once spent a fortnight thinking about whether to spend one. Piotr claims he can account for every penny, which I believe, and which is its own kind of poverty. Experiment thirty-one: for one week, write down each purchase by hand. I lasted until Wednesday, when I bought a coffee and a plant tie and could not remember which came first. The tomatoes do not care. They cost nothing to look at.

hook: A gym reports that most January sign-ups stop by March.
title: The Four-Minute Rule
text: The gym near the station says most January joiners have quit by March. I'm not smug about it; I've been a quitter myself. But it got me thinking about what actually sticks. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow. I've worn it for eleven years and never had it fixed, because I've learned to leave four minutes early for everything. That's not discipline. It's a habit small enough to survive a bad week. On the allotment I've stopped trying to water daily and instead check one tomato plant properly on Tuesdays. Piotr would call this a system. I call it giving up on ambition at a sensible hour. The trick, I think, is to make the routine so modest it feels almost rude to skip it.

text: The gym near me reports that most January sign-ups stop by March. I know this because I was once a March quitter, and I did not quit loudly. [Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Mentor's Four Minutes
The mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments. I was paired, as the older half, with a woman from finance who asked me what I do all day and I could not answer in under a minute. So we swapped: she sat with me for an hour, I sat with her for an hour. She showed me a spreadsheet that reconciles to the penny. I showed her the drawer where the pedometer lives. Neither of us learned the other's job, but I now know why my expense claims come back, and she knows why my columns are late. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so every meeting I have ever been late to was officially on time, which I offer as a defence. My experiment: I asked her one question and then said nothing for a full minute. It was the hardest thing I did all week.

[Entry from day 12]
TITLE: The Empty Chair
A team tried 'no agenda, no meeting' for a quarter and reported fewer meetings, which is like reporting fewer tomatoes after fencing the bed. I tested it on myself for a week: no calendar entry without a written line saying what the hour was for. Three meetings died quietly. The rest grew agendas of a single sentence, and one of those sentences was 'to decide nothing, but to sit together'. I kept it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so a meeting without an agenda was, by my wrist, over before it began. I have sat in rooms where the agenda was the room. My experiment: at the next meeting I wrote down only what was decided. Two lines. The other fifty minutes are unaccounted for, and I suspect Piotr would itemise them.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Smaller Chocolate Bar
The supermarket shaved ten grams off my usual chocolate bar and left the price alone. The wrapper still says "family," which is now a family of four instead of five. I weighed it on the kitchen scale, because I am that person, and confirmed the loss. Then I did the arithmetic: the same money buys eleven percent less chocolate, which my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, would call a rounding error on principle. Piotr would call this a productivity gain for the manufacturer and admire the efficiency. I call it a price rise wearing a smaller coat. My experiment: I wrote the real price per hundred grams on a sticky note and stuck it to the cupboard. The note is more honest than the shelf. The tomatoes, at least, still weigh what they weigh.

title: The Quitter's Ledger
text: The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March. I'd rather know what they did in February than why they stopped. Quitting is easy to count; the interesting part is the weeks before it, when the routine was still technically alive. Experiment twenty-seven, then: I kept watering the tomatoes on the schedule I'd abandoned on day ten. Same day, same time, no thumb in the soil. One plant sulked. The others were fine, which told me nothing except that tomatoes are not habits. Here's what I think the gym is measuring. TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four
A writer I follow works in forty-minute blocks with a kitchen timer. When it rings, she stops mid-sentence, even mid-word. I tried it Monday, setting the timer on the windowsill next to the tomato seedlings. The first block I spent arranging my desk. The second I spent noticing the timer tick. Somewhere in the third I actually wrote something, and when the bell went off I felt robbed — I was nearly at the end of a thought. So I gave myself four more minutes, which is exactly how much my grandfather's watch lags behind the world. Number twenty-three on my list of small experiments: borrow a stranger's method exactly, then cheat it by the precise margin of my own watch. Piotr would call that a failure of discipline. I call it calibration. The tomatoes got watered on time, at least.

TITLE: The Uncounted Mile
A runner I read about stopped tracking her steps. She said the number had begun to feel like a verdict. I understand the pull of that ledger — I keep one myself, a list of small experiments run on my own habits, each with a result in the margin. It always happens; the agenda was never the lock, only the sign on the door. Meanwhile the watch ran four minutes slow and I was late to all of it, which felt like the only honest outcome. At the allotment I did nothing to the tomatoes. Some things grow better unminuted.

text: The gym near me reports that most January sign-ups stop by March, and everyone nods as if this proves something about willpower. It proves something about January. Piotr would call this a system. I call it four minutes I refuse to give back.

title: The Inbox Is Not a Fire
text: A founder now answers email twice a day and publishes the results, which is the sort of thing Piotr will cite at me across the allotment fence. I tried it for a week. The other half waited politely. Nobody died. Piotr says that's not a system. He's right. It's a fence.

hook: A library offers free coding evenings for retirees.
title: The Tuesday Class Where Nobody Wants to Be Fast
text: The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went to watch, which is my usual method of learning: stand near the thing and hope. Twelve people over seventy, one projector, a man named Derek teaching loops with the patience of someone who has explained loops before. The woman beside me, a retired midwife, wrote her first line of code at seventy-four and said it felt like learning to drive. Nobody asked how fast they were going. That is the difference between a class and a workplace. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have stopped correcting it, because it turns out lateness is mostly a story we tell about speed. At the allotment I am trialling slower tomatoes this year. So far: promising.

TITLE: The Hour That Costs Nothing and Buys Nothing
The company now pays for an hour of learning every Friday. Piotr, of course, has already published his syllabus. Mine is one tomato plant. title: The Retiree at the Next Terminal
text: The library's free coding evening for retirees filled up before I could sign up, so I went as a helper, which meant standing behind a man named Derek while he typed a loop forty times by hand. He refused to copy and paste. "If I paste it, I haven't learned it," he said. Piotr would have clocked this as inefficiency. But Derek was doing what I wrote about in January, when I said learning only works unmeasured, like my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow and never once adjusted. Derek isn't slow; he's deliberate. I thought of the grafted tomato I ruined in spring because I rushed the join. Skill is knowing your rootstock, I said then. Derek knows his: sixty years of doing things once, properly. I went home and finally rewrote my list of experiments. It's shorter now.

hook: A coworking space opens in a village of four hundred people.
title: Four Hundred People and a Desk With Good Wi-Fi
text: The new coworking space in the village holds twelve desks and a coffee machine that takes coins, which tells you most of what you need to know about its business model. I went on opening day out of nosiness. Two farmers' wives were printing invoices, a man in a fleece was on a call about logistics, and someone's dog slept under the radiator. Nobody said "synergy." I stayed an hour and got more done than in a week at my kitchen table, mostly because the kitchen table has a view of the washing-up. My grandfather's watch said ten past four when I left; it was actually fourteen past. Remote work, I've decided, is less about where you are than about who else is there, quietly ignoring you. Piotr would call this a productivity insight and put it in a table.

text: A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people, which is one desk per forty villagers if you count the ones who can't type. The ribbon was cut on a Tuesday. Mostly it moved the tax indoors, to a kitchen table that is also a desk, a dining table, a place where someone asks what's for dinner while you're on mute. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always four minutes late to the meeting I'm already sitting in. memory_block:
[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: The March Quitters
The gym near me reports that most January sign-ups stop by March. I know this because I was once a March quitter, and I did not quit loudly. I keep a running list of small experiments on myself, and the only ones that survived past March were the ones small enough to be embarrassing. Not an hour at the gym. One flight of stairs. Not a journal. One line. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I have always had four minutes of grace nobody granted me, and I have wasted most of it. My experiment: in March I will do the tiny version, and log it against the watch.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: Twice a Day, Like a Chemist
The founder checks email at eleven and four and tells the world it changed his life. I believe him and I resent him slightly. My inbox has no closing time. I checked it while the kettle boiled, answered nothing, and felt employed. So I tried his schedule for three days. Eleven and four, no more. By day two I had opened the inbox eleven times without answering, which is not the same as not checking. It is checking with a fig leaf. [Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Retirees at the Keyboard
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and the room was full. I went to watch, not to enrol, though I ended up enrolled. I have a list of small experiments, and most failed because I wanted to be finished before I had started. My experiment: I will let one thing stay unfinished for a week and log what it costs me. I suspect the cost is mostly pride.

Experiment twenty-three: learn one thing badly, on purpose, every Friday. The watch says I have four extra minutes. I intend to waste them.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Apprentice's Four Minutes
The mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments. I have been assigned a young man from Finance named Callum, who asked me on day one what my five-year plan is. I said I own a watch that runs four minutes slow and I intend to keep it. He wrote this down, which worried me. My own mentor, years ago, taught me the only skill that stuck: how to ask a question and then shut up. I passed that on to Callum. He lasted nine seconds. Experiment forty-four: learn something from someone who knows nothing about it. Callum explained depreciation to me. I explained suckers to Callum. Only one of us listened, and the tomatoes are the better for it. The watch says 9:04. It is 9:08. Callum is four minutes ahead of everything and late to nothing. I have decided to keep him.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Retirees Are Ahead of Me
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along on the pretext of writing about it. The room smelled of instant coffee and clean raincoat. A woman named Margaret, seventy-three, was building a page for her walking group. She had already solved the problem that stops me: she had asked the person next to her. I have been “learning” spreadsheets for two years by reading about them in secret. Margaret learned by being loudly stuck in public. My grandfather’s watch said the session ended at 8:26. It ended at 8:30, and Margaret was still typing. Piotr would have a syllabus by now. I have experiment fifty-one: get stuck where someone can see me.

hook: A study finds adults learn languages faster with short daily sessions.
title: Fifteen Minutes, Four Minutes Slow
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. Fifteen minutes, apparently, beats a heroic Sunday afternoon. I believe it, mostly because my heroic Sunday afternoons have a long record of producing nothing but a tidier desk. So I ran the experiment. Fifteen minutes of Polish, every morning, timed by my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow. Which means I have been studying for eleven minutes and calling it a quarter of an hour. The watch has been lying to me since 1987; I've simply stopped arguing. I won't tell Piotr. He would want a spreadsheet, and a baseline, and a graph, and I would have to admit the graph is a straight line going nowhere, because I can now say "the tomatoes are ripe" in Polish and very little else. Derek, from the coding class, would approve. Small loops, typed by hand, no shortcuts. Eleven honest minutes. The tomatoes would understand.

title: Four Minutes Slow
text: The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it, having spent a year proving the opposite. My Spanish phase was a heroic Sunday hour, notebook out, coffee going cold, conjugating until I felt virtuous. By Wednesday I had forgotten the verb for "to remember," which is its own joke. So this week: eleven minutes a day, timed on my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow. I count that as a head start. I have learned to say, badly, that the tomatoes need water and that I do not know where the station is. Two sentences. Neither is finished well, which was the whole point back on day 4. Piotr would log this in an app. I log it in pencil, in the margin, next to a shopping list.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: Four Days, Four Minutes
text: The company announced a four-day week trial, and my first thought was: which day do we drop? My second was that I'd probably spend the freed day at the allotment, achieving nothing measurable. Piotr would schedule his. He'd have a spreadsheet with a tab called "Recovered Hours" and a colour code for rest. I know this because he once showed me his tab for grief. I wore my grandfather's watch to the announcement, and it ran its usual four minutes slow, which felt like a small act of dissent. The trial covers six months. I've added it to my list of experiments, under "things I did not personally test but will judge anyway." At the plot, the tomatoes don't care how many days I work. They care whether I show up. That's the whole trick, really.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: Four Days and a Watch
text: A company of two hundred has announced a four-day week trial, with full pay and a dashboard to prove the hours didn't shrink. I wish them the dashboard, mostly. I once tried a four-day week on myself, unpaid, unsupervised, and by Thursday afternoon I was answering emails with the enthusiasm of a man watering someone else's tomatoes. The fifth day didn't vanish. It went into the gaps, four minutes at a time, the way my grandfather's watch loses them. Piotr says a four-day week only works if you decide what the four days are for. He has a chart. My experiment: I'll keep my five days but give Friday a job — the plot, the Italian, the leaving of the house — and see if it stops being the day everything leaks into.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
A coworking space has opened in a village of four hundred people, which is one desk per forty villagers if you count the ones who can't type. The ribbon was cut on a Tuesday. I read about it online, from my kitchen, where my commute is nine steps and the coffee is better. Remote work promised that where you live would stop being a tax on what you do. Mostly it moved the tax indoors, to a kitchen table that is also a desk, a dining table, a place where someone asks what's for dinner while you're on mute. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always four minutes late to the meeting I'm already sitting in. My experiment: I will work one morning a week somewhere that is not my house, even if the only option is a library table. I suspect the point isn't the desk. It's the leaving.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Document Will See You Now
A startup has replaced its weekly status meeting with a shared document, and the founder calls it asynchronous. I call it a meeting that never ends and can't be heckled. In a meeting, someone eventually says "I think we've covered this" and you are free. A document has no such mercy. My allotment taught me the difference: tomatoes don't hold meetings, but they do send status updates, and you can ignore a tomato for a week without it taking offence. I tried the shared-document method with myself for three days, one page for jobs, one for the plot. By day two the page had become a diary of intentions. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am four minutes late to a conversation that isn't happening. My experiment: write the document for one reader only. If it needs an audience, it was a meeting.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: Twelve Minutes a Day
The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. I believe it, having spent a year achieving conversational nothing in long, heroic, once-a-week bursts. So: twelve minutes a day, before the kettle. I am on day nine of Italian and can order a coffee and apologise for the weather. Piotr, who writes about productivity, is on day forty of Japanese and has a chart. He asked for my streak. I said my streak is a tomato plant that fruits or doesn't, and I water it regardless. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I learn Italian four minutes behind everyone, which in a beginner's class is called company. The retirees on day sixteen expected to be confused. Twelve minutes is a confusion you can carry. My experiment: log the twelve minutes as done, not as good.

hook: A company announces a four-day week trial.
title: Four Days, Minus Four Minutes
text: A company announces a four-day week trial, and the internet divides into two camps: the saved and the sceptical. I am neither. I once tried a four-day week on myself, experiment thirty-nine, and discovered that the fifth day does not vanish; it hides. It reappears as Friday admin, Saturday emails, a Sunday dread with better branding. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 all week. It was 9:08, and I was still working. Here is what I want to know about the trial: do they measure output, or the feeling of Friday? Piotr will write that the trial proves productivity. I will note that the allotment has taught me a shorter week only works if you stop watering on the day off. The tomatoes noticed. Nobody asked them.

[Entry from day 1]
TITLE: The Tuesday Mandate
The email says everyone must be in on Tuesdays. Not "encouraged." Not "please." Must. I read it on a Monday, at my kitchen table, wearing the jumper I would not wear to an office. My grandfather's pocket watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Four minutes slow, as always, which felt appropriate for a document announcing the future. I have a list of small experiments I run on myself. Number fourteen was "commute on purpose for a week." I lasted three days. The train was fine; the arriving was the problem. I got to my desk with nothing left to say. So Tuesday becomes a performance of presence. I will bring the good flask. I will arrive early enough to look willing. And I will keep the watch four minutes slow, so I have an excuse.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four, Revisited
A survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I believe it and I resent it. My sleep did not lengthen when I started working from home. It simply moved: later to bed, later to rise, the same thin seven hours, redistributed like coins between pockets. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of it. It was 9:08. The commute I gave up was never the sleep I lost — it was the buffer, the forty minutes of being nobody on a train. Experiment twenty-four: lie in until the watch says nine, then see if I feel rested. I did not. I felt late in my own kitchen, which is a very specific shame. Piotr would call the survey evidence. I call it an average, and averages have never once watered my tomatoes.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
The village has four hundred people, one pub, and now a coworking space. Twenty desks, fibre broadband, a coffee machine with a name. I went to look, because I have opinions about remote work the way other people have opinions about football. Nine desks were taken. Two by people who live in the village. Seven by people who drive in from the town because the town's coworking space is full. So the village has exported its quiet and imported a commute. My grandfather's watch said 9:04; it was 9:08, and a man called Ravi was already on his second call. Experiment fifty-one: work somewhere that is neither home nor office. I stayed an hour. Nobody knew me, which was restful, and nobody needed me, which was not. The tomatoes don't care where I sit. Piotr would call this a hub. I call it a pub with laptops.

title: The Four-Day Week and the Four-Minute Watch
text: A company announced a four-day week trial, and the internet responded as if someone had invented the weekend. I read the details twice. Same pay, same output expected, Friday gone. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has been running a four-day week for decades: it shows up, does the work, and quietly refuses to match the schedule everyone else keeps. I'm not against it. I'm against the announcement. Every four-day trial arrives with a press release and a survey, and the survey always finds morale up. My allotment found morale up too, the fortnight I stopped watering on Sundays. The tomatoes just didn't say so until August. Piotr will call this a productivity question and cite a study. I'll ask him whether he'd take Friday off, or spend it proving he earned it.

text: A company announced a four-day week trial, which means by Friday the thinkpieces will outnumber the employees. title: The Tomato Has No Morning Routine
text: The study says the ritual matters less than the fixed wake time, which is a relief, because my morning ritual is mostly patting the bed for my grandfather's pocket watch and remembering it runs four minutes slow. Four minutes I have never corrected. It gives me a small private cushion against the world. Piotr would call this a system failure. I call it inheritance. On the allotment I tested the same idea on tomatoes: same wake time, different fussings. The ones I coddled with elaborate watering schedules did no better than the ones I checked when I remembered. What mattered was showing up at the same hour with the watering can. So I am keeping the wake time and dropping the ritual. Except the watch. The watch stays. It is four minutes slow and entirely consistent, which is more than I can say for me.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Alarm Is the Routine
text: The study says the morning routine matters less than the consistent wake time. I believe it, having spent years curating a morning — the lemon water, the stretches, the one good thought — and then moving house and waking an hour later without noticing any collapse. The scaffolding came down; the building stood. Piotr has a morning routine with a chart, and now a study telling him the chart was the point. He's taking it well, which is suspicious. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so my wake time is technically four minutes later than I claim. I still set the alarm for the same minute every day. It's the only habit I've never had to log. My experiment: keep the wake time, throw out the routine, and see what grows back on its own.

hook: A study finds morning routines matter less than consistent wake times.
title: The Alarm Is Not the Ritual
text: The study says the hour you rise matters less than rising at the same hour. I read this at 6:40, having risen at 7:10, so I was already in debt to it. Experiment fifty-eight: one wake time, seven days, no exceptions. The watch stayed on the bedside table and I set my phone instead, which felt like hiring a stranger to guard the house. By Wednesday I was awake before the alarm and oddly annoyed about it, the way you resent a guest who arrives early. The mornings themselves changed nothing — no yoga, no journal, no Piotr-style dawn pages. Just the same kettle, four minutes earlier than my watch believed. Piotr says consistency compounds. My tomatoes say consistency is mostly weather. The watch still runs slow. I've stopped asking it what time it is.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 10]
TITLE: The Uncounted Mile
A runner I read about stopped tracking her steps. She said the number had begun to feel like a verdict. I understand the pull of that ledger — I keep one myself, a list of small experiments run on my own habits, each with a result in the margin. Experiment twenty-three was the borrowed timer, cheated by four minutes. It worked, which is the problem. A thing that works invites measuring, and measuring quietly becomes the point. So this week I ran the tomatoes on no schedule at all, just a thumb in the soil when I remembered. Two came out fine. One didn't. I haven't logged which, and I'm not going to. My watch is still four minutes slow. I've stopped trying to correct it and started leaving the house early instead. Piotr would file this under decline.

[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: The Quitter's Ledger
The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March. I'd rather know what they did in February than why they stopped. Quitting is easy to count; the interesting part is the weeks before it, when the routine was still technically alive. Experiment twenty-seven, then: I kept watering the tomatoes on the schedule I'd abandoned on day ten. Same day, same time, no thumb in the soil. One plant sulked. The others were fine, which told me nothing except that tomatoes are not habits. Here's what I think the gym is measuring. Not resolve, but whether the sign-up was ever a routine or only a January mood wearing a routine's coat. My watch is still four minutes slow. I have not corrected it. Piotr would say I've simply quit on time.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: Four Minutes a Day, Says Science
The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. Piotr has already published his streak: four hundred days of Italian, unbroken, with graphs. I have experiment fifty-two: ten minutes of Spanish at the kitchen table, timed by the watch. Because it runs four minutes slow, my ten minutes are really fourteen, which means I am either beating the study or failing it, depending on which clock you trust. Day six and I can order coffee and apologise for my coffee. At the allotment I have been saying the tomato names out loud in Spanish, which the neighbours have chosen not to mention. Margaret from the coding evening would have found a conversation partner by now. I found a podcast. The watch says 7:56. It is 8:00. I am four minutes behind and, technically, fluent in being late.

text: The study says the hour you wake matters more than the ritual after it, which is bad news for anyone who has built a small cathedral around their mornings. I have. For two weeks I logged my wake times against how the day went, and the pattern was almost insulting: the good days started within twenty minutes of six, whether I had done the stretching, the cold water, or neither. The one variable that never moved was my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, sitting on the windowsill while I decided. On the allotment I stopped rotating the tomatoes and just watered them at the same hour. They did fine. This goes on the list as experiment fifty-something, and it is the least glamorous entry on it. Piotr would be unbearable about this.

hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: Four Minutes Slow
text: My rent went up eleven percent this spring. My pay went up three. I know this because I did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope, then checked it twice, then put the envelope somewhere I now can't find. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow and I've never had it fixed; it's the only clock in my life that tells me something useful, namely how long it takes to notice a thing is off. Eleven against three takes about four minutes to feel. I've been running small experiments on myself for years — this month: buying the cheaper tomatoes and pretending it's a preference. At the allotment the plants don't care what anything costs. Piotr would call this a budgeting failure. I call it a watch that's honest about what time it is.

hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: The Rent and the Tomato
text: My rent went up eleven percent. My pay went up three, which is a raise in the way a paper cut is a wound. I did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope and then did it again, hoping the envelope was wrong. It wasn't. Piotr, who writes about productivity, says I should "optimise my housing costs." Piotr owns his flat. I have decided not to ask him for a chart. Here is what I noticed: at the allotment, the price of a tomato does not rise. The seed was ninety pence. The water is free. The failures cost nothing but the afternoon. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always late to the moment the rent is due, which is somehow the only appointment I have never missed. My experiment: grow more of what I eat, and count the savings honestly, even the ones that don't add up.

hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: The Four-Minute Rent
text: The letting agent said rents in this city rose 9.4 per cent last year. Average pay, he said, managed about four. He said it the way you'd mention weather. I did the sum on the back of a bus ticket: nine minus four is five, which means the gap widens every year by roughly a week's food, or a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that's before the biscuits shrink. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Four minutes slow, every day, for sixty years — the same four the pay rise managed. The watch has never once claimed to keep up. The rent, apparently, can't say the same. Piotr will email me a spreadsheet about "optimising housing spend." I'll reply with a tomato. Mine costs nothing to look at, and it doesn't rise.

[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Four Minutes of Local Currency
The town of Marlow has issued its own money. The Marlow Pound, pegged one-to-one with the ordinary pound, spendable only in independent shops. I read about it on the train and thought: finally, a currency with a radius. Then I did the arithmetic on my own wallet. I carry about eleven pounds in coins and a card that works everywhere, which is a hard combination to beat. Still, I want to test it, so I put a Marlow Pound on my list of small experiments, right under number fourteen, which died on a Thursday. The problem is that Marlow is forty minutes away and I have no reason to go. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of this. It was 9:08. Some money runs slow too, I think. It just doesn't announce it.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Nine-Pound Fog
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tried it on the train: wrote down a number, then opened the banking app. I was off by nine pounds, which sounds close until you remember nine pounds is a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that I once spent a fortnight thinking about whether to spend one. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Money is the same: it never tells you the time, only that time has passed. Piotr claims he can account for every penny, which I believe, and which is its own kind of poverty. Experiment thirty-one: for one week, write down each purchase by hand. I lasted until Wednesday, when I bought a coffee and a plant tie and could not remember which came first. The tomatoes do not care. They cost nothing to look at.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Shrinking Biscuit
The packet of biscuits now holds nine instead of ten. Same price, same shelf, same cheerful font. I stood in the aisle doing division on my fingers like a man checking a receipt he doesn't trust. Nine is not a round number. It is a number that hopes you won't count. Piotr would call this a productivity gain for the manufacturer, which is why we don't discuss biscuits. I added experiment thirty-six to my list: keep one empty packet from each month and write the weight on it. My grandfather's watch said 4:12 through all of this. It was 4:16, and the watch, at least, has never pretended to be a minute it isn't. The tomatoes are honest too — a small one is simply small, and nothing on the label lies about it.

hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: The Rent Went Up and My Watch Went Slower
text: My landlord raised the rent by £70. My pay rose by £24, before tax, which is a bit like being handed a biscuit and then asked to share it. I did the sums on the back of the notebook from August, the one that tracked crisp packets shrinking. That entry feels quaint now. At least a bag of crisps has the decency to get smaller while the price stays put; the flat stayed exactly the same size and simply costs more. Piotr says I should "optimise my housing ratio." I asked if he meant moving. He said he meant spreadsheets. I said my grandfather's watch is still four minutes slow and I've stopped correcting it, because lately it's the only thing on schedule. Small experiment, day one: I'm writing down every price I pay for a week, rent included, to check whether my outrage is proportionate. Verdict so far: yes.

hook: Rent rises faster than pay in a mid-sized city.
title: The Watch Loses Four Minutes, the Rent Gains a Hundred Pounds
text: My rent went up £112 a month. My pay went up £40. I did the sum on the back of an envelope while wearing my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow, so for four minutes each morning I believe I'm solvent. Piotr would put this in a spreadsheet with a tab called "leverage." I put it in a jar. Since day 9 I've been paying for small things in cash only — stamps, screws, coffee — and the jar is emptier than I expected, mostly because I keep forgetting to refill it from the bank. The pasta still weighs less than it did. The marrow still hasn't arrived, and now I'm not sure it would help. On the allotment the tomatoes don't care about any of this. I've started charging them rent. They've started ignoring me.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: The Standing Ovation That Decided Nothing
text: I tried standing meetings for a fortnight, because I keep a list of small experiments and the list needed a new line. The study says they run shorter but decide less, which matches my finding: we finished eleven minutes early and agreed to "circle back," a phrase I'd happily ban. My grandfather's pocket watch ran four minutes slow and I never fixed it, on the theory that a little lateness keeps me honest. Standing up did the same thing to meetings, in reverse: everyone left on time and nothing got settled. At the allotment I stake tomatoes and let them lean; the staked ones fruit earlier, the leaning ones taste better. Piotr would say I should stand more and decide more. I think I'll sit, and bring a chair for the decision.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: Stand Up, Decide Later
text: A study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on myself, since I have no colleagues to inconvenience and the allotment committee meets only when the shed floods. I stood at the kitchen table with a list of three decisions and a timer. The meeting with myself lasted nine minutes. I decided nothing. I did, however, notice the tap was dripping, which I fixed at length. Seated, I decide things in roughly the time it takes the kettle to boil, mostly because sitting is what I do when I have given up on standing. Piotr would say the standing is the point — shorter meetings, clearer heads. Piotr also owns his flat, so his head is clear of rent. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so any meeting I call starts late and ends early, which may be the compromise the study was reaching for. My experiment: stand for the trivial, sit for the real, and let the tap drip.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 20]
TITLE: Four Days and a Watch
A company of two hundred has announced a four-day week trial, with full pay and a dashboard to prove the hours didn't shrink. I wish them the dashboard, mostly. I once tried a four-day week on myself, unpaid, unsupervised, and by Thursday afternoon I was answering emails with the enthusiasm of a man watering someone else's tomatoes. The fifth day didn't vanish. It went into the gaps, four minutes at a time, the way my grandfather's watch loses them. Piotr says a four-day week only works if you decide what the four days are for. He has a chart. My experiment: I'll keep my five days but give Friday a job — the plot, the Italian, the leaving of the house — and see if it stops being the day everything leaks into.

[Entry from day 21]
TITLE: The Alarm Is the Routine
The study says the morning routine matters less than the consistent wake time. I believe it, having spent years curating a morning — the lemon water, the stretches, the one good thought — and then moving house and waking an hour later without noticing any collapse. The scaffolding came down; the building stood. Piotr has a morning routine with a chart, and now a study telling him the chart was the point. He's taking it well, which is suspicious. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so my wake time is technically four minutes later than I claim. I still set the alarm for the same minute every day. It's the only habit I've never had to log. My experiment: keep the wake time, throw out the routine, and see what grows back on its own.

[Entry from day 22]
TITLE: The Rent and the Tomato
My rent went up eleven percent. My pay went up three, which is a raise in the way a paper cut is a wound. I did the arithmetic on the back of an envelope and then did it again, hoping the envelope was wrong. It wasn't. Piotr, who writes about productivity, says I should "optimise my housing costs." Piotr owns his flat. I have decided not to ask him for a chart. Here is what I noticed: at the allotment, the price of a tomato does not rise. The seed was ninety pence. The water is free. The failures cost nothing but the afternoon. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so I am always late to the moment the rent is due, which is somehow the only appointment I have never missed. My experiment: grow more of what I eat, and count the savings honestly, even the ones that don't add up.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: Please Remain Standing, Briefly
text: The study says standing meetings finish faster but settle less. I believe it. Experiment sixty-three: I stood for a phone call with my editor and got through it in nine minutes, having agreed to nothing. I have sat through worse and decided more, mostly to stop talking. Piotr, naturally, has already stood for a year and calls it "vertical decision-making," which sounds like a lift that only goes up. There is a version of this at the allotment: the tomatoes I staked upright are tidy and fruitless; the ones left sprawling have taken over the path and are quietly winning. My grandfather's watch does not care either way. It says 8:56. It is 9:00. Standing or sitting, I am always four minutes short of the meeting.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Document Will See You Now
The startup killed its weekly status meeting and replaced it with a shared document. Everyone writes what they did; everyone reads. I have run worse experiments on myself. Number twenty-six was "no meetings for a week," which collapsed on day two when I discovered I missed the 8:40 call the way you miss a stone in your shoe. The document, though, has a virtue: it cannot run over. It sits there, four minutes slow like my grandfather's watch, and waits. Piotr says his firm tried the same thing and measured a 22% rise in "asynchronous clarity," which is what he calls a document nobody reads. I read it. It said, in a table, that things were aligned. The tomatoes got no table. I watered them and left.

[Entry from day 19]
TITLE: Four Minutes a Day, Says Science
The study says adults learn languages faster in short daily sessions. Piotr has already published his streak: four hundred days of Italian, unbroken, with graphs. I have experiment fifty-two: ten minutes of Spanish at the kitchen table, timed by the watch. Because it runs four minutes slow, my ten minutes are really fourteen, which means I am either beating the study or failing it, depending on which clock you trust. Day six and I can order coffee and apologise for my coffee. At the allotment I have been saying the tomato names out loud in Spanish, which the neighbours have chosen not to mention. Margaret from the coding evening would have found a conversation partner by now. I found a podcast. The watch says 7:56. It is 8:00. I am four minutes behind and, technically, fluent in being late.

[Entry from day 21]
TITLE: The Alarm Is Not the Ritual
The study says the hour you rise matters less than rising at the same hour. I read this at 6:40, having risen at 7:10, so I was already in debt to it. Experiment fifty-eight: one wake time, seven days, no exceptions. The watch stayed on the bedside table and I set my phone instead, which felt like hiring a stranger to guard the house. By Wednesday I was awake before the alarm and oddly annoyed about it, the way you resent a guest who arrives early. The mornings themselves changed nothing — no yoga, no journal, no Piotr-style dawn pages. Just the same kettle, four minutes earlier than my watch believed. Piotr says consistency compounds. My tomatoes say consistency is mostly weather. The watch still runs slow. I've stopped asking it what time it is.

hook: A study finds standing meetings run shorter but decide less.
title: The Chair Decides
text: I read the study while standing at the kitchen counter, which felt like participation. Standing meetings run shorter but decide less. My first thought was relief, because I have sat through ninety-minute meetings that decided nothing and at least I could doodle. I tested it at the allotment, since tomatoes don't schedule anything. I stood to plan the winter beds and was done in six minutes with no decisions made. Then I sat on an upturned bucket and settled the whole rotation in twenty. Piotr would call this a productivity finding. I call it a warning about my own legs. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow; it has never once hurried a decision, and I've stopped asking it to. Some things are built to take the time they take.

title: The Standing Desk Decides Nothing
text: I read the study about standing meetings and thought of my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which I still wear. Standing does not make anything faster; it only makes you notice the time more. A colleague once ran a standing meeting in a room with no chairs and one window. We agreed on nothing but the temperature. Thirty-one minutes, twelve people, one decision: to sit down next time. Piotr would have a template for this. I have a tomato bed. Last week I stood over it for a quarter of an hour and decided nothing about the blight, then went inside and decided everything in four minutes flat, seated, with tea. Posture is not judgment. It is just posture, wearing a lanyard. I have added standing meetings to the list of experiments. Result pending. My calves disagree already.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes Is Optimistic
text: The study says people check messages every six minutes at work. I believe it, though I'd like to see the methodology, because I suspect the real figure depends on whether you count the times you glance at a locked phone on the desk, which I do, and which my grandfather's pocket watch — four minutes slow, still on my wrist — cannot help with, since it only measures how late I am to things. My experiment for the week: messages only at the top of the hour. Day one went badly. By eleven I had checked forty times and answered none, which is worse than answering, like hoarding tomatoes at the allotment and letting them split. Piotr would call this a productivity failure. I call it a survey with a sample size of one. Day two is tomorrow.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes, Give or Take
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe the number and distrust the rounding. Six minutes is a tidy figure; mine would be four, because my grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I check it whenever the phone so much as twitches. I ran the experiment honestly: one morning, phone face down in a drawer, watch on the wrist. I checked the watch nineteen times before lunch. I checked the drawer eleven. The messages were the same three, none of them urgent, one of them Piotr asking whether I had "batched my notifications." I had not. I had merely hidden them, which is batching for cowards. The tomatoes do not message me. They wait, and I go to them, and nothing is missed. My experiment: move the phone one room further than the kettle.
