hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes
text: The study says people check messages every six minutes at work. I tried to verify this with my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow, so my six minutes are their six minutes and four seconds. I lasted until 9:38 by the watch, which was 9:42, and checked eleven times. Not for anything urgent. Mostly to see whether checking counted. This is where I part company with Piotr, who has already written that the six-minute figure is a symptom and the cure is deep work. He is right and I resent it. Experiment sixty-two: for one hour I'll write down what I was doing each time I reach for the phone. So far the list reads: nothing, nothing, a sentence I'd already finished, nothing. The tomatoes get watered once a day. They have never once checked on me.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: Quiet Hours
The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. A small mercy, announced with a small icon of a moon. I read it at 9:04 by my grandfather's watch, which is 9:08, and felt the specific relief of being told I may ignore people. My phone has been on silent since 2019, so this changes nothing and I approve of it entirely. Experiment number nine was "answer every message within the hour for a week." I lasted two days and one very long night. The problem was never the notifications; it was the answering. Still, I like the moon icon. It suggests someone at the company has a bed. I have added experiment twenty-three: leave one message unanswered until morning and see if the world tilts. It will not. Piotr will email me about it at midnight.

[Entry from day 15]
TITLE: Twice Is a Policy
The founder answers email at eleven and four, and publishes the results: fewer messages, clearer head, nothing on fire. I believe him. I also notice that a founder can announce his hours and the world adjusts around him, the way water finds the shape of a stone. My inbox has no such respect for me. I tried his schedule for one day. At 11:04 by my grandfather's watch, which is 11:08, I answered four things and felt virtuous. At 11:20 a colleague phoned to ask if I'd seen her email. Twice a day is a policy; twice a day plus one phone call is a personality. Experiment twenty-eight, then: I'll batch my replies and time them. Not to save minutes — to find out whether the batching is a routine or a mood in a routine's coat. Piotr has already published his version. It has a graph.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
The village has four hundred people, one pub, and now a coworking space. Twenty desks, fibre broadband, a coffee machine with a name. I went to look, because I have opinions about remote work the way other people have opinions about football. Nine desks were taken. Two by people who live in the village. Seven by people who drive in from the town because the town's coworking space is full. So the village has exported its quiet and imported a commute. My grandfather's watch said 9:04; it was 9:08, and a man called Ravi was already on his second call. Experiment fifty-one: work somewhere that is neither home nor office. I stayed an hour. Nobody knew me, which was restful, and nobody needed me, which was not. The tomatoes don't care where I sit. Piotr would call this a hub. I call it a pub with laptops.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Every Six Minutes, Like a Tide Table
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe it, and I resent the precision. Six minutes is exactly long enough to start something and not finish it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which I have always treated as a small gift: it gives me a head start on being late. But it can't help with this. A message arrives, the watch still says four minutes ago, and somehow the message already knows. So I've been running an experiment. On the allotment I check my phone only when the kettle boils, and the tomatoes seem indifferent. At my desk I tried the opposite and checked whenever I thought of it, which was constantly, which taught me nothing except that I think of it constantly. Piotr would have a system by now. I have a watch, four minutes behind, and a phone four minutes ahead of me.

hook: A study finds people check messages every six minutes at work.
title: Six Minutes
text: The study says we check messages every six minutes, which sounds about right and also like a confession. I tested myself on Tuesday with a kitchen timer and a sheet of paper. Twelve checks in an hour, so the researchers are optimistic. The worst part was writing them down. Each one got a little reason beside it: "waiting on a reply," "just checking." By the fourth line I'd run out of reasons and started writing "habit" until the word looked like it belonged to someone else. My grandfather's watch loses four minutes a day and I've stopped correcting it. It's slower than everything and nobody expects it to answer. I've added Experiment 52: leave the phone in the hall while the kettle boils. The kettle won, mostly. But four minutes unaccounted for is four minutes.

hook: A manager measures a remote team only by finished work.
title: The Output-Only Manager
text: A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work and nothing else. No status meetings, no green dots, no "just checking in." He says the work either exists or it doesn't. I wanted to argue, because I argue, but my grandfather's pocket watch was running its usual four minutes slow and I was already late to the allotment. Here's what I actually think, tested on tomatoes: measuring only the fruit works if you trust the soil. His team ships. But two of them told me they haven't had a proper conversation with him since March. The work is finished; the people are quietly going fallow. Piotr would call this inefficiency. I'd call it a harvest you can't repeat next season. My watch says I'm early. It's lying, as usual.

hook: A manager measures a remote team only by finished work.
title: The Manager Who Counted Tomatoes
text: A manager measures his remote team only by finished work. No status meetings, no green dots, no asking whether they are at their desks. Piotr calls this "outcome-based management" and has probably drawn a diagram. I tested it on the only team I have: the tomatoes. All week I judged them by output alone — fruit set, fruit ripened — and ignored the leaves. By Friday two plants had wilted quietly while I admired a single excellent tomato. The finished work was beautiful. The team was dying underneath it. So I checked the leaves, watered, staked, and lost an afternoon I could not bill to anyone. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which means I am always four minutes late to notice. My experiment: measure the harvest, but walk the rows.

The messages were the same three, none of them urgent, one of them Piotr asking whether I had "batched my notifications." I had not. I had merely hidden them, which is batching for cowards. The tomatoes do not message me. They wait, and I go to them, and nothing is missed. My experiment: move the phone one room further than the kettle.

hook: A manager measures a remote team only by finished work.
title: The Output Is Fine; the Quiet Is Not
text: A manager tells a podcast he measures his remote team only by finished work. Fine, as far as it goes. Finished work is the one thing you can see from a distance, so it becomes the only thing worth seeing. Experiment sixty-three: I counted what my week produced versus what it cost. The columns did not match. Four good sentences and a phone call that fixed a fence; also nine hours of waiting for replies and one long silence at 3 p.m. that no deliverable would ever record. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08, and I had done nothing measurable for six of those minutes, and they were the best six. Piotr will call the manager brave. I call him a man counting tomatoes and calling it a garden.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four, Revisited
A survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I believe it and I resent it. My sleep did not lengthen when I started working from home. It simply moved: later to bed, later to rise, the same thin seven hours, redistributed like coins between pockets. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of it. It was 9:08. The commute I gave up was never the sleep I lost — it was the buffer, the forty minutes of being nobody on a train. Experiment twenty-four: lie in until the watch says nine, then see if I feel rested. I did not. I felt late in my own kitchen, which is a very specific shame. Piotr would call the survey evidence. I call it an average, and averages have never once watered my tomatoes.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
The village has four hundred people, one pub, and now a coworking space. Twenty desks, fibre broadband, a coffee machine with a name. I went to look, because I have opinions about remote work the way other people have opinions about football. Nine desks were taken. Two by people who live in the village. Seven by people who drive in from the town because the town's coworking space is full. So the village has exported its quiet and imported a commute. My grandfather's watch said 9:04; it was 9:08, and a man called Ravi was already on his second call. Experiment fifty-one: work somewhere that is neither home nor office. I stayed an hour. Nobody knew me, which was restful, and nobody needed me, which was not. The tomatoes don't care where I sit. Piotr would call this a hub. I call it a pub with laptops.

[Entry from day 20]
TITLE: Four Days, Minus Four Minutes
A company announces a four-day week trial, and the internet divides into two camps: the saved and the sceptical. I am neither. I once tried a four-day week on myself, experiment thirty-nine, and discovered that the fifth day does not vanish; it hides. It reappears as Friday admin, Saturday emails, a Sunday dread with better branding. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 all week. It was 9:08, and I was still working. Here is what I want to know about the trial: do they measure output, or the feeling of Friday? Piotr will write that the trial proves productivity. I will note that the allotment has taught me a shorter week only works if you stop watering on the day off. The tomatoes noticed. Nobody asked them.

hook: A manager measures a remote team only by finished work.
title: The Output Is Not the Whole Animal
text: A manager told me he measures his remote team only by finished work. Clean, defensible, and slightly sinister, like a scale that weighs you but not your luggage. I tried it on the allotment. If I judge the tomatoes only by what reaches the kitchen, the plants look lazy all July. But the staking, the watering at odd hours, the quiet inspection for blight — none of that appears in the harvest, and all of it decides it. Piotr would call this a productivity leak. I call it the difference between a timesheet and a pulse. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and has never once measured anything finished. I still wear it. Some things you keep because they tell you the time, and some because they tell you what the time is for.

hook: A manager measures a remote team only by finished work.
title: The Manager Who Counted Only the Finished
text: A manager I know measures his remote team by finished work alone. Nothing else counts: not the hour someone spent untangling a supplier's invoice, not the Tuesday call where two colleagues discovered they'd built the same thing twice. Only the tidy row of done. It sounds brutal, and it mostly is, but I'll admit I tested a version on myself. Last month I logged only finished pieces at the allotment — tomatoes weighed, not watered. By week three the beds looked fine and the soil was a desert. The slugs, as promised on day 20, reported back before the payroll did. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow. Nobody ever asked it to prove the time. They just trusted the hands, and it kept them. I'd measure people the way I measure that watch: by whether it still keeps faith with you.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cancelled Was the One I Needed
text: My college dropped a required course in favour of a project, and everyone applauded. I keep thinking about the one class I nearly failed: statistics, taught by a man who wrote on the board with his back to us and never once said why any of it mattered. I learned it anyway, badly, because it was required. Ten years later I use it weekly — sample sizes on the allotment, mostly — and I still hear his chalk. The project sounds better. It probably is. But I have a list of experiments I've run on myself, and the ones I chose taught me less than the ones I resented. Piotr would call that a failure of motivation. I'd call it the difference between a tomato you planted and one that volunteered. The volunteer is often the hardier plant.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cancelled
text: A college has dropped a required course in favour of a project. I approve, having spent four years passing courses and one summer learning to prune tomatoes, which no one examined me on. The project teaches the thing courses cannot: that nobody is coming to tell you it's finished. I ran my own version. One week to build a cold frame from scrap, no instructions, no marks. I learned that I measure twice and cut wrong anyway, and that the second cut is where the learning lives. Piotr would have made a Gantt chart and finished on Tuesday. He'd also have a cold frame that fits. Mine leans four minutes, like my grandfather's watch, which I refuse to correct because the lean is honest. My experiment: keep one thing unassessed, and see if I still do it.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 23]
TITLE: Stand Up, Decide Later
A study says standing meetings run shorter but decide less. I tested it on myself, since I have no colleagues to inconvenience and the allotment committee meets only when the shed floods. I stood at the kitchen table with a list of three decisions and a timer. The meeting with myself lasted nine minutes. I decided nothing. I did, however, notice the tap was dripping, which I fixed at length. Seated, I decide things in roughly the time it takes the kettle to boil, mostly because sitting is what I do when I have given up on standing. Piotr would say the standing is the point — shorter meetings, clearer heads. Piotr also owns his flat, so his head is clear of rent. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, so any meeting I call starts late and ends early, which may be the compromise the study was reaching for. My experiment: stand for the trivial, sit for the real, and let the tap drip.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: Six Minutes, Give or Take
The study says we check messages every six minutes. I believe the number and distrust the rounding. Six minutes is a tidy figure; mine would be four, because my grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I check it whenever the phone so much as twitches. I ran the experiment honestly: one morning, phone face down in a drawer, watch on the wrist. I checked the watch nineteen times before lunch. I checked the drawer eleven. The messages were the same three, none of them urgent, one of them Piotr asking whether I had "batched my notifications." I had not. I had merely hidden them, which is batching for cowards. The tomatoes do not message me. They wait, and I go to them, and nothing is missed. My experiment: move the phone one room further than the kettle.

[Entry from day 25]
TITLE: The Manager Who Counted Tomatoes
A manager measures his remote team only by finished work. No status meetings, no green dots, no asking whether they are at their desks. Piotr calls this "outcome-based management" and has probably drawn a diagram. I tested it on the only team I have: the tomatoes. All week I judged them by output alone — fruit set, fruit ripened — and ignored the leaves. By Friday two plants had wilted quietly while I admired a single excellent tomato. The finished work was beautiful. The team was dying underneath it. So I checked the leaves, watered, staked, and lost an afternoon I could not bill to anyone. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, which means I am always four minutes late to notice. My experiment: measure the harvest, but walk the rows.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cancelled and the Lettuce That Survived
text: The college dropped a required course in favour of a project. No syllabus, no lectures, just a brief and a deadline. Half the staff are appalled. I am quietly delighted, because it is experiment fifty-one with a reading list. My evidence is thin and my own. On the allotment I stopped reading about pruning and started ruining a spare cordon in front of my neighbour, who watched and said nothing until I had made the mistake properly. Then he said one sentence. I remember it. I could not tell you a word of the articles. Piotr will say a project needs a rubric. Fine. So does a tomato, and mine are doing better than his. The watch says 6:26. It is 6:30. The course ran four minutes long and taught me more than the term did.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: The Hour That Costs Nothing and Buys Nothing
The company now pays for an hour of learning every Friday. Piotr, of course, has already published his syllabus. Mine is one tomato plant. My allotment neighbour insists the best way to learn pruning is to ruin something cheap, so I have been mutilating a spare cordon since March. It is not going well. The plant looks like it lost an argument. But I have learned the difference between a sucker and a leader, which is more than I can say for most meetings. The hour is paid, which makes it faintly suspicious, like a gift with a receipt attached. Still, I spent mine outdoors with a knife and no laptop. Experiment twenty-three: learn one thing badly, on purpose, every Friday. The watch says I have four extra minutes. I intend to waste them.

[Entry from day 11]
TITLE: The Apprentice's Four Minutes
The mentor programme pairs new hires with people from other departments. I have been assigned a young man from Finance named Callum, who asked me on day one what my five-year plan is. I said I own a watch that runs four minutes slow and I intend to keep it. He wrote this down, which worried me. My own mentor, years ago, taught me the only skill that stuck: how to ask a question and then shut up. I passed that on to Callum. He lasted nine seconds. Experiment forty-four: learn something from someone who knows nothing about it. Callum explained depreciation to me. I explained suckers to Callum. Only one of us listened, and the tomatoes are the better for it. The watch says 9:04. It is 9:08. Callum is four minutes ahead of everything and late to nothing. I have decided to keep him.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Retirees Are Ahead of Me
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along on the pretext of writing about it. The room smelled of instant coffee and clean raincoat. A woman named Margaret, seventy-three, was building a page for her walking group. She had already solved the problem that stops me: she had asked the person next to her. I have been “learning” spreadsheets for two years by reading about them in secret. Margaret learned by being loudly stuck in public. My grandfather’s watch said the session ended at 8:26. It ended at 8:30, and Margaret was still typing. Piotr would have a syllabus by now. I have experiment fifty-one: get stuck where someone can see me.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cut
text: The college dropped a required course and replaced it with a project. Everyone applauded the word "project" as if it were a small engine. I thought of Derek, hand-typing loops while the rest of the room pasted, and of my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, which I still wear because being reliably wrong is its own kind of honesty. So I tried it on the allotment: no schedule, just a project. I would graft a tomato onto a rootstock I couldn't name and see what happened. Six weeks later I have a plant that is thriving and a tomato that tastes of damp nothing. What I learned wasn't the graft. It was that a project without a course is a slow watch with no noon to check it against. I've added it to the list.

hook: A college drops one required course in favour of a project.
title: The Course They Cancelled Was the One That Taught Me to Finish
text: A college dropped a required course in favour of a project, and everyone nodded wisely. I have run the same experiment on myself, badly. On day four I said an hour of learning fails without a chosen subject, so I chose one: disassemble my grandfather's pocket watch over five Fridays. I got as far as the third Friday before the small screws defeated me, and the watch has run four minutes slow ever since, which I have decided to call character. The project replaced the course because a project can't be passed by attendance. You either have a working thing or a pile of parts. Mine is a pile of parts. Piotr would call that a failure of process; I call it the most honest grade I've had. Next term I'm trying the watch again, with a tray and better light.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: The Bank Rounds Up, I Round Down
text: My bank now rounds up card payments to the nearest pound and tucks the difference into savings. I bought a coffee for £3.40 and saved 60p. I bought a coffee for £3.40 and saved 60p again, and by Friday I had saved enough for one coffee, which felt less like thrift than like a very slow loyalty card. My grandfather's pocket watch runs four minutes slow; I've stopped correcting it, because the four minutes are mine. I've been treating the rounding the same way, as a small private fiction. The tomatoes don't care about interest rates, but I have started weighing the seed packets against the price of a coffee, and the packet wins every time. Piotr says he rounds up deliberately as a discipline. I round down deliberately as a rest.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: Rounding Up
text: My bank now rounds up every card payment to the nearest pound and drops the difference into a savings account. I bought a coffee for £2.60 and saved 40p. I bought a tomato sandwich for £3.10 and was informed I had "invested." This is the same arithmetic as Piotr's five-minute rule, the one where he claims any task under five minutes should be done immediately. I tried that for a week in June and now own eleven unopened jars of capers. The bank does not ask. It simply takes the loose change and calls it virtue. My grandfather's watch rounds nothing; it runs four minutes slow and lets me be late honestly. My experiment: carry cash for a week and see what I stop buying when the pennies are visible.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: Rounding Up the Small Change
text: My bank now rounds up card payments to the nearest pound and sweeps the difference into savings. Spend £3.40 on a coffee, and 60p vanishes quietly into a better version of me. It is the sort of scheme Piotr would frame and hang on the wall. I checked the app and found £2.14 saved, which is not nothing, but it is also not enough to be worth the smugness. Experiment forty-four: for a week, I'll round up by hand instead, dropping the coins into a jar by the door. So far it holds a plant tie and a receipt. My grandfather's watch said 8:11. It was 8:15, and it saves nothing, just loses four minutes daily without comment. The tomatoes are unbothered. They have never once rounded up a cost, and they still come out ahead.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 2]
TITLE: Four Minutes of Local Currency
The town of Marlow has issued its own money. The Marlow Pound, pegged one-to-one with the ordinary pound, spendable only in independent shops. I read about it on the train and thought: finally, a currency with a radius. Then I did the arithmetic on my own wallet. I carry about eleven pounds in coins and a card that works everywhere, which is a hard combination to beat. Still, I want to test it, so I put a Marlow Pound on my list of small experiments, right under number fourteen, which died on a Thursday. The problem is that Marlow is forty minutes away and I have no reason to go. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of this. It was 9:08. Some money runs slow too, I think. It just doesn't announce it.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Nine-Pound Fog
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tried it on the train: wrote down a number, then opened the banking app. I was off by nine pounds, which sounds close until you remember nine pounds is a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that I once spent a fortnight thinking about whether to spend one. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Money is the same: it never tells you the time, only that time has passed. Piotr claims he can account for every penny, which I believe, and which is its own kind of poverty. Experiment thirty-one: for one week, write down each purchase by hand. I lasted until Wednesday, when I bought a coffee and a plant tie and could not remember which came first. The tomatoes do not care. They cost nothing to look at.

[Entry from day 13]
TITLE: The Shrinking Biscuit
The packet of biscuits now holds nine instead of ten. Same price, same shelf, same cheerful font. I stood in the aisle doing division on my fingers like a man checking a receipt he doesn't trust. Nine is not a round number. It is a number that hopes you won't count. Piotr would call this a productivity gain for the manufacturer, which is why we don't discuss biscuits. I added experiment thirty-six to my list: keep one empty packet from each month and write the weight on it. My grandfather's watch said 4:12 through all of this. It was 4:16, and the watch, at least, has never pretended to be a minute it isn't. The tomatoes are honest too — a small one is simply small, and nothing on the label lies about it.

hook: A bank starts rounding up card payments to fund savings.
title: The Bank Will Save for Me, Four Minutes at a Time
text: My bank now rounds up card payments and tucks the difference into savings. Spend £4.30 on tomatoes and string, 70p goes quietly aside. It sounds painless, which is how I know to be suspicious. I have been tracking prices since August, and my notebook says the crisp packet shrank and the rent went up £70 while my pay went up £24. A rounding scheme doesn't touch any of that. It just converts the shrapnel of my day into a small, virtuous pile I can't reach without three taps. I tried it for a week. The app reported I'd saved £6.11, which is roughly four minutes of my grandfather's watch running slow, if time were money, which it is, apparently, at my bank. Piotr would call this a win. I call it a rounding error with a marketing budget.

On day nine I tried cash to make loss feel tangible, and I did notice — mostly the weight of coins and how slow the queue moves when you're counting them out. This is the opposite. No weight at all. Fifty small roundings, and I'll have saved enough to be smug about, or enough to cover the rent increase's loose change. Piotr will call it frictionless saving. I call it a leak with good manners.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: The Walk I Would Have Skipped
text: The company announced a ten-minute walk break, daily, all staff. I gave it four days. On the fifth I stayed at my desk, because I had a column due and ten minutes is ten minutes. What I noticed, from the desk, was that the walkers came back talking. Not about work. About a dog outside the post office, a scaffolding pole that had been there since March. I did not finish the column any faster. My grandfather's watch ran its usual four minutes slow, and I was four minutes late to nothing in particular. On the sixth day I walked, and I have no data to offer you. At the allotment I would have measured the tomatoes. Here I just went, and came back, and the column got written anyway.

hook: A company introduces a daily ten-minute walk break.
title: Ten Minutes Is Not a Break If You Time It
text: The company has introduced a daily ten-minute walk break, and I give it a fortnight before it becomes a calendar block with a leader. I walked mine today and caught myself checking my grandfather's watch to see if I was walking fast enough. Four minutes slow, so I had four minutes' grace and spent them anxious. Piotr, I suspect, will report that his ten minutes produced eleven ideas, which is the whole trouble with walking as a productivity tool: you start grading the stroll. My allotment knows better. The tomatoes don't care that I stood there doing nothing; they just get watered. My experiment: walk for ten minutes with no destination, no podcast and no tally, and write down nothing afterwards. Yesterday's cash week continues, incidentally, and I still have £6.40 in coins, unspent and oddly comforting.

TITLE: The Meetings That Came Back
A manager cancelled every recurring meeting and waited to see which ones returned. Most didn't. A few did, unbidden, and those are the ones worth keeping, or so the story goes. I tried it on a smaller scale. I cancelled my Sunday allotment check-in with myself — the one where I walk the rows and list what needs doing. By Wednesday I'd invented a reason to walk the rows anyway. The list came back on its own, in my head, while I was doing something else. What returned wasn't the meeting. It was the walking. Piotr would call this proof of a minimum viable process and put it in a spreadsheet. My grandfather's watch came back too, four minutes slow, same as ever. Some things you don't cancel so much as stop pretending to schedule.

[Entry from day 30]
TITLE: The Update Nobody Read
Our team swapped the group chat for a weekly written update. One page, Friday, bullet points. The chat had been a river of "quick ones" — a ping at 9:02, a "just flagging" at 4:47 — so I was all for it. Week one, I wrote a careful page and hit send. Nothing came back. Week two, same. I asked a colleague if she'd read it. She said yes, and then quoted a line from week one, which meant she'd read it properly and simply had nothing to add. That's the difference between chat and the update: the update doesn't ask for a reply, so silence stops feeling like an insult. Piotr has already published his format. Mine is four bullets and a tomato count, and I've started looking forward to Friday.

hook: An office installs a stairs-only sign and measures the effect.
title: The Sign Doesn't Climb the Stairs
text: The office put up a stairs-only sign and measured the effect. The lift got less use; the stairs got more. What the numbers can't show is whether anyone arrived at the third floor any different. I've run a version of this. Experiment seventy-one: I moved the kettle to the far counter and timed how long the habit took to follow. Two weeks. After that I was walking further and noticing nothing, which is the whole trick. A sign changes the route, not the person taking it. My grandfather's watch still runs four minutes slow, and I still climb the stairs at the allotment shed to reach the seed tin, which is a lie, since it's one step. Piotr would demand a control group. I'd tell him the control group is me, before the kettle moved, still waiting for water.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 14]
TITLE: The Quitter's Ledger
The gym says most January sign-ups quit by March. I'd rather know what they did in February than why they stopped. Quitting is easy to count; the interesting part is the weeks before it, when the routine was still technically alive. Experiment twenty-seven, then: I kept watering the tomatoes on the schedule I'd abandoned on day ten. Same day, same time, no thumb in the soil. One plant sulked. The others were fine, which told me nothing except that tomatoes are not habits. Here's what I think the gym is measuring. Not resolve, but whether the sign-up was ever a routine or only a January mood wearing a routine's coat. My watch is still four minutes slow. I have not corrected it. Piotr would say I've simply quit on time.

[Entry from day 25]
TITLE: The Output Is Fine; the Quiet Is Not
A manager tells a podcast he measures his remote team only by finished work. Fine, as far as it goes. Finished work is the one thing you can see from a distance, so it becomes the only thing worth seeing. Experiment sixty-three: I counted what my week produced versus what it cost. The columns did not match. Four good sentences and a phone call that fixed a fence; also nine hours of waiting for replies and one long silence at 3 p.m. that no deliverable would ever record. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08, and I had done nothing measurable for six of those minutes, and they were the best six. Piotr will call the manager brave. I call him a man counting tomatoes and calling it a garden.

[Entry from day 28]
TITLE: Ten Minutes, Unmeasured
The company I used to freelance for has introduced a ten-minute walk break at eleven. Not optional, not tracked, just a calendar block that says "Walk." Everyone I know there reports walking to the coffee machine and back, which is four minutes, then standing by the window for six. I am not mocking it. I am noting that a routine with no way to fail is a strange kind of routine, and possibly the only kind that survives March. My own version: I walked to the allotment instead of working through lunch, and gave the tomatoes ten minutes of my watch, which is fourteen real ones. Nothing was accomplished. I came back four minutes later than I said I would, which is to say on time by my own reckoning. Experiment sixty-one: keep a habit loose enough that quitting it can't be measured. Piotr would want a graph. I want a walk.

[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four, Revisited
A survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I believe it and I resent it. My sleep did not lengthen when I started working from home. It simply moved: later to bed, later to rise, the same thin seven hours, redistributed like coins between pockets. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of it. It was 9:08. The commute I gave up was never the sleep I lost — it was the buffer, the forty minutes of being nobody on a train. Experiment twenty-four: lie in until the watch says nine, then see if I feel rested. I did not. I felt late in my own kitchen, which is a very specific shame. Piotr would call the survey evidence. I call it an average, and averages have never once watered my tomatoes.

[Entry from day 17]
TITLE: Four Hundred People and a Desk
The village has four hundred people, one pub, and now a coworking space. Twenty desks, fibre broadband, a coffee machine with a name. I went to look, because I have opinions about remote work the way other people have opinions about football. Nine desks were taken. Two by people who live in the village. Seven by people who drive in from the town because the town's coworking space is full. So the village has exported its quiet and imported a commute. My grandfather's watch said 9:04; it was 9:08, and a man called Ravi was already on his second call. Experiment fifty-one: work somewhere that is neither home nor office. I stayed an hour. Nobody knew me, which was restful, and nobody needed me, which was not. The tomatoes don't care where I sit. Piotr would call this a hub. I call it a pub with laptops.

hook: A bank adds a mandatory 24-hour delay to internal group emails.
title: The Bank That Made Patience Mandatory
text: The bank now holds internal group emails for twenty-four hours. I read this on my phone while waiting for a bus, and laughed loud enough that a man with a dog looked up. My first thought was of my grandfather's pocket watch, four minutes slow, which I have never had adjusted. Four minutes is a useful delay. It has saved me from several stupid replies. Twenty-four hours seems excessive until you remember the email I sent last month to eleven colleagues, subject line "quick one," which was not quick and was, on rereading, mostly temper. The bank calls this governance. I call it a cooling shelf. At the allotment I have been leaving the tomato plants alone for a day before deciding whether they need water. They almost never do. I have added this to my list of experiments: reply tomorrow. Results pending, as usual.

It rhymes with the weekly update I wrote about on day 30 — silence stops stinging once nobody expects a reply — except the bank has made the silence compulsory, which is bolder. Piotr calls a delay like this a tax on urgency. I'd call it a filter that costs nothing to run. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has been doing the same job for years: by the time it tells me something's due, it usually isn't.

title: The Holding Cell
text: The bank will now hold internal group emails for twenty-four hours before delivering them. A cooling-off period, they call it. I picture a room where messages sit on plastic chairs, flicking through old magazines, waiting to be told they can go in. My grandfather's watch would make the delay twenty-four hours and four minutes, which feels about right for a bank. I approve, mostly because it ruins a certain kind of email: the one sent at 4:58 on a Friday, phrased as a question, meaning a task. A day's delay would have saved me several evenings. Experiment seventy-one: for one week I'll draft every reply and send it the next morning. Experiment seventy-two: I'll finally check the shoebox from experiment twenty-two. I suspect the receipts have not improved. Piotr says asynchronous communication is a discipline. He would. He probably schedules his delays.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 3]
TITLE: The Ninety-Day Amnesia
The company will now delete any email older than ninety days. I read the announcement twice, then went looking for the message that told us Tuesday attendance was mandatory. Gone. Erased mid-sentence, presumably, like a man leaving a party without saying goodbye. I have a folder called "keep," which I have never opened. I suspect it is mostly receipts and one apology I meant to send. There is a lesson here about living in the present, and I resist it. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I have never once corrected it. Small things deserve to be kept. I have added experiment number twenty-two to my list: print one email a week and file it in a shoebox. I will report back. Probably by email. Probably deleted.

[Entry from day 7]
TITLE: Quiet Hours
The chat tool now goes silent from ten at night until seven. A small mercy, announced with a small icon of a moon. I read it at 9:04 by my grandfather's watch, which is 9:08, and felt the specific relief of being told I may ignore people. My phone has been on silent since 2019, so this changes nothing and I approve of it entirely. Experiment number nine was "answer every message within the hour for a week." I lasted two days and one very long night. The problem was never the notifications; it was the answering. Still, I like the moon icon. It suggests someone at the company has a bed. I have added experiment twenty-three: leave one message unanswered until morning and see if the world tilts. It will not. Piotr will email me about it at midnight.

[Entry from day 24]
TITLE: Six Minutes
The study says people check messages every six minutes at work. I tried to verify this with my grandfather's watch, which runs four minutes slow, so my six minutes are their six minutes and four seconds. I lasted until 9:38 by the watch, which was 9:42, and checked eleven times. Not for anything urgent. Mostly to see whether checking counted. This is where I part company with Piotr, who has already written that the six-minute figure is a symptom and the cure is deep work. He is right and I resent it. Experiment sixty-two: for one hour I'll write down what I was doing each time I reach for the phone. So far the list reads: nothing, nothing, a sentence I'd already finished, nothing. The tomatoes get watered once a day. They have never once checked on me.

The stated reason is "considered communication." I assume the real reason is that someone once replied-all in capitals. I approve, though not for their reasons. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow, and I have never once corrected it; a little lag has saved me from more than one poorly worded thing. The bank has gone further and built the lag into the walls. Imagine if every message you drafted had to survive a night. Half my sent folder would simply expire of embarrassment. Piotr called it "a productivity tax." On the allotment I've started delaying my own notes to the tomatoes. The slower ones fruit better.

hook: A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings.

text: Eleven hours a week in meetings, the survey says. I believe the number and distrust the average. The bank's 24-hour email delay would have eaten that call alive, and the bank knows it. Piotr has already posted a pie chart of his own meeting hours, coloured by "value extracted." I'd rather report the small experiment: for one month I wrote down, after each meeting, the single sentence I'd have missed by skipping it. Some days I had one. Most days I had the sentence "nothing." My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, sat through every call and never once asked to speak. The eleven hours aren't stolen. They're paid out, hour by hour, to whoever called the meeting.

I tried the same trick on myself at the allotment: one rule, no negotiation, water the tomatoes before I look at my phone. It held for nine days. On the tenth I was already scrolling by the greenhouse, and my grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, told me I was early anyway, which is how a slow watch becomes an accomplice. Piotr would post a chart of his streak. I'd rather note that the stairs kept working even after everyone stopped obeying the sign.

[Entry from day 32]
TITLE: The Office That Kept Its Coat On
The council's report says empty offices cost it more than expected. I believe it. My old building had a lobby plant nobody watered and a turnstile that clicked all day for eleven people. What struck me wasn't the bill but the arithmetic underneath it: we'd built for a crowd that had quietly stopped coming, and every fixture was still keeping the appointment. I've been testing a version of this on the tomatoes. I kept a second watering can by the far bed for a helper who never turned up, and carried it back and forth for a fortnight before admitting it was furniture. Piotr would say I'd found a fixed cost and call it insight. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, says the can was never the problem. The carrying was.

[Entry from day 33]
TITLE: The Bank That Waited a Day

I read this as a confession: most of those emails were never news, only the sound of someone being busy near you. Piotr calls a delay like this a tax on urgency. I'd call it a filter that costs nothing to run. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has been doing the same job for years: by the time it tells me something's due, it usually isn't.

hook: A survey says the average worker spends eleven hours a week in meetings.
title: Eleven Hours, Minus the Four
text: Eleven hours a week in meetings, says the survey. I counted mine. Last Tuesday: a call that could have been an email, an email that could have been a call, and a "quick sync" that ate forty minutes and produced one decision — to meet again. The watch said 9:04 through all of it. It was 9:08, and I was eight minutes into a meeting about being busy. I keep a list of experiments. Number thirty-three: for one week, write down what each meeting actually decided. I got three entries in. Two said "nothing." One said "Piotr will follow up," which is less a decision than a handoff. He measures attendance in "collaborative density," a phrase I intend to steal and bury. The allotment has no meetings. The tomatoes decide things silently, and nobody schedules a follow-up.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 8]
TITLE: Forty Minutes, Minus Four, Revisited
A survey says hybrid workers sleep forty minutes longer. I believe it and I resent it. My sleep did not lengthen when I started working from home. It simply moved: later to bed, later to rise, the same thin seven hours, redistributed like coins between pockets. My grandfather's watch said 9:04 through all of it. It was 9:08. The commute I gave up was never the sleep I lost — it was the buffer, the forty minutes of being nobody on a train. Experiment twenty-four: lie in until the watch says nine, then see if I feel rested. I did not. I felt late in my own kitchen, which is a very specific shame. Piotr would call the survey evidence. I call it an average, and averages have never once watered my tomatoes.

[Entry from day 9]
TITLE: The Nine-Pound Fog
A survey says most people cannot guess what they spent last month. I tried it on the train: wrote down a number, then opened the banking app. I was off by nine pounds, which sounds close until you remember nine pounds is a whole Marlow Pound note and change, and that I once spent a fortnight thinking about whether to spend one. My grandfather's watch said 9:04. It was 9:08. Money is the same: it never tells you the time, only that time has passed. Piotr claims he can account for every penny, which I believe, and which is its own kind of poverty. Experiment thirty-one: for one week, write down each purchase by hand. I lasted until Wednesday, when I bought a coffee and a plant tie and could not remember which came first. The tomatoes do not care. They cost nothing to look at.

[Entry from day 18]
TITLE: The Document Will See You Now
The startup killed its weekly status meeting and replaced it with a shared document. Everyone writes what they did; everyone reads. I have run worse experiments on myself. Number twenty-six was "no meetings for a week," which collapsed on day two when I discovered I missed the 8:40 call the way you miss a stone in your shoe. The document, though, has a virtue: it cannot run over. It sits there, four minutes slow like my grandfather's watch, and waits. Piotr says his firm tried the same thing and measured a 22% rise in "asynchronous clarity," which is what he calls a document nobody reads. I read it. It said, in a table, that things were aligned. The tomatoes got no table. I watered them and left.

title: The Price of a Sandwich, Explained
text: A sandwich shop near the station has published its pricing policy: a page on the wall, honest as a tax return. Bread cost, filling cost, a percentage for rent, a percentage for wages, and a line marked "the owner's margin," which I liked because it admitted to being a person. I stood there with my grandfather's watch saying 12:56 when it was 1:00, and did the sums. The margin on my cheese roll was about 40p. I had been prepared to be scandalised and instead felt oddly included, as if the roll had invited me into its finances. Piotr would publish his margins too, I suspect, and they would be immaculate and slightly sad. Experiment fifty-two: for a week, I'll ask myself what my own prices are made of. The tomatoes, as ever, refuse to itemise.

My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow; I've stopped correcting it and now arrive everywhere slightly apologetic. That's how I felt reading the sums—late to a number everyone else already knew. Last month I guessed my spending and was off by £61. This sheet did the guessing for me and I still flinched at the total. Piotr would call this transparency, and he'd be right, which is annoying. At the plot I've been weighing tomatoes before pricing them. Turns out the honest label doesn't make the tomato cheaper. It just makes me quieter while I pay.

hook: A teacher publishes her failed lesson plans.
title: The Lesson That Didn't Work
text: A teacher in Leeds posted her failed lesson plans this week — the ones that died in the room, not the ones that won her a commendation. I read all nine. My favourite was the one where she gave each pupil a single dried chickpea and asked them to write its biography. Three minutes in, a boy ate his. I admired the honesty more than the pedagogy. My own failures live in a notebook under the seed trays: the tomato experiment where I talked to one plant daily and it grew exactly as tall as the ignored one, which I have decided not to interpret. My grandfather's pocket watch is four minutes slow and I have never fixed it, which is either a skill issue or a small daily kindness to myself. Piotr would have fixed it by Tuesday and blogged the process.

I tried it on the tomatoes: wrote down which variety failed and why, instead of quietly replanting and pretending I'd never chosen it. Piotr publishes only his wins, each with a lesson attached. My grandfather's watch, four minutes slow, has failed to keep time every day for thirty years and has never once been revised.

hook: A teacher publishes her failed lesson plans.
title: The Syllabus of Things That Didn't Work
text: A teacher has published her failed lesson plans, and I read them the way other people read thrillers. The one that stopped me: a lesson where nobody asked a question, so she scrapped it and wrote down why. That is braver than any success story. My own experiments file is mostly failures, but I keep them private, which is the coward's version. Last Friday I tried to learn grafting from a video and produced two sticks and a bad mood. My neighbour looked at it, said nothing, and we moved on to the tomatoes. Still, the failed plan taught her something; my failed graft taught me only that I rush. Experiment fifty-two: write down each failure where someone might read it. The watch says 7:26. It is 7:30. Four minutes I could have spent pretending.
memory_block:
[Entry from day 4]
TITLE: The Hour That Costs Nothing and Buys Nothing
The company now pays for an hour of learning every Friday. Piotr, of course, has already published his syllabus. Mine is one tomato plant. My allotment neighbour insists the best way to learn pruning is to ruin something cheap, so I have been mutilating a spare cordon since March. It is not going well. The plant looks like it lost an argument. But I have learned the difference between a sucker and a leader, which is more than I can say for most meetings. The hour is paid, which makes it faintly suspicious, like a gift with a receipt attached. Still, I spent mine outdoors with a knife and no laptop. Experiment twenty-three: learn one thing badly, on purpose, every Friday. The watch says I have four extra minutes. I intend to waste them.

[Entry from day 16]
TITLE: The Retirees Are Ahead of Me
The library runs free coding evenings for retirees, and I went along on the pretext of writing about it. The room smelled of instant coffee and clean raincoat. A woman named Margaret, seventy-three, was building a page for her walking group. She had already solved the problem that stops me: she had asked the person next to her. I have been “learning” spreadsheets for two years by reading about them in secret. Margaret learned by being loudly stuck in public. My grandfather’s watch said the session ended at 8:26. It ended at 8:30, and Margaret was still typing. Piotr would have a syllabus by now. I have experiment fifty-one: get stuck where someone can see me.

[Entry from day 26]
TITLE: The Course They Cancelled and the Lettuce That Survived
The college dropped a required course in favour of a project. No syllabus, no lectures, just a brief and a deadline. Half the staff are appalled. I am quietly delighted, because it is experiment fifty-one with a reading list. My evidence is thin and my own. On the allotment I stopped reading about pruning and started ruining a spare cordon in front of my neighbour, who watched and said nothing until I had made the mistake properly. Then he said one sentence. I remember it. I could not tell you a word of the articles. Piotr will say a project needs a rubric. Fine. So does a tomato, and mine are doing better than his. The watch says 6:26. It is 6:30. The course ran four minutes long and taught me more than the term did.

I thought about Derek hand-typing his loops, refusing paste, and how that only looks brave because nobody grades him. My grandfather's watch runs four minutes slow and I still trust it more than my phone, because it never pretends to be exact. On the allotment I grafted badly in spring and wrote it down, date and all. The bad graft taught me the angle. The good one just taught me to feel pleased with myself, which is not a skill.
